A LOATHLY TILE. Little chickens, one, two, three, They went oat to take their tea, Brisk and gay as gay could be, Caekle, mackle, mackle. . Feathers brushed all smooth and neat, Yellow stockings on their feet, Tails and tuftings all complete, Cackle, mackle, mackle. "Very seldom," said the three, " of as the weld can see, Beautiful exceediuglee, Cackle, Mal:kite, mackle. Such our form and such our face, Such oar Cochin-Ch,na grace, We must win in beauty's race, Cackle, mackle, mackle." Met an elephant huge and wise, Looked at them with both his eyes, Caused these chickens great surprise, Cackle, mackle, mackle. "Why," said they, "do you suppose Elephant doesn't look out of his nose? So very conveniently it grows, Cackle, mackle, mackle, "Elephant with nose so long, Sing us now a lovely song, As we gaily trip along, CaelKle, mackle, mackle Slug of us and sing of you, Sing- of corn and barley too, Be viteous beast with eyes of blue, Cackle, mackle, mackle !" Elephant sang so loud and sweet, Chickens fell before his feet, For his love they did entreat, Cackle, mackle, mackle! "W 11-a-day, and woe is me! Would we ;tII could elephants be! Then you'd marry us, one, two, three, Cackle, mackle, mackle!" Elephant next began to dance. Capered about with a stately prance (Learned from his grandmother over in France), Cackle, mackle, mackle! Fast and faster 'gan to tread, Trod on every chicken's head, Killed them all uncommonly dead, Cackle, mackle, mackle! MORAL. Little chickens, one, two, three, When you're walking out to tea, Don't make love to all you see, Cackle, mackle, mackle Elephants have lovely eyes, But to woo them is not wise, For they are not quite your size, Cackle, mackle, mackle!

The Western merchant who sold a great many goods to replace things destroyed by the cyclone, called it a trade wind. A well-known litterateur andhumorist modestly says that his chief literary acquirements are the books he has bor- rowed and never returned. WILBERFORCE'S 0 %K. t Holwood, five miles south of Bromley, stands a Yeller tble oak, conspicuous for its gnarled and projecting root,on which two men sat one day, earnestly conversing about on of the most iniquitous systems that over cursed the human race. It was there and then that William Wilberforce, urged by Will Pitt, determined to lead theitiovetn.ent for the aliolition of the slave trade. In his diary he says, "1 well remember, after a conversation with Mr. Pitt in the open air, at the root of an old tree at Holwood, just above the steep descent into the vale of Kes- ton, I resolved to give notice on a fitting occasion, in the House of Commons, of my intention to bring forward the abolition of the slave trade." The tree is still known by the name of " Wilberforce's Oak." To this interview it is owing that on May 12th, 1789, Wilberforce brought the question before the House of Commons, " in a manner," to use the words of Burke," the most masterly, impressive, and eloquent ;" and so headed an enterprise which issued in the complete destruction of slavery in all parts •of the British dominkins.:—The Quiver. Time Potrricara.v Awtawn.—There is a better story on record than that told in the House of Lords the other even- ing, when itrwas said that a priest illustrated his views of the decision of the sob-commissioners under the Land Act by preaching a sermon from the text, "And the rent is made Worse." • Almost exactly a Century ago, the borough of Bed- ford was disturbed by a hotly-contested election. The popu- lar party- sVaa represented by the philanthropist, John Howard, of pardington, and his relative, Mr. Whitbread. On the other hand, the Corporation was suspected of having sold the representation to a couple of strangers—Sir William Wake, Bart„ and Mr. Robert Sparrow. The feeling against these Purchasers of the electors honour was so high thaton a Sunday when the election fever was hottest a clergyman of the Established Church took as his text—" Are not two sparrows-old /or one farthing? Fear ye not, therefore, ye are of more 'value than many sparrows." The result, never- theless,_of the poll was that Wake and Sparrow were re- turnedaorrall Mall Gazette. A RussuanAN MAY QITEEN.—At the suggestion of Mr. Ruskin, who takes great interest in the National Society's Training College at Whitelands, in Westmorland, the old festival of May-day has been observed during the last two or three years at this college by the selection from the junior students of a "May Queen." The queen is elected by the votes of the whole body of students, and according to hirAluside's directions, " she may be the cleverest and the prettiest, but she must be the likeablest and the love- ablest." The ceremony begins with service in the college chapel, which is beautifully adorned with flowers and ferns. After the service Is over the governesses and students meet in the lectaire room, where the principal having given per- mission, and each student being provided with a slip of paper, the election of the queen takes place. Each girl writes on her paper the name of the student she would choose, acid all voting papers having been handed to the head governess they are scrutinised, and she who obtains the Largest number of votes is proclaimed Queen. This year the selection fell on Miss Edith Martindale, formerly of Staveley National School. After election the Queen names her maidstof honour, and she and they are robed in white dresses, the Queen wearing a crown of moss and flowers, and having a sceptre tipped with flowers. She is placed upon the throne receives the homage of her subjects,' is presented in Mr. Rus,kin's name with a jewel of gold, and for a short time holds her mimic court. The festivities close with the singing of the National Anthem, after which the Queen makes a gracious proclamation of a holiday till seven in the evening. ScAornreAmiN Basios.—The peasants like grand names for their little ones, much as Adolph, Adricin, Gotfried, Gustavus, for boys • artd Josephine, Thera, Ingeborg, for girls; and if they ta'ave no name prepared, they seek one in the almanac for the particular day of baby's birth. It is baptised the next Sunday, and taken to church by the gal- mother, who provides the christening-garments, which are often trimmed with coloured bows; whilst the infant has beads round its neck, and wears a cap with very little border. The Clergyman holds it well over the font, and pours water over the back of the head three times, then wipes with a towel. As the baby is swathed in six-inch- wide bandages, so that it cannot move its legs, and some- tirnea not even its arms, it is obliged to lie very passive during this ceremonial. The peasants have their reasons for this swathing, the first of which is that they think it makes thelimbe grow straight; the second that it turns baby into a compact bundle to carry. When swathed thus, infants have been said to resemble the tail of a lobster, or even its whole body. In the north they are often hung from a long, springy pole stuck in the wall, to be out of the 9.y; and, being by nature quiet, they are supposed not to mind it. Their cradles, which are very primitive, are also frequently suspended by a spiral spring from the roof, which innst be mote comfortable than the pole. Both in Swedish and Norwegian Lapland people take these "swaddlings" to church. But instead of carrying them into church they make a hole in the snow outside in the churchyard, and bury them in it, leaving a small aperture for breathing pur- poses. The babies are kept !splendidly warm, while their friends within the sacred building have their beards frozen to their fur coats by the freezing of their own breaths. As soon as a peasant boy can walk, he is put Into trousers, but- toned outside his jacket; and these are so baggy behind that it is often amusing to see him. This baggmem is fre. gamey due to the fact that the trousers originally be. longed to his father, but were cut off at the legs, and simply drawn round the boy's waist, without reducing their size. Add to this, that the feet are shod either with little jack- boots or wooden shoes, and we have a strange picture. Their stockings have either leather heels or no heals at all, so that the mother is spared the trouble of mending them. Neither has she much labour with their heads, the hair of which is cropped as close as a convict's. The girls, also, wear wooden shoes; but they have gingham kerchiefs or caps on their heads, frocks down to their heels, and quaint pinafores Folks Magazine. It is possible that the matter may be brought before the next meeting of the British Association, and lead to the appointment of a*Conunittee for a systematic investigation of the waters on the coast of the island. The Athenseunt says that Mr. Beck, the compiler of "The Drapers' Dictionary," is printing a work entitled "Gloves, their Annals and Associations." The book deals with gloves in the church, gloves on the throne, gloves on the bench, hawking gloves, gauntlets, perfumed glovee, chicken abyss, companies of glovers, &c.; also with gloves as pledges, gloves as gages. gloves as gifts, and gloves as favour. It appears to be at last decided that the electric light is to be used for the illumination of the Grand Opera at Paris. About 1,800 Edison lamps will be employed, but the motive •nachinery will not be placed on the premises. It is proposed to erect the works somewhere in the 9th arrondissement, and to eneelv from the sense source the distric-t seirround- ing the opera house and the 800 lamps required by the Opera Comique. In a communication to the Physical Society,'Mr.W. Lent Carpenter recently criticised the present arrangements for science teaching in Board Schools, and peinted out the marked advantages of the system folloe-ed in Birminghain and Liverpool, where skilled lecturers are appointed to go from school to school, and provided with an assistant demo istrator and proper apparatus. Mr. Carpenter advo- cated the extsnsian of this system to the country in general. Franz Liszt.has given 2,490 gulden to the Coneervatorium of Vienna to found an annual scholarship of 100 gulden for the beet pianoforte player. The aged Abbe,who is-to spend the summer in Weimar, was present on the let of this month at a performance of his " Heil ige 'Elisabeth" in Marburg to celebrate the 600th anniversary of the comple- tion of the church of Saint Elisabeth. The new Conserve- corium of Music at Frankfort on the MAine, founded and named in honour of the composer itaff, who was head of the Hoch Conservatorium there at the time of his death, has now been opened, and begins with the names of more than onchundred students on the register, A SCIENTIFIC Veereasees.—About a year ago I succeeded, with some difficulty, in obtaining a copy of an old classical treatise, Chevreul's " Recherches Chimiques stir le Corps Gras d'Orizine animate," a series of pspers published in a collected form in 1823,-and I aSeumed, as a matter of ceurse, that the author had bag since joined his contemporaries, Cavendish, Priestley, Lavoisier, Woollaston, Davy, Dalton, Berzelius, &c. This is by no means the case, for enly the other day he read a paper at the Academy of Sciences, in the coarse of which he said : "Moreover, gentlemen, the observation is not a new one to me. I had the honour to mention it here, at a meeting of the. Academy, on the 10th May, 1812." Here is a chemist who was born before phlo- giston was dead and buried, when the composition of air and water was newly discovered, and who is therefore just as old as modern chemistry, and is now vigorous enough in body and brain to still contribute to its advancement. May his venerable voice long continue to be heard from his old, old place in the Academy !—Geatleinan's .lbegazide. Eeecrrac Ftsntese.—When July has ended, and the dark- ness of night conies over the lakes and fjords, the sturdy Scnnd'nevian bonder patches and caulks his rough home- made boat. and fixee opise bow an eyeeharegleg fie; grate prepare ory to tne.prolitie sport of fish-Veering ley night. The fire, made of resinous pine knots and beech bark, is lighted on the grate, which is placed as near to the surface of the water as possible. The fish swim towards the light, are speared and captured easily. A trial has been made in France, by "Government permission," of a great improve- ment upon this. An electric light, enclosed, like Swan's, Edison's, &c., in a small glass globe, is sunk in the water, and the fish come to it with very commendable docility (from the fisherman's point of view). Other boats then sur- round them with the nets, and the fete concludes fatally for the guests. The account I read states that this method of capture is so deadly that " there seems to be much doubt whether it will ever be allowed as a recognised kind of fish- ing within territorial waters." This appears to me a very odd mode of looking upon the question, much about the , same as doubting whether an improvement in the mode of winning coal from the seam too easily, or extracting gold from quartz reefs with superlative facility, should be per- , mitted. If it prove to be practically as effectual as imagined, it might be made a means of preserving and en- riching the fisheries, for with such advantage on the side of the fisherman, tlee.Government might introduce most desir- able restrictions, as regards the meshes of the nets and the sale of fish, whereby the wasteful destruction of young half-grown fish should be prevented. THE DIVINING ROD AT AVON-I'M-TM—A not unnatural desire has for some time existed to discover the-presence of water springs at Avonmouth, and that -desire has been quiekened by a recent report that an American company of sugar refiners had intimated their readiness to establish , works at that place, provided that the requisite supply of fresh water could be ensured irrespective of the Bristol Waterworks Company. In these circumstances Mr. W. S. , Lawrence, who has long enjoyed a reputation for his power to detect the sites of hidden springs, and who is said to have detected their presence in many altogether unlooked- for places, was retained to go over the ground. He was accompanied during his investigation by Mr. E. Prudhoe, the mechanical engineer who superintends the machinery of the Avonmouth Dock. We append a copy of the letter con- taining the report of that official to the dock-master, Capt. Pomeroy :—" When Mr. Lawrence came down to try to find water I went with him. He had a piece of fine spring steel about 12 inches long, inch wide, and about 1-30 inch thick. He held the ends in his hands, and bent the steel in the form of a horse-shoe, and, placing his elbows close to his side, began to walk slowly about the field. He told me to take particular notice sof his hands, and see that he did not move any of the muscles or cause the spring to move mechanically. I was very sceptical as to there being any virtue in the steel, so I watched him very closely. We ' walked for some distance, the steel remaining perfectly until we came to the place where the bore-hole is now,, when the steel became violently agitated, and twisted itself ' into rings with such violence that it cut his finger. He then said if we bored at that spot we would find water, and a good quantity. We have since bored through-about 107 feet of strata as per sketch. We got no water until we were dewn 70 feet. When we touched the spring it at once rose to within 17 feet of the surface, and has remained at that level, never sinking any lower. We kept on boring, down to 107 feet, when we stopped and began pumping. I The bore-hole is 21 inches in diameter, and we put a 2-inch suction-pipe down 24 feet into the hole, and after 8A- hours' pumping with a double-action pump, throwing 1,00-0 galls. per hour, we drew the suction-pipe, and found the water I still.standing at 17 feet from surface, showing that there is a good supply. While pumping the pump never gave the slightest indication of sucking." The spring is still yield- ing 1,000 gallons of fresh water per hour.—Land.

GLADSTONE'S EXAMINATION FOR HIS DEOREE.—V'e come to the Michaelmas term of 1831, when Gladstone was going to pass the examination for his degree. Moderations were not instituted until 1852 ; so that under the old system an undergraduate's scholarship was never subjected to any pre- liminary tests, save at the terminal collections or college examinations. But these were insignificant, because if a man did badly in them he incurred nothing more than a mild reproof from his tutor. The consequence of all this was that men were generally seized with a panic in the last term before their examination. This may be the ease still to a certain extent, because so much of a man's prosperity in life may depend on his University honours, that the dread of failure is enough to unstring ordinary nerves. But in Mr. Gladstone's time the terrors of examination came from the feeling that success or the reverse would be a matter ef chance. The best scholars could not command success ; they could only deserve it. They went up as men for a race imperfectly trained, having had no means of accurately ascertaining what were their strong or weak points. They knew more than enough of some things and not sufficient of others. Then first-class honours were very sparingly bestowed—the average number of first-class men being about seven, reckoning the statistics of a dozen ex- aminations together. In the classical schools men had to take up Aristotle's "Moral Philosphy," Eferodotae, Thucy- d ides, Xenophon, Livy, Tacitus, Virgil, Horace, and Juvenal. There was never much doubt that Gladstone would take his first-clam in classics. He himself felt pretty confident about it; and he succeeded easily though only five were placed in the first-class that term. One of his examiners was Mr. R. D. Hampden, afterwards Bishop of Hereford, and one of his colleagues in Ow first-class was Henry Denison, of Christ Church, wko became 8i5.1'..9p of Salisbury. Denison, like Gladstone, took a first-class in IruithVmatic.s also. This last honour was a most important addition to t 6 ether; it had been earnestly coveted, aad yet almost despaired of. Cilad- stone had been obliged to study optics, hydrostatics, spher- ical trigonometry, something of astronomy, and it is a wonder hew he managed to do it all, even by working so regularly as he did. It must be remembered that two ex- aminations in classics and mathematics had to be passed in the same term. For all this the taking of a double first was not a very rare achievement, seeing that it had been per- formed more than 20 times since 1807, when class lists in the two schools were first issued. The name which heads the list of double first class men is that of Sir Robert Peel. It was perhaps because so many others had succeeded that Gladstone felt nervous lest he should not be able to do like them. From this extract it appears that Professor Custance has a considerable edu- cational work in front of him, and the colonist a great deal to learn. An Agricultural College is on the tapis in the colony, and great things are expected to come of it. It is to be established on the lines of similar institutions which exist in the United States and Canada, so far as we can dis- cern the plan. There will be two departments—department A, for practical students, and department B, for science students; and there will be also out-students, who, not re- siding in the college, will attend courses of lectures. The first-named--that is, the practical students—" will be re- quired to work regularly on the farm," though a portion of each day will be devoted to instruction in the college. The project is an important step in the right direction, and should result in considerable benefits to the colony, for, as the Adelaide Observer remarks "the example of half a dozen students who can leave the college and give ocular proof of the advantages which follow from a systematic culture of the soil, based upon the methods of science, would do more good in convincing the agricultural com- munity generally of the superiority of scientific over slovenly farming, than scores of reports from a learned pro- fessor."—Land.

"Thank heaven!" exclaimed a faded actress as she turned from her looking-glass, "my shop-window picture can never grow old." The meanest slight a girl can put upon an admirer is to use a post-card in refusing an offer of marriage. It proves that she dosen't care a halfpenny for him. There are two reasons why some people won't follow the advice of "mind your own business." First, they haven't any business; and second, no mind to bring to it. Just before the commencement of evening service at Breightmet Church, near Bolton, on Sunday, a married woman named Martha Yates, who was present with her family, became suddenly ill. She was removed to the porch, where she immediately expired. A tradesman lately sent out his accounts, one of which was returned marked on the postal cover—" Dead." Not lhaving written it off in his books, the account was again sent out, and was again returned, marked this time—" Still I dead." An imaginative Irishman gave utterance to this lamenta- tion, "I returned to the hall of nay fathers by night, and I found them in ruins. I cried aloud, 'My fathers, where are they?' and echo responded, 'ls it you, Patrick M'Glathery !' " A polite little girl was shown a set of playthings and a doll, and was asked which she would have. She looked at the doll 4 which was a fine one, and then, drawing her mother's head down, whispered, "1 would rather have the playthings, but please don't tell the doll." The famous Bishop Burnet, like many authors of later days, was veryipartial to tobacco, and always tmoked while he was writing. In order to combine the two operations with due comfort to himself, he would bore a hole through the broad brim of his large hat, and putting his long pipe through it, puffed and wrote, and wrote and puffed, with philosophical calmness. Professor Porson being once at a dinner party where the conversation turned upon Captain Cook and his celebrated voyages round the world, an ignorant person, in order to contribute his mite towards the social intercourse, asked him, "Pray, was Cook killed on his first voyage ?" "I be- lieve he was," repied Porson, "though he did not mind it much, but immediately entered upon the second." A story is told of a distinguished Prelate of the Church of England, who, on first accepting a country benefice in the gift of his college, urged a friend to pay him a visit as soon as he got into residence, and added, is perfect good faith, "I have a nice little green field attached to the rec- tory. I mean to keep a couple of sheep, and we shall have mutton kidneys fresh every morning for breakfast." THE BURDEN OF A BIG Foterrrss.—One requires educa- tion for a big fortune. Sit down, brother of mine, whose income tax remains small, whatever rate Mr. Gladstone may impose, and consider what you would do if you were to be- come the possessor, say, of twenty thousand pounds a year. You cannot eat more than you do now; you might drink more, but it would not be good for you; you do not want to dress yourself any finer; you do not wish to dazzle your friends with the splendour of your wife's dresses; you would not desire to give entertainments; you do not want to keep a troop of hulking servants. What would you do, in short, with so great an income ?—Good Words. THE OLDEST TREE IN Tull Wosztaa.—The oldest tree on earth, so far as any one knows, is the "Bo" tree in the sacred city of Amarapoora, Burnish. It was planted in 288 n.c., and is accordingly 2,171 years old. Its great age is proved by historic documents. according to Sir James Emerson Tennett, who says :—" To it kings have even dedi- cated their dominions, in testimony of belief that it is a branch of the identical fig tree under Which Buddha reclined at Urumelya when he underwent his apotheosis." Its Ivaves are carried away as streamers by pilgrims, but it is too sacred to touch with a knife, and therefore they are only gathered when they fall. THE PRINCESS LOCISE AND TEE " OLE Mme."—The American journals relate an interesting incident in connec- tion with the sojourn of the Princess Louise in Bermuda. On the day before the reception tendered her at St. George's, Bermuda, the Princess Louise went for a solitary stroll along the shore; and after a time, becoming thirsty, she stopped for a drink at the cottage of a negro fisherman. No one was there but "auntie," and she was as busy as could be ironing a shirt for the "Ole man" to wear at the recep- tion. The Princess asked for a drink. " I'se no time to bodder getting water fo' you," was the reply, "I'se fea'ful busy, for I'ae bound to see the Queen's chile to-roorrow." But if you'll get me a drink, I'll iron while you do so," said the thirsty Princess. The offer was accepted, the Princess r finished the shirt, and got her drink, and then revealed her identity. When the old negress recovered from her surprise she declared that neither her " ole man" nor any one else should wear that shirt again. THROAT IRRITATION AND COTTON. _ A CURIOUS NEGRO CUSTOII.—A custom almost universal among the African tribes is to rub their naked bodies over with grease until they shine. This fashion prevails both in the interior and on the coast, and is probably due to the grease acting both as a protection against the sun's rays and against cold, for naked men have all the world over wqrmed in their pnoverbial philosophy that "dirt and grease are the poor man's clothing." They are not at all particu- lar as to the grease used; rancid butter is not uncommonly used, and if not rancid it soon becomes so when transformed to the Negro skin. Hence the varied but ever detestable odours which greet the uneducated nose of the traveller as he plods his weary way across the African continent. They will tear the tallow out of an animal killed in order to use the grease for this purpose, and an admirable story—whe- ther strictly true or not it is hardly worth inquiring too closely—is told of a native, whose desire to possess a shin- ing skin overruled any little honesty he might have been possessed of, stealing a pot of varnish under the idea that it was oil, and dressing his sable skin with it. The result was not entirely satisfactory. The thief, resplendent in his odoriferous coat of varnish, landed while a cloud of wind was blowing. The consequence was that in a short space of time he VMS the observed of all observers, his body looking as if enveloped in a tight-fitting suit of sandpaper. He is understood for long to have had a prejudice against white men and all their crookedliways.—The Peoples of the rf orld.

_ I RELIGIOUS INFLI7ENCE AMONG THE TURCOMAN WOMEN. —I never trusted entirely to my character as a holy man, , who wrote amulets, and who bestowed blessings on the sick, except in the case of the female portion of society, who showed implicit faith in my doings, and who frequently sheltered me against the rudeness of their unbelieving hus- bands or brethren. Imagine, gentle reader, an isolated tent in some dreary portion of the desert, at whose door I arrive after a tiresome march of several hours in deep sand and under a scorching sun, without a drop of refreshing water, and without an animating breeze. My salutation, " Es- eelam Aleikum " i.e., "Peace be over thee," resounds far in the distance, and makes the grazing ca tie raise their heads, as if bewildered at the unaccustomed voice. At once a yentig Qr an elderly woman appears at the entrance of the ragged and Form-worn tent, the felt pieces of which have been bleached by rain and stio"; whilst belt, ropes, and pegs are sadly out of repair. It is a poor tent? The male in- habitant is out on some predatory or hunting expedition, whilst his wife has to tend the flock in close proximity tO the dwelling, or is engaged in spinning or rolling a new piece of felt ro be laid under the new member of the family whose arrival is expected soon. On perceiving7the pious stranger from a distant land she utters a few words of joy- ous surprise, and soon comes forward with a wooden dish of sour milk, with a piece of cheese, or with a bundle of sun- dried fish. The visitor partakes of the offering with a loud " Vismillah," i.e.," In the name of God," whilst his hostess sits opposite shedding tears because God has given her the opportunity of feeding a guest. As soon as he has satisfied his hunger she brings before him the plain coloured camel- • hair, the material for the new carpet, in order to have be- stowed upon it his blessings, as a sure sign of happiness to her coming child. For a while the Turcoman woman will remain quite motionless, her eyes fixed upon the movements of your lips, every sound of which is most anxiously caught, and it is only after having finished the recital of the Koran, of which she does not understand a single word, that she gives vent to her blissful satisfaction, by uttering a sigh from the depth of her heart, or by a tear. I have often wit- nessed scenes of this nature that were indescribably touch- ing, and it may he easily understood how this comes back to my memory, whenever I have to picture the lights and shadows of life amongst the primitive inhabitants of the desert. No wonder, too, that during my abode amongst the Turcomans on the Gurg:3n feelings of admiration were mingled with the deep aversion and horror that agitated my iseart.—Good

Essex, is on& of the finest mansions in the country. We have to consider how the land was obtained, and how the mansion

Lord Chancellor Audley is fitly describ,d by Lord Camp- bell as "a sordid slave,' who further declares that "no eunuch in a seraglio was ever a more submissive tool to the caprice and vengeance of a passionate and remorseless master." This jihigment is not at all an exaggerated one; his whole ignoble career is unrelieved by any touch of up- rightness or manliness. He was born to poverty, and he rose to wealth and power by the basest means. His first pl ices were earned by defending, in the House of Commons, the worst abuses of the Royal Pri-regative, and supporting Wolsey's demand for extortionate subsidies. Wnen Sr Thomas More was disgraced Audley was appointed Lord Keeper, and subseq nutty Lord Chancellor. This pliant, servile tool of tyranny never shrank from the basest deeds in order to please his master. It was he who presided at the shameful trial of More, and at the still more shameful trial of Bishop Fisher, in which his conduct as a judge was simply infamous. It was he, to.), who presided at the trials of Queen Anne Boleyn and the Marquis of Exeter and Lord Montagu. It was he, too, rho took an active part not only in the spoliation of the ecclesiastical houses, but in "the division of the plunder among those who planned the rob- bery." It was he, too, who was one of Henry's chief instru- ments in raising money by illegal expedients, the commis- sions being issued under the Great Seal ; in short, he was a willing tool in executing all the worst measures of that evil reign. And he hid his reward. His own repeated applica- tions to Crcenwell are still extant, his chief desire being to secure for himself the lands of the rich A )bey of Saffron Walden He hid sbld himself to the devil apparently with- out remorse, and he was not slow in claiming whatever gain he could hope from the bargain. "I have," he writes, "in this world sustained great damage and infamy in serving the King's Highness. which this grant (Walden Abbey) shall recompense." He obtained his desire, and was also farther rewarded with a priory at Aldgate, where he built a mansion, and with four or five other confiscated monastic houses. Thus the lands were gained,

Audley is mentioned by Air Henry Spe!man as one of the persons who were punished for sacrilege by having no male heirs. If the failure of male heirs is a mark of Divine dis- pleasure, it is clear that not a few royal .nd noble houses must have been exceedingly wicked. Be that as it may, And ey left behind him only one daughter, who lived to mature years; and she married the unfortunate Duke of Norfolk who was beheaded for treason in the reign of Eliza- beth. One could almost wish that Aadley had lived long enough to see the daughter of the Queen upon whom he had pronouncet sentence of death sign the death-warrant of his own daughter's husband. The eldest son of the marriage, IThomas Howard, was subsequently restored in blood, and inherited from his mother the Barony of Walden which had been obtained by Lord Chancellor Audley. One of his daughters married William Cecil, the first Earl of Salisbury; another the Earl of Essex, and subsequently Carr, Earl of Somerset, the favourite of James I. It is not at all surpris- ing, then, to find that, soon after the accession of James, h was created Earl of Suffolk, and that he held for some years the lucrative post of Lord filth Treasurer. In the first years of that reign he was Lord Chamberlain; and, in company with Lord Monteagle, who had received kwarning of the Gunpowder Plot, he inspected the cellars beMath the Houses of Parliament, where he discovered Guy Fawkes, with his stores of gunpowder. After the fall of the favourite Somer- set, whose connection with the Countess of Essex is known to every reader of English history, the Earl of Suffolk fell into disgrace. According to Rapin, his Countess "made no scruple of taking bribes with both hands." According to the same authority, 'lt was discovered that the Treasurer has converted to his own uses part of the money received for the cautionary towns frau Holland." This was an old claim which we had upon the Dutch, which was settled by the payment of 2,728,000 florins, and eighteen years' interest. The Earl was fined A 30,000, and sentenced to be imprisoned in the Tower during the King's pleasure. Whether the fine was paid I know not; but, after a short confinement, he was released. But, in the meantime, he had erected the magnificent mansion of Audley End, which he named after the Lord Chancellor, and which is said to lime cost £l9o,ooa—an enormous sum in those days. Thus the house was built. The third Earl of Suffolk sold the mansion and park to Charles 11. for £5OlOO, two-fifths of the purchase-money being allowed to stand over. After the Revolution of 1688 he was allowed to re-purchase it at the same price which he had actually received from Charles. This nobleman having no male heirs, the Earldom ef Suffolk devolved upon his next brother. The Barony of Walden, which for a time fell into abeyance between his daughters and their heirs, is now held by the present Lorn Howard de Walden, who is descended from his younger daughter. His elder daughter, hnwever, married Lord Griffin of Braybrooke, in Northamp- tonshire, and her descendant, John Griffin Whitwell, in- herited her share of the Saffron Walden estates, and for his lifetime the Barony of Walden. He, having no issue, obtained during his lifetime a new patent of peerage as Lord Braybrooke, with remainder to his relative, Richard Ald- worth Neville, of Billingbere, in Berkmhire, who, after his death, became the second Lord Braybrooke. These Nevilles are an offshoot of the Abergavenny Nevilles. I have been unable to discover how they obtained billingbere, in Barks, which is still held by Lord Braybrooke. The first who is spoken of as possessed of it was Sir Henry Neville, who is several times mentioned by Burnet as a courtier in the latter part of the reign of Henry VIII., and, according to a MS. written by the father of Sir Thomas Overbury, he was a bastard son of that monarch. He married the daughter and heiress of Sir John Gresham, by whom ho had a son, Sir Henry Neville, who narrowly escaped becoming a prominent statesman. That Sir Henry was employed by Elizabeth as Ambassador to France' but, being implicated in the conspiracy of Essex, he was fined £5,000, the penalty being rigorously exacted. In the following reign, he filled some subordinate posts, and his further progress was retarded by the hostility of the favourite Carr. The Richard Aldworth Neville before spoken of was the son of a Mr. Aldworth, by a Neville heiress, and assumed the maternal name. It is worth notice that the Lords Braybrooke are Hereditary Visitors of Magdalene College, Cambridge, and that younger sons of the second and third lord both became masters of the College. The first of these, the Rev. George Neville, was also Dean of Windsor and Chaplain in Ordinary to the Queen. Of his sons, one became Prebendary of Wells and Vicar of Butleigh ; another Vicar of Wyrardisbury. The other, the Hon. and Rev. La,itner Neville, Master of Magdalene College, is also Vicar of Haydon (1681 and a house), a family living, and a Bishop's Chaplain. The third Lord Bray- brooke is best known as the editor of "The Diary of Samuel Pepys."

BARNUM AND Jumno.—The finest advertisement in the worid continues to run its triumphant career. There is no end to the variety of Mr. Barnum's methods of calling Heaven and earth to witness that he is possessed of the big- gest and the most eccentric mammal in existence. His latest device (says the Pall Mall Gazette) bee been to offer the trusters of Brooklyn Bridge 4,000 dole. if they would grant Jumbo the privilege of walking over it," quietly and secretly, late on Saturday night," because he objected to the ferry-boat. The quietness and the secrecy of his pro- ceedings are evidently very dear to Mr. Barnum. It is within the recollection of most people how these virtues were exemplified in Jumbo's removal from the Zoological Gardens last year, when only 200,000 extra vieitens, as we learn from the report of the Zoological Society read last Mcnday, were attracted by Mr. Barnum's "quiet and secret " manoeuvres. What would not the society give for such another £5,000 worth of quietness and secrecy ? Mean- while, the great Jumbo has evidently come to constitute a fresh and one of he strongest links between the Old World and the new. CANAL BOATS.—In the Canal Boats Bill, Mr. Butt, M P. proposes to make the registration of canal boats annual. The renewal of a certificate of registration would then be granted only on proof that the conditions of registration have been duly complied with as regards the boat. The Bill ilso prohibits the employment of children under the age of 13 in a canal boat, or for the purposes of one, unless they have attained the third standard, or some other to be fixed by the Local Government Board with the consent of the Education Department. And on Sundays no child whatever under the age of 10 is to be so employed for hire. For the contraven- tion of the last two regulations the penalty to which the owner of the boat is liable, and also the master if he is in default, is a fine not exceeding 20s for each day on which the illegal employment takes place. And a maximumt penalty of 40s. is imposed by the Bill for every default in complyment with the regulations made by the Local Govern- ment Board and the Education Department under the Acts, one half of the penalty being paid to the informer. More- over, the Board and the Department are requested to make enquiries as to the due observance of the Acts. Power also is given by the Bill to the Education Department.to.make regulations with respect to the payments or rerntsstnn of fees in elementary schools for children who by reason of their living in canal boats are unable to attend a school for the whole of a week. Every canal boat that contame ac- commodation for cooking or sleeping is to be deemed to be used as a " dwelling " within the meaning of the Act of 1877 ancleof this amended Act. And it is to be epeeially noticed, the expression canal boat " in these Acts is to be made very comprehensive by ircluding " all trav,lling and temporary dwellings not rated for the relief of the poor."

div.head: CZAR'S CoRONATION.
div.p: THE CZAR'S CoRONATION.

The Moscow correspondent of the Times writes :—" The external preparations for the grand procession and po- pular festivities here are now rapidly approaching comple- tion, under the favourable conditions of brilliant summer weather and the full certainty as to time and place obtained by the official publication of dates aril programmes. Both within and without the walls of the Kremlin a vast quantity of wood has been employed in the erection of tribunes, grand stands, pavillions, and screens for lamp illumination and fireworks ; necessary precautions for checking the pressure of crowds are observable in the shape of strong barricades on most of the side streets leading out of he main thorough- fares through which the Emperor will enter the holy city. As to the prohibitory regulations which were reported to have been issued against the letting oat of windows and bal- conies on this route and various other vexa- tious orders, supposed to have been devised as precautionary measures of safety against the designs end threate of Anarchists Ana Nihilists, One te obliged to entertain causiderable doubt. At least, General Kozleff, the head of the police has informed me that no such regulations have been made. The Emperor hag no desire to enter a city of people locked up within doors, and every facility, it seems, will be given in order to gratify popular curiosity. Particular favours are tobe shown , to the representatives of the native and foreign Press. Besides receiving a handsome silver badge and souvenir, about four times the slat of an ordinary war medal, board and lodging will be offered them as guests of the Czar. Surmises of a most absurd and alarming nature have late;y been going the round of the foreign press, attributing all kinds of ridiculous reasons for the fact that nothing definite was known as to the date of the coronation ceremony. But 47 have only to look at the history of former coronations to see that tho date was always published only a few days previous to the actual event. If we

take into consideration the • immense number • of important and trivial circumstances which are con- noctod with toe ceremony, the thousands of mrsons who are :ipp3inted to takc a c,rtain part in it, the absence of one of whom, if it does not cause an actual delay, will at least.lead to a certain amount of disorder, it is not surprising that the marsha's of ceremonies postpone as long as possible the fix- ing of the date. We have a proof of this even to-day in the alarming telegrams announcing the critical state of Count
Peter Schouvaloff, who was to hold the important post of standard bearer in the Imperial procession into the Cathe- dral of the Assumption. Ile was to have returned from Parts

to-day, but there is now no chance of his being able to take part in the forthcoming ceremony. Several members of his family have to-day started for Paris. The late Emperor's c wonation was announced four months beforehand, but no d ite was fixed. Fls Majesty had expressed a desire to be crowned on August 18, but almost at the last moment the ceremony had to be postponed until the 26th. This time we have nothing to complain of, as the dates have just been published, and are as follow: The arrival at Peter's Palace, May 20 • the Imperial entry into Moscow, May 22; the ceremony of coronation, May 27. The 28th, 29th, and 30h will b taken up in receiving congratulations. On June 2 will be given the grand festival cn Kodinsky Common, arranged for 400,000 The inauguration _ _
of St. Saviour's—C,ithedral is fixed for June 7, and the de-

parture for St. Petersburg will take place on June 19. The foreign guests will soon begin to arrive. Eight princes of royal bload are expected. It has been found that the ac- commodation afforded by the Palace, notwithstanding its immense size, will still be inadeqbate ' • and consequently the President of the Moscow Ceremonial Cominiss'on, Prince Droutski Lubetski, has been obliged to hire a great number of detached villas, each of which will cost on an average 5.000 roubles. The Emperor will, be accompanied by a suite of about 100 generals and adjutants. In all his escort will consist of nearly 2,000 men. The foreign diplo- matists, who have all found houses for themselves, will number about 200, the marshals of nobility 70, the nobles 250,

the deputies from territorial assemblies 100, the mayors 300, the Moscow merchants 150, and various other persons having the right of entry into the Palace 1.000. A correspondent of the St. James's Gazette says :—"The regalia to be used on the 27th of May represent a very con- siderable sum of money. The Crowns to he placed on the heads of the Emperor and Eawress, the two collars of St. Andrew, and the globe and sceptre are said to be worth about £400,000; but from an artistic point of view the modern gold and silver work of the Russian Court has no particular value. The Emperor's crown was made for Catherine 11., and has done service at five coronations; it is set with 50 large diamonds and 4,878 brilliants, as well as 54 magnificent pearls. The sceptre is adorned with the famous Orloff dia- mond, and the globe is set with a sapphire of rare size and beauty. One of the most remarkable events succeeding the coronation will be the consecration of the Church of Our Saviour of Moscow, which Alexander I. began to build in commemoration of Moscow's deliverance from Napoleon. The policy of panem et circenses will be well carried out in free banquets and spectacles to the moujiks and soldiery, who, if they do not surfeit themselves with food and drink, will not be able to blame their Little Father, the Czar. There will be plenty of tobacco to assist digestion. One tobacco merchant alone has contracted to supply thirty million cigarettes of the best Crimean and Caucasus tobacco."

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.
The anrual Tichb-o-rn-e-d-e-mo;t'tra-tiOU -took place on Mon- !lay in Trafalgar-square, when the usual resolutions protest- ing against the continued incarceration of the claimant were Passed.

A fire occurred on Saturday night at the oil works of Mr. -John Parker, Port Dundas, Glasgow. Several tanks becom- ing ignited burned until Sunday morning. The damage is estimated at £6,000. The weather was tine, on Monday, for the celebration of Whit-Monday, riad in all parts of the country the people took advantage of the favourable conditions to enjoy the holiday. At a male meeting of workingmen in Hyde Park, London, on Monday, a resolution was passed requesting the Govern- ment to facilitate the passing of a measure for the closing of Public-houses on Sundays. Ann Frost, a servant, at Paignton, was committed for trial, on Monday, for concealment of birth, having, it was alleged, destroyed the remains of the child by burning it in the kitchen range of her employer's house. A brassfounder, named James Goxv, residing at Kirk- caldy, died on Monday morning from the effects of drink- ing aquafortis. Gow, it appears, got out of bed for the Purpose of taking a drink of beer, but by mistake took 11Pa bottle containing aquafortis, and drank part of the con- tents. , A 1121 w 13stomer.—Dr. William Chambers, of Edin- burgh, bas, it is stated, been offered and has accepted a baronetcy. He was born in Peebles in 1800; he was Lord Provost of Edinburgh from 1865 to 1869, and re- anived from the University of Edinburgh the honorary degree of doctor of laws. Dr. Chambers has spent a large 411171 on the restoration of St. Giles's Cathedral, which is now nearly completed. .13mts or SALE AND FAILURES.—In the week ending May 13, 1883, there were 240 bills of sale in England and Wales, decrease of 727 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 213 Totals for the portion of year to May 12, 1833, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 4,462, a decrease of 13,698 ; the failures gazetted number 4,092, a decrease of 101.—Stubbs's Mercantile Gazette.

The Mayor of Barrow (Mr. John Fell) on Monday laid the Memorial stone of a new shelter for the public which the Corporation of Barrow are erecting on Biggar Bank, a large recreation ground on the west shore of Walney Island, lately purchased by them from the landowners. Biggar Rank is one of the most beautiful undalatinggrass plots, some two or three miles long by half a mile wide, which border the Irish Sea. THE Boyar, AGRICULTURAL StlOW.—The entries for the forthcoming show of the Royal Agricultural Society at York are as follow :—Horses, 614; cattle, 468; sheep,4l6; Pigs, 193; making a total of 1,691. As was expected, the entries of horses are very much larger than at any show of the society for some years past. At Reading last year there were 239 horses, 598 cattle, 442 sheep, 158 pigs; total, 1,467. In 1881 at Derby there were 156 horses, 392 cattle, 414 sheep, and 167 pigs; total, 1,229. At the Carlisle show in 1880 the entries were 487 horses, 434 cattle, 434 sheep, 146 pigs; total, 1.501. At London in 1879 the animals numbered 2,874; at Bristol in 1878, 1.354; at Liverpool in 1877,1,305 ; and at Birmingham in 1876, 1,499. ATTEMPTED GIGANTIC JZIVELLERY ROBBERY IN MAN- CRIMER: CLEVBR CAYTURIL—A jeweller's shop in Cross- street, Manchester, was forcibly entered during the small hours of Sunday morning. The robbers, two men supposed to have come from America, and who give the names of -10lan Warren and Joseph Toner, effected an entrance into the premises through gaps they made in three brick walls of Xreat thickness, one of them plated with iron, and, with the eid of jemmie., chisels, halnmere, and other implements they had just succeeded in breaking open a safe containing about £20,000 worth of jewellery and precious stones, when they ware interrupted by the police, who afterwards cap- tured them on the roof of an adjoining block of buildings. The prisoners answer to the descriptions given of two men Who recently committed an extensive robbery from a jewel- ler's shop in High-street, Birminghana. They were brought before the city magistrates on Monday, and remanded. THE NaTioNat.. SECULAR SOCIETY. The annual con- ference of the National Secular Society was held on Sunday, iR Manchester. Mr. Bradlaugh, the president, was in the Chair. Mrs. Besant, the vice-president, and the Misses Hradlangh were also present.—Mr. Bradlaugh, in presenting the report of the execetive, said the past year had been OlOfts important to the Freethought party than any similar period daring the last 40 years. In returning thanks for his re-election as president, Mr. Bradlaugh said their party had Yet to fight, and at least he could say that he could join in the Part of the work. They were a militant body, a fight- ing body, and the wand of OffiCll which they gave him was sword, and he would strike with it. A resolution was Passed thanking Messrs. Fuote, Ramsey, and Kemp for their defence of free publication, offering their sympathy in their " annterited suffering."

" Cl/EAP AND GOOD LIVING."—On Friday evening Dr. and Mrs. Norman Kerr gave a vegetarian supper to 100 Persons, consisting of employs of the Vestry of Sfat7lebone aM their wives and relatives, at a tavern, in Marvlebone- tYad, the object, as stated on the invitation card, being "to Illustrate cheap and good living."
