A party of excursionists were driving into the country on Tuesday from Kidderminster, when the carriage was over- turned. A lady named Roden was killed on the spot, a gentleman named Hepworth had his leg fractured, ami two others were badly hurt. The party of lacrosse players, consisting of fifteen Can- adian gentlemen and thirteen Indians of the Iroquois tribe, the whole under the command of Dr. Beers. of Montreal, arrived at Liverpool on Tuesday in the Dominion Line steamer Sarnia. On Saturday, nearly 10,000 colliers and ironstone getters in North Staffordshire went out on strike against the pro- posed reduction of 10 per cent. in their wages. The notice of redaction was originally for 15 per cent, but the employers consented to change it to 10 per cent. A youth named Harrison was drowned in the ornamental lake at Roundhay Park, Leeds, on Tuesday, by the cap- sizing of a canoe in which he had been sailing. His struggles were witnessed by a crowd of excursionists, and an unavailing attempt at rescue was made by one of their number. Major Hatton, senior major of the Sheffield Artillery, at present encamped on Scarborough Castle Hill, was super- intending the firing of a 64-pounder on Tuesday afternoon, when he failed to get clear of the gun as it recoiled after discharging. His right foot was terribly crushed, and it is feared that amputation of the limb will he necessary. FINE rou SELLING NEWSPAPERS ON 6ITNDAY.—The Worcester magristrates fined two Birmingham lads on Tues- day ss. and costs, under the Lord's Day Act of Charles 11., for "exercising their worldly calling" on Sunday by selling the Birmingham. Sundae/ Echo on Sunday in the streets. The lads stated that in Birmingham and districts they tied never been interfered with. The conviction under the obso- lete statute caused much surprise in court The Protestant Dissenting Ministers of Warwickshire and the neighbouring counties, at their recent meeting, adopted a resolution recognisiag the services rendered to the cause of civil and religious liberty by Mr. Gladstone's speech on the affirmation Bill, and regretting that that measure was not carried. The Premier, in reply to the resolution, ex- presses his gratification at having the views of an important Nonconformist gathering so emphatically recorded in favour of the bill. . .

A telegram from Rome, published by the Journal Catkolique, states that the Pope has addressed a strongly- worded letter to the Irish bishops desiring them to forbid the clergy to take part in any political meetings or subscrip- tions in aid of any agitation, and recommending that res- pectful laogu3ge should be held towards the State digni- taries. The telegram adds that Dr. Croke, the Archbishop of Cashel, left Rome on Saturday little satisfied with the result of his visit.

A DISGR.SCEFCL HOAX ON AN OFFICIATING OLER,IY- MAN.—X disgraceful hoax has been played on the Rev. F Metcalf, curate of St. Bartholomew's Church, Claycroas. On Tuesday morning, when about to administer the Sacrament, ment, the rev, gentleman poured the contents of the wine bottle into the silver cup, and it was then found that the wine had been abstracted and ink substituted. The trick was at once detected, and, when another bottle had been pro- cured, the service proceeded as usual. DETERMINED ATTEMPT AT MURDER.—A determined at- tempt at murder was made near Stockton on Saturday night. Christopher Curry, who left Stockton market near midnight with a horse and trap for Thorp, was accosted on the road by a man, who asked for a ride. Before he could reply the man lifted a gun and fired, the charge taking effect in Curry's hand. The horses set off ata furious pace, and the man again fired, the shots this time taking effect in Curry's body. Four slugs have been extracted by Dr. 01liver from the wounded man, and it is hoped he may recover. THE STRENGTH or PARTIES IN THE HOUSE OF Cox- MOWS—The following figures may be of interest just now. The number of members of the House of Commons at the present time is 639—there being thirteen seats vacant through the action of the election judges. The gross strength of the Liberal party is 329. In addition there are twenty Home Rulers who sit on the Liberal side and usually vote with the Ministry, which brings its strength up to 349. The Tories whip 248 members, and the Irish party proper 42, in all 290. It follows that the Government have a no- minal majority of 39, or, adding the moderate Home Rulers, of 39.

MADAME RACHEL'S WILL—The French Court of Appeal gave judgment on Friday in a case which turned on the will of the great tragedienne Madame Rachael. She left a life annuity of 6,900 f. to Sarah Felix, known to fame as the patentee of cosmetics, and bestowed the reversion upon her own natural children. When, however, Sarah Felix die., the two surviving sisters of Rachael stepped in and obiected to the reversion going to the children, urging that the clause in Rachel's will was a covert means of favouring her natural children, while eluding the law. The Tribunal of First In- stance dismissed the claims of the sisters ; but this decision has now been reversed on appeal, and Rachel's own children will not get what she intended for them. Mr. BRADLAUGH'S APPEAL TO TICE CONSTITUEN- CIES. Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P' . addressed a large Lilteral, meeting held on Saturday, at 'Witten- stall. His charge against the House of Commons was that they had been guilty of treason to the Constitu- tion, and he intended, he said, to preach a crusade against them all over the country. "Wherever there was a hill that had an echo he would try to wake it, that it might speak to the people of rights infringed and liberties in- sulted." He thought it was a disgrace to the century that one man should be driven to measure himself with the majority of the House of Commons, but, the law being powerless, he meant to go on with the btttle. AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' DRMONSTRATION.—The SDRUaI demonstration of the National Agricul aril Labourers' Union was held at Fording Bridge, Wilts, on Monday. The attend- ance was small, owing to rain. Sir John Bennett, who was expected to preside did not attend, and letters expressing sympathy were read from several members of Parliament, including Messrs. Burt, Bradlaugh, Broadhurst, Cowen, Col- lings, &c On the motion of Miss Helen Taylor, a resolu- tion was carried in favour of the extension of the franchise to counties, and urging the Government not to defer this pressing reform. A petition was adopted, demanding redis- tribation of political power, the equalization of the fran- chise in boroughs and counties, and the payment of election expenses out of the publi.c purse. Miss H -len Taylor spoke in support of the extension of the franchise, and said the laws, which were remnants of feudality, prevented the legiti- mate fruits of our land being produced. Mr. Geo. Mitchell, who presided, said the present laws forced men to emigrate, leaving the land uncultivated. _

DISCOTEUY OF GOLD COINS AT PENDLETON.—lnforma- tion has been given to the Salford police of the finding of a considerable sum of money at Pendleton. It is stated, that some £3O has been found buried beneath the trunk of a tree near Mr. Chadwick's glassworks, in Seedley Fields, and that it was discovered by some boys who were playing on the spot on Sunday. A boy, 13 years old, found the first lot, and communicated the fact to his relatives, and the police got to hear of it. It is stated that two other boys and a man also found some gold at the same place on the same day. When the matter came to the knowledge of the police, the Chief-Constable (Mr. W. L. Marshall) had the parties interviewed, and ordered that the money should be given up to the police, into whose hands only a portion of it has yet come. Several officers, under the direction of Inspector Shenton (of Pendleton) searched the place, and they were successfnl in finding more gold. Most of the coins, it is said, are very old—some bearing the date 1820—and they have the appearance of having been buried a good while. DINING IN THE VESTEY.—The Bishop of Winchester, a Salisbury correspondent writes, has been in communication with a committee of parishioners during the past month on the question of the legality of the vicar of Portchester (the Rev. Mr. Knight) and his wife taking their meals in the vestry. The parish churchwardens wrote to the Bishop complaining that the vicar and his wife had hot dinners in the vestry, which was thus converted into a dining-room, and urging that "the vicar's home should be with his flock." The Bishop, in reply, wrote—Though I think the vestry is not the right place for dinners, I.do not think I could desire Mr. Knight to take a lodging for the sake of getting refreshment on a Sunday. If Mr. and Mrs. Knight had to remain in the vestry between the services. I should not think there was much desecration of the House of God in the eating of a sandwich, tic., in the vestry, which I sup- pose is a distinct apartment from the church, and in which secular business is commonly transacted. I quite think the vicar ought to reside in the parish, but it is difficult to force him to reside if he has no house of residence. TRH CO-OTEUATITE WHOLESALE Socerrx.—The 75th quarterly report shows sales £995,879. being an increase of £152,28.5, or 18 per cent, on the corresponding quarter of last year. The net profit amounts to £9,281, which it is proposed to be divided as follower—Dividend on members' sales at 2!,,-d in the pound, £8,671 • dividend on non-members' purchases at 11d in the pound, £304; and the balance £304, to reserve. The increase in business is shared by all the three branches. In Manchester the rate of increase is 18, at Newcastle 81, and at London 11 per cent. The turnover la the bank department during the quarter has been £3,448,540, and upon this business there is a net profit of £7OO. 'The number of retail co-operative societies compos- • ing the federation is now 639, with an individual member. ship of 405,866, an increase of 19 societies and of 34,890 individuals compared with the corresponding quarter of last year. The capital of the socie-ty, iacluding shares, loans, deposits. reserve, and insurance, now amounts to £641.841, an increase since March. 1882. of £53.877. During 1882 the society did a business of £4,038,238, at a cost of 30 the pound, and realised a net profit of £49,058. AN ELOTEMENT AND ITS CONSEQUENCES.—At the Liver- , pool Police Court, on Tuesday, before the stipendiary magis- trate Edward Biggs, a respectably-dressed man, was charged with obtaining food and lodging at the Angel Hotel, Dale- street, under false pretences. It wits stated in evidence that the prisoner, accompanied by a young lady, came to the hotel a fortnight ago, and said he was a medical man, but had retired from practice, and was than engaged in a specu- lation in horses, seven of which animals he expected over from Ireland for sale either at Lucas's Repository, Liverpool, or at Tattersall'e, London. The young lady he represented to be hie wife. In due time the bill for his maintenanc! was presented, and the prisoner deferred payment, explaining tha• he had sold a horse for £5O but had not got the money. The bill being again presented some days afterwards the produced a document purporting to be a bill of exchange, but the leedlord on examining it found it was a fietitiousdocu- ment. end charged the prisoner to this effect, when the pri- soner admitted it was so, stating he had written it in order to gain titne for the arrival of a remittance from Ireland. The prieoner wasthen given over to the police. His portman- teaus, on being searched, were found to he empty. It was now stated that the prisoner was a married man, and bad left hie wife in Ireland, having run away with the girl who ac ee-npanied him, and who Naas the daughter of a respectable innkeeper in Ireland. The prisoner was remanded for a week, bail being accepted.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAT 19, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAT 19, 1883.

A Paris correspondent says :—" I have reason to believe that the French Government has ordered reinforcements to be prepared in case China should oppose France in Tonquin." M. Waddington has, it is reported, discharged a delicate mission at Berlin. He has assured the Emperor and Prince Bismarck of the "good and peaceful intentions of France towards Germany." The Ameer of Afghanistan has convinced the people of Jellalabad of his triumph over the Shinwaris by the same means as were employed in London early in the last cen- tury to show that the Jacobites were buten. He has had 150 Shinwaris' heads fixed in spikes on the walls of the fa- mous city. A despatch to the Daily News from a correspondent at Khartoum, announces the defeat of the False Prophet with great loss. The telegram says :—" The enetnyilled to Kor- doffan. We followed them and met them at Gebaline. Many were killed, and all their chiefs were defeated. 'We hare taken a number of cattle."

ADVENTURES OF AN ITALIAN WEAVER.—A young Italian, originally a weaver, has just been tried at the Turin Assizes for robbing the mails. He had, it appears, been passing himself off as the son and heir of Napoleon 111. He suc- ceeded in getting a rich widow to believe in him; but on her finding him out, he toolr to the road. His conduct at the preliminary examination led to his being sent to a lunatic asylum. He has now been condemned to 21 years' penal servitude. SUICIDR OF Two Lovints.—lntelligence has been re- ceived from Hamburg of a sad case of double suicide there. Some watermen fishing in the River Alster discovered at a secluded spot the dead bodies of a man and woman both tightly interlaced in the woman's mantilla. They were in full evening dress, the woman wearing her jewels. She was 19 years old, the daughter of a very wealthy and respected family. Being definitely forbidden to marry the man of her choice, who was socially her inferior, she committed suicide with him.

• A TERRIBLE CRIME.—A terrible crime is reported from Paris, and unfortunately no clue has been discovered as to the identity of its perpetrators. It was committed in broad daylight in the Paldis Royal by daring thieves, who broke into the shop of a jeweller named Prestot, in the Montpensier Arcade, and were engaged in rifling the windows of their vintents when a servant sarprided them. This hapless indi- vidual was at once attacked and murdered, and then the robbers escaped with booty, chiefly in the shape of diaomonds amounting to the aggregate value of forty-five thousand fr4ncs.

Nows FROM Sorra AFRICA.—News from South Africa is even less satisfactory than it has been for a considerable time past. Cetewayo has been drilling some regiments, with the intention, it is believed, of making another attack on Usibepu, who so severely defeated the restored king's young braves recently. Fighting has been renewed, too, in Basutoland between Joel and Jonathan, and Masupha and Lero•hodi are again on the war-path. The war on the Trans- vaal border is not yet terminated, and the Orange Free State Government looks to this country, as well as to the Colonial Governments, to protect it against incursions by the Basutos.

TORNADO IN MISSOURI.—A tornado which swept across Kansas City, Missouri on Sunday, cleared a path nearly three miles long and 300 yards wide. It caused damage to property to the amount of $300,000; and six lives were lost. Fifty buildings were destroyed, and 200 more were much injured. Oatside of the city the path of the tempest extended for 15 miles, causing serious losses in several vil- lages. Another tornado later in theAvening almost des- troyed Webb City and Ornogo in Situth-Weat Missouri. Several persons were killed. Both of these tornadoes are describPd as having the appearance of dark, funnel-shaped, whirling clouds.

1110127BLES ON THE WEST AFRICAN COAST.—The West African mail steamer brings information of some troubles on the coast. A French naval officer has, it is stated, been trying to conclude a treaty with the natives of Bonny, in the absence of Consul Hewitt, and the annexation of some land near Porto Novo by a small French force is also reported. Owing to a serious case of robbery and outrage by natives, an armed force has destroyed one of their villages on the Sherbro river. The King of Dahomey. alarmed at the rumoured cession of Whydah to the English by Portugal, has (mused all the white people in his kingdom to be con- fined to their houses, whereby trade is entirely stopped. THE RESULT OF GAMBLING.—A Hamburg correspondent writes :—" The gambling hell at San Carlo has put one of the first Schleswig-Holstein families into mourning. The second son, a promising young nobleman visited Monaco during his journey through Italy. He hada large sum with him, which he lost at roulette, and he had to telegraph to his family for more. Having received a supply he again took part in the play. but ill-luck pursued 'him. When the last franc was gone, and his watch, studs, and rings, he tried to borrow 500 f. to pay the bill at his hotel; but, not being known, he got only a trifle. Exasperated, and ashamed to ask his family a second time, he shot himself."_ . .

The movement in favour of a second Suez Canal is at- tracting great attention in Paris, and some of the journals are endeavouring to create ilbfeeling against England on the ; subject. The project is regarded by some as merely "a ' threat levelled at the Suez Canal Company with the hope of inducing it to give England a preponderating share on the direction," and the Paris and other journals call upon the Ministry to prevent England from planting" both her feet" in Egypt. On the question of concession, it is announced that coausel to whom the subject was referred by the Khe- dive have given a qualified opinion that it creates a monoply, which. however, " ceuld not be maintained if a single canal should prove inadequate." AFFAIRS IN ManaGasce.R.—The special correspondent of the Standard in Madagascar says preparations fel war con- tinue to be made on an exteasive scale, and are even more manifest in the interior than on the coast. Everything points to the certainty of a desperate resistance being offered to any attempted aggression on the part of France. England is in high favour with the people and the Government. It is expected that the French will begin their operatiens by attempting a landing at Passandava Bay, where there is a good Barbour and coal is abundant, and the Malagasy military leaders arc preparing to despatch an army to that ' point. The forces at the command of Queen Ranavalo seem amply sufficient. The regular army now amounts to 20,000 wcil-drilled troops, partly armed with breech-loaders, beside:, a horde of 50,000 spearinen. J)EATII OF NEDIM PASHA. It is stated in a telegram from Constantinople that Malimoud Nedim Pasha has died at the age of 68. His Highness began his career in the Grand Vizierate, and was afterwards appointed Governor- General of Barbary, where he realised a considerable for- tune. Abdul Aziz made him Grand Vizier, and Mahmoud, to strengthen his own position, released his master from the restraint of the Porte, and taught him to govern as well as to reign. A few months after the famous financial decree of October, 1875, Mahrnoud was virtually exiled by being appointed Governor-General of Adana, where he contracted a fever, the effects of which he had never been able to shake off. He was recalled by Sultan Abdul Hamid in 1879, and nominated Minister of the Interior. Nlahmoud had been in a precarious state of health for some time, having injured his constitution by excessive doses of quinine. PHOTOGRAPHING SEASON TICKET HOLDERS.—A novelty in the form of a railway ticket has been introduced in the Netherlands. In connection with the Amsterdam Exhibi- tion certain invited guests have each been presented with free passes over the whole network of Dutch railways, and for the purpose of identification each ticket holder's portrait is shown upon the back of the ticket. It appears also that the Baltic Railway Company have dechled upon this method of identifying passengers, and that upon an issue of vason tickets for the summer months, that has just been announced, it is stipulated that on the back of the ticket there shall appear a photographicoportrait of the rightful owner, and that duplicate portraits shall be deposited with the corepany. With these tickets in force the words "not traneferable " ! will be altogether unnecessary, but the work of the ticket ! examiners will be very considerably increased if each pas- senger's features are to be carefully scrutinised in compari- son with the portrait upon the ticket.

A National Society for the Repeal of the Blasphemy Laws was inaugurated in London, on Thursday af:ernoon. Among the speakers were Mr. Bradlaugb, M.P., and several minis- ters of different denominations. At a meeting of the Boyle Branch of the National League held on Monday, a resolution was adopted strongly censor- ing Dr. Commins, M.P., for being absent from the division on the Affirmation Bill, and for neglecting his parliamentary , duties. Dr. Commins is the Parnellite representative who unseated the O'Connor Don in Roscommon at the general elution.
THE PWENIX PARK I\IIIRDERS.
EXECUTION OF BRADY.

The sentEnce of death passed on the Irish " Invincible," Joseph Brady, on the fith of April last, for the inurder ef Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Thomas H. Burke, in Pficeuix Park, Dublin, just a year and eight days ago, was carried into effect within the precincts of Kilnaainharn tiaol at eight o'clock on Monday morning, and thus the chief assassin of the Invincibles has been the first to pay with his life the penalty of the terrible crime which first brought him into notoriety. The morning in Dublin was wet, but an enormous concourse of people assembled outside the goal, and some estimates place the number at not fewer than ten thousand. An accurate estimate of a crowd is seldom made, but the number of people was undoubtedly very large. The authorities had taken complete precautions to guard against any disorder, hut these were not obtruded upon the popu- lace, and fortunately there was no attempt at any demon- stration. Some perturbation was at one time caused by the appearance of a hearse, it being supposed that an attempt at a mock funeral was contemplated, but it subsequently transpired that a funeral was really to take place frora a house opposite the gaol, ani when the crowd had dispersed it was duly proceeded with. Notwithstanding the culprit's clearly-prove( complicity hi the crime—a crime which was described in Monday's Freeman's Journal as "perhaps the most atrocious that has ever stained the annals of Ireland" —there were not lacking many sympathisers with the assas- sin. "Expressions of condolence" ate said to have "poured in " upon Brady and his fellow-culprits from many quar- ters. Amongst others a cross of white ro•es and camelias was taken over from England to Brady's relatives by a dele- gate specially deputed from Liverpool. Accompanying the cross was a slip of notepaper, upon which was inscribed, "A token of grief from the Irishmen of Liverpool," Mourning cards were also issued to the members of the Liverpool Branch of the Irish National League, requesting them to attend mass on behalf of Brady at St. Patrick's Church, Park Place, at 8-30 a.m., on Monday morning, the concluding words on the card being "All members of the branch intend wearing a token of mourning. God save Ireland." There were numerous marked tokens of sympithy in certain parts of Dublin, including what are described as mourning arches, bearing the culprit's name. Brady is sajd to have derived very great comfort from the ministrations of the Roman Catholic clergy, and Canon Kennedy, who I regularly visited him from the time of his condemnation and accompanied him to the scaffold, is reported to have stated that "Brady's demeanour, as, indeed, that of the other condemned men, was very consoling as viewed from a religious standpoint." Brady met his death with extraor- dinary coolness, but with no display of bravado.

div.head: EXECUTION OF -CURLEY.
div.p: EXECUTION OF -CURLEY.

Daniel Curley, the Invincible, who superintended the Proenix Park assassinations was executed in Kilmainham Gaol at eight o'clock yesterday morning. At a quarter to eight the gaol bell tolled for his approaching doom, and the chaplain whispered in Curley's ear, on seeing the warder apprsaching him, that time was up. Simultaneously out- side the gaol groups of people began to say the Litany for the dying. Curley's father and father-in-law were in the centre of a large crowd on the bridge opposite to the black flag. Curley's father had expressed an intention of addressing the people, but, yielding to the advice of friends, he resolved to say nothing. There were groups in all directions saying the rosary. By permission of the police, Curley's father and his father- in-law got into a field apart from the crowd, and they were praying earnestly. Precisely at eight o'clock, in a blaze cf sunshine, the black flag was run up, indicating that Curley was no more. A wail of grief was raised, and the crowd, numbering two thousand, rushed across to the prison boundary, where prayers were said. Cur. ley's father and father-in-law assert their son to be a patriot and martyr. Curley wrote a letter to his wife, which is practically an admission of his guilt. SECOND TRIAL OF "SKIN-TM-GOAT."

James Fitzharris, alias" Skin-the-Goat," was again put on trial in Dublin on Tuesday, charged this time with being accessory after the fact to the murder of Mr. Burke. Fitz- barris it will be remembered, has already been tried for the capital offence and acquitted. The Solicitor-General, Mr. Murphy, Q.C., and Mr. P. O'Brien, Q.C., prosecuted for the Crown; and the prisoner was defended bv Mr. J. O'Byrne and Mr. M'lnerney. In opening the Crown case, Mr. ISaish referred to the formation of the Invincible organisation, and said the prisoner would be proved to have attended its meetings in Brunswick-street. On the 6th of May be drove Smith, Carey, and Hanlon t) the park. It was impossible that the prisoner could not have known the nature of the business in which those men were engaged. Evidence was then called, and the approvers Joseph Smith, James Carey, Peter Carey, Michael Kavanagh, and Joseph Hanlon de- posed to the prisoner's presence with the Invincibles on sevcral occasions previous to and on the 6th of May. At the trial on Wednesday, four independent witnesses were called, who proved that the prisoner was in the park, near the scene of the murder, on the evening in question. No witnesses were called for the defence. It was urged in behalf of the accused that he was only in the park in pursuit, of his ordinary calling as a cabman. The jury, after de- liberating about forty minutes, returned a verdict of guilty, and Mr. Justice O'Brien sentenced the prisoner to penal servitude for life. THE CONSPIRACY PRISONERS.

Edward M'Caffrey, Daniel Delaney, and Thomas Martin afterwards pleaded guilty to conspiring to murder Govern- ment officials, and sentence upon these prisoners was de- ferred. In respect of Martin, Mr. Mutphy, on behalf of the Crown, pointed out that though he was present on the quays on March 28, it was believed that be had not participated in any acts of the Invincibles since that day, and be was, too, the sole support of an aged father, who was unfit to work. Upon this the judge remarked that be would con- sider the case in the most favourable light, but Martin then destroyed some of the good feeling that had been created by the Crown on his behalf by specially directing the attention of the judge to the fact that though he had been twice examined by Mr. Curran he had never given the Crown any information. Mr. Murphy gave full corroboration to this statement. •

div.head: MURDER OF POOLE.
div.p: THE MURDER OF POOLE.

True bills were found against Sylvester Kingston and Thomas Gibney for conspiring to murder Joseph Poole, and also against Matthias Brady (brother to Joseph Brady) for sending a threatening letter to Mr. King, juryman. Kingston and Gibney pleaded not guilty, and they were put back un:il Thursday. CLOSE OF THE COMMISSION. SIX MORE PRISONERS SENTENCED.

At the Dublin Commission Court, on Thursday, Mr. Justice O'Brien passed sentence on the prisoners who had pleatb-d guilty to conspiracy to murder. A conversation between the Crown lawyers and Judge was the first incident which attracted attention, and from what could be gathered it would appear that the question at issue was, whether or not Peter Doyle should be placed in the dock. The prisoner has been in bad health for some time, and Dr. Carte, the Kilmainham physician, now stated that he would be unable to undergo at present the strain which a prolonged trial might impose upon him. It was decided, however, to ask the prisoner whether he was prepared for his trial, and with this obj.-ct prisoner was assisted into the dock by two warders. As he appeared at Kilmiinham Doyle was one of the best-looking men among the Invincibles in the dock, but now appeared a broken-down invalid, and was barely able to stand on us feet. His lordship intimated to the prisoner that his trial would be postponed out of con- sideration for his delicate health. Doyle bowed, and ex- pressed his thanks to the judge and retired. James Mullett, Edward Weaffrey, Edward O'Brien, William Moroney, and Daniel Delaney were then eacq sentenced to ten years' penal servitude, and Thomas Doyle to five years.' Thomas Martin was next put in the box, and his Lordship said, owing to the intervention of the head of the detective department he would allow him cut on his own recogni- zances to come up for judgment when called upon. The prisoner, who appeared much astonished, thanked his lord- ship, andentered into the required securities. After an interval Matthias Brady was put forward, and pleaded pay to a charge of sending a threatening letter to the foreman of the jury who convicted his brother. At the request of the gen- tleman to whom the letter was sent, and by the consent of the Crown, the prisoaer was allowed out on his own recog- nizances to come up for judgment when called upoi.

div.head: VIGILANCE u0:1111ITTFE.
div.p: THE VIGILANCE u0:1111ITTFE.

The prisoners Sylvester Kingston and Thomas Gibney, who have pleaded not guilty .to tne charge of conspiracy to murder Joseph Poole and others, will be tried at the next commission, which will be held in June. DISCHARGING THU JURY PANELS.

His lordship in discharging the first special panel of jurors paid a high tribute to their intelligence, fearlessness, and impartiality. They had been engaged in unravelling a conspiracy which had been supported in that court by another conspiracy, that of an organised system of false swearing, but in spite of all difficulties the law had triumphed and verdicts had been returned which were not only just, but so undeniably certain, that it was impossible to dispute them. The result had shown the supremacy of the law when it came to a trial of strength between it and crime. In reply to a number of applications, his lordship announced that he would remit the tines that had been imposed upon all jurors with the exception of those who had not attended at all dur- ing the Conunission. The members of. the second jury panel were also discharged. SUMMA la' OF THE SENTENCES ON THE I N VINCI BLES.

The inviocibles who stood together in the dock at Kil- mainharn have thus been disposed of :—There were sen- tenced to death besuks Brady, Curley, Fagan, Kelly, Caffrey, and P. Delaney. As it is understood that Delaney will not suffer the extreme penalty of the law, the capital sentences are live. Thcse sentenced to penal servitude for life are Fitzharris, Joseph Mullett, and Laurence Hanlon. Those s,intenced on Thursday for the conspiracy to murder are James Mullett, 'l'. Doyle, O'Brien, Mooney, M4caffrey, I). Delaney, and Marlin. James Carey, R. Farrell, .Kavanagh, Joseph Smith. Peter Carey, and Joseph Hanlon became approvers, of whom there were thus six. Hawks died in the prison, and George Smith was liberated. Twenty- four men forming the Invincible Society have thus been ar- migned and dealt

A Lisbon telegram says that on Tuesday evening, at a popuhr fete which was being held in a village near Oporto, dynamite bomb used in the firework display exploded, killing four and wounding twenty persons. At Brack on Thursday, Edward Iligbam, of Evdon. aged twenty three, was committed for trial charged with the wianl murder of his father. During an altercation on :•iatiirday night pris.mer knocked the deceased down with a boot, and kicked him savagely while on the floor.

div.head: TIIE STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: TIIE STATE OF IRELAND.

A herd. named Greevy' his wife, and five children have hcen accidentally poisoned near Elphin, county Roscommon, bf7,i7rikmg of -a eakelrrrnaking 'Which arsenic hatt—beer used in mistake for bread soda. Greevy died in great agony shortly afterwaeds, and hts.wife and children are in a most critical state.

According to a New York correppondent of the Daily Telegraph, the reports that the extradition of Walsh had been -demanded are regirded as totally devoid of foundation. It is also stated to be untrue that P. J. Tynan is in close hiding. The correspondent is credibly informed that the British Government are quite cognisant of his whereabouts. CONSPIRACY TO MURDER LANDLORDS.—Six rrrests were made in Ballina, county Mayo, on Wednesday, the prisoners being charged with conspiracy to murder certain landlords and agents in that district in 1882. In searching the houses of some of the prisoners an infernal machine and some arms were found. Formal evidence having been given, the prisoners were remanded until Wednesday next.

At the Dublin Police Court. on Saturday, Patrick Kin- sella, who was arrested on his own confession of the mnider of Lord Leitrim, was brought up, on remand, bet it was abundantly evident that he had nothing to do with the crime. his story was, in fact, disbelieved from the first, the impression being that he was a harmless lunatic. He was about to be discharged or sent to the workhouse, when he said he was afraid of being shot, and was again remanded. DESPERATE ATTEMPT TO MURDER —A caretaker named Walsh, employed to protect an evicted farm on the property of Miss Busteed at Carker, near Castleisland, was fired at and wounded on Tuesday morning. Walsh was usually accompanied by an escort of police from a neighbouring protection pet, but on Tuesday morning he dismissed them when they had gene part of the way. l'he assassins must have been for a long time watching their opportunity, for the moment they found Walsh alone they made a furious attack, firing several shots, and wounding him in the back and neck. Assistance came to hand, and the assailants re- tired. Eight arrests have been made. TRAITORS IN THE FENIAN CAMP.—The latest and most sensational story with regard to " traitors in the Fenian camp" is furnished by the New York correspondent of a Plymouth paper, who says it has been known for same weeks that the English Government had received information of an important nature both as to the plots of the Invincibles and the movements of the dynamite party from a person occupying a position of trust among one set of the conspira- tors. Suspicion has pointed to the notorious "No. 1," but it now passes, the correspondent save, with terrible accuracy to the "I.ld Man" of the dynamite plot. O'Donovan Rossa. The correspondent adds: "This double treachery was nut in Tynan's power; but by accident in the one case, and by de- sign in the other, Rossa was in possession of bath secrets. Rossa has always sought gain and safety. He is now utterly discredited, and his early 'removal' may be expected." _ _ _

THREATENING JIIIIORS.—Most of the tradesmen in Dublin received on Sunday morning, by post, a printed circular termed "An analysis of the special juries serving on eighteen trials under the Crimes Act," containing the names of the persons convicted and of the jurors who convicted them. Appended to this list are some notes setting forth the names of jurors to whom special attention is de- sired to be drawn, and enclosed with the circular is a slip bearing the words "Woe to von if you have any of the goods of these jurors in your house, for you, as they, will have the blood and sufferign of the innocent people on your head." The envelopes containing these documents bear the Manchester postmark, and the circular is signed "By Hook or by Crook." Similar circulars have been circulated throughout Tipperary. Their circulation hae created quite a sensation.—The circulars have been traced to Liverpool. Michael Hynes, Patrick Slater, printers in that city, and Patrick O'Brien, secretary of the local branch of the National League, were on Wednesday remanded by the Stipendiary Magistrate 'on a charge of conspiring to defeat the ends of justice. O'Brien ordered the circulars, to the number of 10000, and paid ten guineas for them. A printer, named Dalby, in the employment of liyhes said that O'Brien took away the circulars, which were afterwards posted in Manchester and Liverpool. Dr. Commins, M.P., who appeared for the prisoners, considered that the object they had in view was merely that of exposing the system of "jury packing."
TERRIBLE RAILWAY COLLISION IN
SCOTLAND.
SEVEN PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED

A terrible railway collision, which has resulted in 7 deaths occurred about midnight on Monday near Lockerbie, a station on that portion of the Caledonian line which lies between Glasgow and Carlisle. The mail train which leaves Glasgow for Carlisle at 9-15 in the eveeing, and which on Monday was more than usually freighted with returning holiday makers, dashed with terrible force into a goods train which had left Carlisle about ten minutes after nine. The front carriages of the mail train were telescoped, while the fireman and driver of the goods train and six other persons were killed. The mail train which ran into the goods car- riages consisted of first, second, and third class carriages. It was travelling at a great speed, having gone without stopping after leaving Glasgow until it reached Motherwell Junction, and again from Motherwell having gone without stoppage as far as the junction of Carstairs, where some passengers changed from the Dum- fries and Stranraer line. At Carstairs, also, passengers for Beatock and for the market town of Lockable are rtquired to change carriages so that they may be slipped at their desired stations while the train proceeds without stopping. Until this catastrophe Lockerbie was chiefly knee n to the public as a small market town of Dumfries, at which, how- ever, is held the largest lamb fair in all Scotland. It was when quite near to this place that the driver saw suddenly through the dam knees that a goods train was meeting him upon the same track of rails. So close were the trains that a desperate attempt to reverse the engines entirely failed to avert th ecollision. A great part of the mail train carriages (which were manufactured by the West of England Joint- stock Company, and designed especially for work on the joint London and North-Western and Caledonian system) were completely wrecked, and several of the passengers, who were booked for Carlisle, were killed by the shock. Many others in the mail train were fearfully shaken, and several had their limbs injured. The driver of the goods train, named Menzies, and his fireman, who both stuck to their engine, were also killed, and the contents of the carriager were scattered far and wide all along the line, while 5°01014 the trucke were heaped upon each other by the force of the concussion. The whole of the mail train did not equally suffer, some of the hind carriages being comparatively un- hurt. Without a moment's delay news of the collision was conveyed to Lockerbie, and also to other places rather more remote, and the telegrams to Carlisle very quickly resulted in the despatch- of a train with a number of doctors and with a large breakdown gang, who were quickly on the scene of the accident. The wounded were lifted into the doctors' train and were quickly conveyed to the nearest hospitable shelter. On every hand the utmost readiness to assist the sufferers was manifested. In Glasgow and Car- lisle a most painful sensation was produced, and crowds gathered at the various stations eagerly inquiring for the names of the killed and injured. Telegrams were of -course despatched from Glasgow and Carlisle to the superintendents at, the various stations on the combined systems of the London and North-Western and Caledonian Railways. At Ruston a telegram was received at about 2a.m. which briefly mentioned the occurrence, without explanation of the cause, or even details as to the number who bad lost their lives. Later on it was found that the accident was of an en more serious character than was at first supposed. The main cause of the catastrophe was the overrunning of the Lockerbie junction signals by a passenger train coming from Btranraer. This train ran .into a goods train which was proceeding on the up line, thus fouling both lines. Before any effective warning could be given the auxiliary mail train from Glasgow, coming at full speed, dashed into the wreckei waggons, which had been thrown by the first collision on to the up line. In an instant the alarm and ex- citement created by the first collision was intensified ten- fold. ' •

The scene presented at daybreak on Tuesday morning, after the passengers had all been remot ed from the train, was of a most extraordinary character. The express had been drawn by two engines. The first of these left the line about the middle of the station. On becoming detached from the train it rushed into the platform on the east side of tbe station, first of all crushing through a wooden plat- form for about twenty yards, then plunging for forty yards .farther into the solid masonry, of which the remainder of the platform is built. It then fell upon its side, emitting smoke, steam, and flame in a most alarming manner. It was the driver and fireman of this engine who were 'Hied. The other engine, with the express attached, rushed on for about 80 yards further, through the station, maintain- ing its position on the metals, but as it careered along the west side of the station nearly the whole of the carriages and waggons were thrown on to the other line. The Liverpool and Mancheerer portion of the train escaped with compara- tively little injury, hut eight or ten other carriages were terribly damaged. Windows, panels, and doors were broken almost entirely, seats were smashed completely, glass and pieces of carriage were strewn about in all directions, and the whole scene was one of terrible wreck. Gangs of work- men were engaged all the morning in removing the ruins of the carriages and restoring the line. Major Marindire of the Board of Trade, held on Wednes- day an inquiry which occupied nearly nine hours, during which the drivers, firemen, and guards, as well as the station master, signalmen, and other officials were examined at con- siderable length in regard both to the collision and the general working arrangements at Lockerbie station. Very minute inquiries were made respecting the causes of the colli- sion between the Dumfries train and the goods train, the particular points being whether the signals were against the train before it entered the cutting, or whether the signalman delayed warning the driver not to advance until he was within a comparatively short distance of the main line. As to he rzsult of the evidence on these points the railway officials and Major Marindin declined to make any statement, owing to the Procurator Fiscal's desire to keep the proceedings private. Major Marindin indicated that be did not anticipate he should require farther oral evidence, but that he had c tiled for copies of the regulations and some special rules foe certain classes of traffic. He did not anti- cipate his report would be prepared for ten days. A message was received on Wednesday requesting that the latest particulars with reference to the accident should be forwarded for the information of the Queen. Her Majesty desired also that she should be informed fully as to the pro- gress of the injured. The interest in their sufferings thus manifested by the Queen was highly appreciated by the sub- jects of Her Majesty'a sympathy, and the Royal coramane, was fully and immediately complied wit!),

The following official list has been supplied by Mr. Thompson, general managAr of the. Caledonian Railway Killed: Mr. Wynne, G laegow; Edward Annam, Glasgow; [ferny Mackenzie, Newcastle: James Foster, Carlisle; a .;hild named 131ackniere; Wm.. Menzies, engine driver; Lileorge Sowerby, fireman.—lnjured Seriously: Wm. Hay, traveller to %V. Ceiling and Co., Glasow ; Colin 'Ross, tfanchester (leg lyoken) • Daniel Campbell, Clydesdale Bank, Carlisle; George Forsyth Merchieton, Edinburgh; Rev. Mr. Halliday, Taypart; Mrs. Blacktnore. Slightly Injured: H. Carrol, Liverpool; Mrs. 'Yonne, Carlisle; Mr. md Mrs. Coirnack and child, Port Glasgow ; George Rae, Carlisle; Mr. Blackenore ; eqephen Spanon and Wallace '4ayers, boys, from Greenock •, Mr. and Mrs. Linn, Fort George; Mr. Liddell an I Andrew Taylor, District Bank, Manchester. David McLeod (with Hutchison and Dixon), Glasgow; Duncan McDougal, spirit merchant, Greenock. Mr. Wynne. whose name is mentioned amongst the list of those killed in the accideet was we understand, a cigar merchant in Glasgow, where he had been residing for tome few years. At the time the accident happened he was journeying to town in order to be present at the funeral of his mother, which %vas fixed for yeaterday (Friday). The 'nether. who was 87 years of age, died on Sunday, and Mr. Wynne, who was the eldest son. was immediately telegraphed for. Two brothers and two sist.ers, all unmarrie(t, were living with Mts. Wynne, while there is also a married sister. The first information of the sad news reached the bereaved family about five o'clock on Tuesday morning, in the shape of a telegram stating that a collision had occurred, and that the deceased was included in the list of those injured. A sub- aft:pent telegram reached the relatives of the deceased about half-past seven, stating that be bad died.

div.head: DYNAMIIE CONSPIRACY.
div.p: THE DYNAMIIE CONSPIRACY.

The-man Dalton. who had been charged with Dr. Galla- gher and others with conspiracy and was discharged on Fri- day by the Bow-street police magistratts, was on Saturday charged before Mr. R the Lives pool stipendiary magi- strate, with having in his possession explosive substances with intent to commit a felony, and also with censPiring with Denis Deasey, Patrick Flannigan, and others to com- mit felonies. It was stated for the proseeutkn that in a pocket-book found in the prisoner's possession was the address of Daniel O'Herlihy, who is already in custody on a serious charge in connection with the dynamite plots. Another piece of evidence will be that this pocket-book con- tains a number of prescriptions and directions in the pri- soner's writing, one of which describes in exact detail the articles found upon Deasey, one of O'llerlihv's associates. There is a promise of mach more damaging evidence than this. The prisoner was remanded for a week.—lnformation in the possession of the police authorities has led to the adoption of precautions against any attempt to rescue-VI, prisoners Deasey, Flannigan, O'Herliby, Featherstone, and Dalton, who are at present detained in Walton Gaol in con- nection with the dynamite discoveries.

div.head: OPENING OF THE FISHERIES EXHIBITI.iN.
div.p: OPENING OF THE FISHERIES EXHIBITI.iN.

The International Fisheries Exhibition in London was opened on Saturday by the Mace of Wales. The Princess accompanied His Royal Highness, and nearly all the mem- bers of the Royal Family were present. The•ceremeny was attended with a courtly display which was originally in- tended in honour of the Queen, but Her Majesty was not sufficiently recovered from herxecent accident to be present. There can be no doubt now that crowds of visitors will be attracted to South Kensington during the summer months. ' All parts of the United Kingdom are represented, many of our own colonies, and most foreign countries in which fish- ing is an industry. The British section is, of course, the most prominent and important, but it is not improbable that the Chinese will prove the moat attractive. Amongst the classes embraced in the catalogne are sea and fresh water fishing, the condition of fishermen, the conamercial and eco- nomic position of the industry, pisCcaltetre, natural history as shown in numerous aquaria, and the history and litera- ture of fishing as illustrative of fishery laws and commerce. In addition to competitive exhibits there are also loan collections on view, inclining many art specimens and wondrous curiosities, and all ' coming within the scope of the foregoing classes. The Duke of Richmond, as President of the Exhibition, read an address to the Prince of Wales, in which it, wee stated that the buildings, large as they are, had proved hardly adequate to contain the vast contributione, w4i4 have poured in. Every article of ceininerce yielded by fisheries is represeetc.d, and the agencies lay wlitdß these articles are transported, distributed, and prepared for use are exemplified. The consumer may not only becomeatc- quainted with the organisation of a fish market, btit may also forrn a judgment, based on practical examination of the vast possibilities open to judicious fish cookery. It examination, been the especial aim of the Committee to direct the atten- tion of the public at large to the perils and hardships necessarily connected with the mode of life of those sea fishermen by whose labours they profit so largely; and they were not without hope tkat the creation of a general in- terest in their affairs may have a favoui able influence on the condition of the fishing population. It was also intimated that an International Congress for the discussion of ques- tions connected with fish and fisheries will be held. 'I he Prince of Wales suit- ably replied. A banquet was held at the Fishmongers' Hall in the evening, in celebrition of the opening of the Exhibition. Mr. Humphrey Foidham (prime warden) pre- sided. The guests included the Prince ot Wales, the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Con- naught, the Duke of Teck, and the Lord Mayor. The Prince of Wales, in the course of his speech, announced that the honorary freedom of the Fishmongers' Corporation would be conferred on Mr. BirkbPck, M.P., who had done so much to promote the Exhibition. The Doke of Edinburgh. in pro- posing the toast of "The foreign Arlib,atliallorB and repre- sentatives," mentioned that during his absence abroad the Prince of Wales had undertaken to read a paper which he had prepared on the euhject of fisheries aryl the fishing population of the United Kingdom, the information in which wet derived entirely from personal experience during the period of his command of the Royal Naval Reserve. The Duke of Connaught and the Duke of Albany were also amongst the speakers.

div.head: POPE AND THE IRISH BISHOPS.
div.p: THE POPE AND THE IRISH BISHOPS.

The following is a text of a letter addressed by Cardinal Simeoni, Prefect of the Propaganda Fide, to the Irish Bishops:—" Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord,--What- ever judgment may be formed on Mr. Parnell and his ideas, it is certain that many of his partisans have followed in many cases a line of conduct which is absolutely con- trary to what the Sovereign Pontiff has set forth in his let- ters to his Eminence the Cardinal Archbishop of Dublin, and to what is contained in the instructions of the Sacred Congregation of the Propaganda unanimously accepted by the Irish Bishops at their last assembly in Dub'in. In fact, pursuant to these prescriptions, the Irish are permitted to seek the amelioration of their unfortunate condition, they ' are allowed to struggle for their rights, but they are ever to observe this Divine precept, that we roust seek first the king- dom of God and his righteousness; that it is shameful to defend a just cause by unjust means. Now it belongs to the whole of the clergy, and principally to the Bishops, to appease the over-excited spirits of the multitude, and to bring them back by means of opportune exhortations to the justice and moderation necessary in all things, lest, carried away by their passions, they should judge falsely of the advantages to be reaped from events, and rest their hopes for the public welfare on shameful crimes. It follows, there- fore, that it is not allowable for any member of the clergy to depart from these rules nor to mix himself up in, or favour I an agitation which is contrary to prudence and to the duty incumbent on the clergy of restating peace to souls. It is certainly not forbidden to collect sums.of money to relieve the condition of tae Irish, but in accordance with the injunction of the Holy See above quoted those subscrip- tions are to be absolutely reprobated which lire publicly announced with the object of inflaming the passions of the people, and of thus being able te.turn them easily to the account of violent and seditious desTns. Such subscriptions are above all to be abstained from when it is clear that hatred and dissensions are aroused by them, that distinguished persons are loaded with insults, that never in any way are censures pronounced against the crimes and murders With which wicked men stain themselves; and es- pecially when it is asserted that the measure of true patriot- ism is in proportion to the amount of money given or re- fused, so as to bring the people under the pressure of intimi- dation. This being established. your lordship must compre- hend that the subscription called the Parnell Testimonial Fund cannot be approved by the Sacred Congregation of the Propaganda, and that it is not allowable for ecclesiastics, and especially for bishops, to recommend or favour it in any way whatever meanwhile.—Given at the Palace of Propa.- ganda, May 11, 1881"

FINANCE is a favourite theme with Tory orators, who never seem tired of endeavour- ing to make their deluded followers under.: stand that the present Government is vet' much more extravagant than their predecesi sors were. How far they succeed we do Oa pretend to know. Not long ago there was sharp passage-at arms between Lord Gn t.'s' HAMILTON and Sir JOHN LUBBOCK. On tb? very question, the former of whom essayed Ic, , prove that the expenditure of the prestens Government is a good many millions in excesct of what it was when the Conservatives office. Sir JOHN LUBBOCK had no difficut-e whatever in showing that if the sum paid by tu,t present Government in liquidation of debt I°4 by their predecessors be deducted, as it Ours. to be, from the expenditure, then the gru.sil expenditure of the present Government No" compare very favourably indeed with the e%; penditure of the last Administration. It 11 be remembered that when the present CI-lA< CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER introduced lue,' Budget this year he took occasion to rentnv some of the fallacies regarding finance fro,llle the Tory mind, and as his figures had ti'f effect—conclusive on the face of thent—tt putting the Government in a favourable lig"A before the public Mr. CHILDERS was assaile' with a torrent Of abuse for introducing de; bateable matter into his statement. SincAt then Mr. GLADSTONE has given us the bene" of his critical examination of the accounts' and as the figures which he has quoted havf, never been challenged, though they have ne" been before the public for some time, wet think them of sufficient importance to warran us reproducing them in a limited W; It is very desi.able that they shOw' not be lost sight of ; and they are so strikingly arranged that they canon`, fail to leave a deep impression upon those who care to peruse them. In the la!', three wars of the late Governineu`' from 1877 to 1880, the gross 1; penditure was £253,300 000 ; while in t"- • first three years of the present Governments from 1880 to 1883, the expenditure wasi ' £259,000,000, an apparent increase (3' £5,700,000. When, however, we deduct the "expenses of collection, because," as Mr', GLADSTONE says, 'Sour establishments service are not establishments of taxation, the expenditure of the late Government for, the three years in question stands afr £229,693,000, while the expenditure of the present Government is found to be, £233.44.8,000. There is still a balance again-` us, but that is reduced by this process of de- duction from £5,700,000 to £3,755,000. balance will presently disappear altogether The nation, just in the same measure as• all, individual, is all the richer for the pavinen` of its debts, and therefore it is necessary tc: take into this reckonins , the money spell' annually in squaring old 'scores. In the three years of the late Government the real par merit of debt was £7,987 000, while in the three years of the present Government the real payment of debt has been £z0,448,000. If these items be deducted from the total C' penditure given above, the Conservative e,! penditure will stand at £221,706,000, and the "' Liberal expenditure at £213.000,000, a balance in the Liberal favour now £8,706,000. If the investigation of te accounts be carried still further, it is not di"" cult to increase this balance very consider" ably. For instance, the Liberals have had t° make repayment to India of, in round nurn: bers, £3,000,000 in respect of the burclet recklessly and needlessly cast upon her bY Afghan war; and if to this be added, whjcps we think may fairly be done, the war charg,T, in South Africa and Egypt, which were incurred in dealing with the state of affaLr" handed over to the Liberals by the late Government, and which amount in the aggre:r gate to £600,460,000, the balance "41; £8,706,000 is at once increased el_ x 8,000,000, a sum which faithfully rePr,e sents the actual balance in favour of the a' Liberals on their management of the expenss of the country during the past three Years 01 compared with the previous three years _0 Conservative management. There is .te denying the fact that the expenditure of the country is very high, much higher than it wa_ . some years ago, and if any means can devised for reducing it the present Gove. to; ment are pledged to give effect to them; Du;.; it is interesting to ascertain what mainly responsible for this increase. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DIMS'S IN LANCASHIRE.—The return made up on Wednesday at the office of the Clerk of the Peace at Preston shows the during last week there was one fresh farm affected in Amounderness Hundred, four in the Hundred of Blackburn, two in Salford Hundred, and one in West D..rby Hundred. Not a single farm was declared free, so that the numb,,r movr infected in the county is 46, as against 33 in the previous week. There were 21 fresh cattle affected in the Amounderness Hundred; Blackburn, 27; Salford, 11; and West Derby, two, making a total of 61; but 70 cattle rec wered, letvi rig 132 now suffering from the disease, as compared with 141 at the end of the previous week.

PROTECTING THE PUBLICANS AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Polk!! Court on Wednesday, before Messrs. John Brundrit and Alfred Thom as, Henry Jones, a boatman, was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of Tnotnae Harrison, Stanley Arms, and also with refusing to gait. Oa Monday evening the defendant entered the house aiel asked to be served wiih liquor,.but the landlord, seeing his drunken state, declined to do so. whereupon the de- fendant created a disturbance. P.S. Whalley was sent fer, and c nuing on the scene ej •cted the defendant, who is a big, powerful fellow, with the aid of the landlord.—Mr. Brun- drit add the Bench were determined, support the pubicans in maintaining order in their houses, and people brought be- fore them charged with offences of this kind would be severely dealt will. The defendant was fined £1 anircosts 8e 41, or a month's hard labour.—At the same court Ellen Nolan was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on Monday night. RETIEW OF THE LANCASHIRE HUESARS.-011 Saturday Lord D 4. Ker, of the 10'h Royal Hussars (the Prince of Wales regiment), reviewed the Lancashire Hussars at South- port. At the conclusion of the inspection, Lord Ker said he wished to express to them the very great satisfaction which he felt in all he had seen that day. He had always heard of the Lancashire Hussars as a regiment wertby the example of all yeomanry regiments, but he mast confess he was not prepared to see what he had that day. He was very much pleased to see the horses they brought on parade, as well as the stateof the saddlery. He hid not a word to say against the recruits of the Lancashire Hussars. They were a fine body of men, and he only wished he could see recruits of the same stamp in the regular army. The attention of the men in the ranks was remarkable. They were fully ready now to take part in all brigade movements of the regular cavalry. He was exceedingly delighted to find that that regiment bad gone in for the course of signalling, and he hoped more signal men would qualify. He hoped that as long as be was inspecting officer he would find them continue from good to better. POOH RATES AND PAUPERISM.—The following figures have been supplied to the Local Government Board by the clerks to the guardians of the county of Lancaster showing their receipts and expenditure for the year 1882 :—ln this county, with a population of 3.485,611, £753,975 was ex- pended in relief to the poor. against £782,756 in 1881, being a decrease of £28,809, or 3.7 per cent. The receipts from poor rates amount to £1,506,976, from the Treasury £32,411, and £56,676 from other sources. The expenditure amounted to £1,592,381. Of this £213,404 was for mainte- nance, £174,175 for out-relief, £93,631 fer the maintenance of lunatics, £57,821 for workhouse loans, £106,598 for salaries, dm., of officers, and £108328 for other expenses. £2.684 for law proceedings, £621.860 for the police, £35,315 for highway boards. £16.250 for burial boards, £7,288 for sanitary purposes, £39,598 for school boards, £1,468 for school committees, £11,914 for fees to clergy- men and registrars, £10,170 fer vaccination, £13,752 for Parliamentary. ke:, registration, £9,938 for Assessment Committees, £7OOB for school fees for non-pauper children, £55.181 for all other purposes. The loans outstanding at the end of 1882 amounted to £68,816. div.p: • THE EXAMINER, SA T.LIRDA.Y, MAY 19, 1883 THE FARNWORTH BUTCHER AND SINGULAR BOAT ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY THE POLICEMAN. RUNCORN. AUTHORITY. CURIOUS CASE. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse Before Mr. 11. L. Eves and Mr. Jetn l!r.ler, at Widnes A MOTHER AND TWO CHILDREN DROWNED. on Tuesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there . _ _

Petty Sessions, on I'Velnesiay, Oharki T.,ylor, butcher, Church-street, Farrworth. was clnrg,A wit 11 !.:e in g drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap.—lnsp...-ct,.'r Btrnett said that about a quarter to four o'clock oa 3 afternoon of Monday, the 16th April, he met the def,niant it Birchfield- road, farnworth, in charge of a 1101,' :07,! The defen- dant, who was drunk and lvin 4 on hi:, it 1;2!-- in the trap, was q•iite incapable, and the inspector jurniwd in' o the vehicle. _

'lle lifted the defendant into a sitting posi,j2n and endea- voured to drive him home, but after driving some distance down the road the defendant became very awkward. He at- tempted to seize the reins, and the inspector found that lie could not drive in consequence, and returned to the Black Horse, where he knew P.C. Palmer was. The defendant was in a helpless state of drunkenness, and was unable to sit up, so he was lifted out of the trap. Inspector Barnett instructed the constable to take charge of the defendant, and himself drove the horse and trap home. The horse was a spirited one, and if the defendant had not been removed from the trap he would either have been thrown or fallen out.— P.C. Bryan Palmer was then charged with assauTtin.g Mr. _ _ _

-5 Taylor, and he was defended by Mr. Knowles, solicitor. Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, represented Mr. Tiylor, and in his opening statement observed that early on Monday morning, the 16th April, Mr. Taylor went to Liverpool Cattle Market, travelling the distance in his own trap. After tran- sacting his business be had some drink, and on his way home be called at the Bin.. Ball, Huyton, and at the Black Horse, near Rainhill. At the latter place he visited the asylum, where he saw his son, who was confined there.

Mr. Taylor admitted that he was the worse for think, but he was not so bid but that he could drive, and he did so properly to the Black Hotel at Farnworth. A man whom he had picked up on the way alighted there. The landlord of the house refused to serve Mr. Taylor with beer, and be replied "All right," and immediately drove away. At the corner of the street Palmer, who was attired in plain clothes, was standing, but he took no notice of Mr. Taylor, who, it must therefore be aseumed, was driving -properly. After he had proceeded about two or three hundred yards, Inspector Birnett met him, jumped into the trap, arid in- stead of taking Mr. Taylor home, which would sern to have been the more reasonable course, turned the horse's head and returned to where Pilmer was standing. inspector Barnett told Palmer to pull Mr. Taylor out, and the con- stable, seizing the latter by the legs, dragvil him from the trap to the ground, his body coming in contact with the step. Palmer then took hold of Mr.' Taylor by the arms, shook him several times, and ultimately gave him a push, which, no doubt assisted by the drink, caused him to fall heavily backwards to the ground. His head was cut open, a wound two inches long being inflicted. Apparently frightened at what he had done, the constable accompanied Mr. Taylor half way home, the latter's son coming up when that distance had been traversed. Mr. Taylor lost a great deal of blood, and was compelled to remain in bed until the Sunday, but erysipelis set in, and he was confined to bed for another week. Mr. Swift's state- ment was corroborated by the complainant, Joha Birket, teamsman, Farnworth ; —. Ellison, landlord of the Black Horse, Farnworth ; Mrs. Elizabeth Beasley, of Bold; Wm. Dntton, toolmaker; and Robert Taylor, son of the com- plainant. These witnesses saw the occurrences at various distances, Dutton stating he was 70 yards distant, but like Mrs. Beasley he stated he saw Mr. Taylor's head rebound from the pavement when he was pushed to the ground.—Mr. Knowles, for the defence, said tke police had a difficult duty to perform, and they must he protected. The complainant admitted that if he had not been summoned for being drunk, he would never have brought this case before their worships, and his action therefore savoured of vindictive- ness. It was not likely that a policeman, under the eyes of his inspector, would he guilty of an offence of this hind, for it would mean his dismiss il from the force. He should have no hesitation in asking the Bench, after they had heard the evidence to dismiss the case.—lnspector Barnett was called, and stated that when Mr. Taylor was removed from the trap he held him by the coat collar, and the policeman held his feet. The horse was "jumping about," and Mr. Taylor fell to the ground. Palmer raised him three times, and then he struggled as if he wanted to get to the trap. At that time Palmer had his arms round Mr. Taylor's body, but releasing his grasp, the latter fell to the ground and cut his head slightly. Palmer did not exceed his duty in any way, but on the contrary did all he could to help the man. —Charles Macbeth and Charles Smith, insurance agents, corroborated the Inspector's statement. The complainant was very drunk, and the policeman did not exceed his duty.—Mr. Evans said tl:a Bench had decided to dismiss the case against ttn officer. The injury Mr. Taylor had re- ceived was tlie result of his own conduct, and they were sur- prised at a man occupying his respectable position being in such a conditien. He would be fined ss. and costs for being drunk.—Mr. Swift observed that Mr. Taylor bad paid a doctor's bill amounting to £2 10.
MURDEROUS ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN POLICEMAN.

Before Mr. John Brundrit and Captain C. W. Hazle- burst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph Heys, James Clabby, and John Henry O'Neil, young men, were charged with assaulting P.C. Morris whilst in the execution of his duty. Heys pleaded guilty, as did also Clabby, with the reservation that the constable deserved it ; and O'Neil pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Johnson (magistrates clerk) said Clabby's vias a plea of guilty, but Superinten- dent Williamson remarked that if there was anything against the police he had no wish to screen them, and preferred to take it as a plea of not guilty.—This wat done, and P.C. Morris was called. He stated that on the previous night about 11-20 be was on duty near the Post Office when he heard a person shouting " Murder." He went into Mersey - street, where he found a man bleeding from the face, who told him that the men standing arround had been kicking him. The prisoners were there. He ordered them to go quietly away, but they would not, and he took in custody a drunken man who was shouting. Immediately about six men rushed upon him and knocked himself and the prisoner to the ground. He was savagely kicked by about 12 persons, and his prisoner was rescued. He could not see ivho kicked him, but he had three or four wounds on his head, and one on his back. O'Neil struck him in the face with his fist. There were a lot of women there, who, he believed, " belonged " to the fair ground.—Mr. Brundrit asked if he said anything or did anything to provoke the prisoners? No, sir. I only ordered them away, and they would not go.—Samuel Edwards, labourer, Pool-lane, stated that hearing a noise in the "Rookery" he went there. He heard the con- stable order the wen off, when they rushed at him, knocked him down, and kicked him, witness tried to help him, and also got kicked. Someone behind shouted "Give it him, Clabby," and he saw Clabby kick Morris Had not witness protected the constable's head the latter would have been much more severely injured. —William Abrams, blacksmith, Cooper-street, deposed that he went into the Strand with some women at half-past 10 o'clock. The prisoners were al sa in the house, and on leaving at 11 o'clock O'Neil and Clabby struck a man in the street. The officer then came up and asked them to go home, giving one man a little bit of a shove. They all then rushed upon Lhim and kicked him, and witness ran to the police station. Sergeant Walley came on the scene and arrested Heys, who had been on the floor with P.C. Morris. Clabby and O'Neil both kicked the officer.—Agnes Lewis, a single woman, residing in Trinity - street, deposed to seeing O'Neil strike the constable in the face. The constable did not do anything to provoke the men.—By Superintendent William- son: Morris had O'Neil in his custody, but Clabby struck at him. O'Neil's shirt was torn". Dr. MacDougall said he had examined P.C. Morris that morning. On his head were three bruises which might have been produced by kicks. These was behind the left ear. The left side of his face and 11 his hand were scratched, and there was a bruise in tbe 11 middle of the back. All the bruises bad the appearance of having been caused by kicks, a great deal of violence must have been used.—Clabby stated that the constable seized a young fellow and put him on the floor before he could speak a word. lie and his fellow prisoners were stopping the constable from hurting the young fellaw. O'Neil denied that he was on the scene at all. At the time it took place he was some distance away talking to a man who worked at the locks. He had not the witness present.—Mr. Brundrit said if he had told the police they would hlve seen that the witness was present.—O'Neil : The policeman didn't forget to bit me with his stick.—Mr. Brundrit said it was quite time that young men such ea the prisoners were taught that they could not take the law into their own hands, and as an example to themselves and their associates each prisoner would be imprisoned for six weeks, with hard labour.—Clabby: Thank you, sir.—As Heys was being taken to the cells, he was heard to threaten the witness Wm. Abrams. He was again placed in the dock, and charged with using threats. Abrams stated that when being taken to the cells, Heys shook his flat in his face, and said " By Christ, I will warm your head when I come out."—P.C. Walley and P.C. Boesons corroborated, and the Bench bound the prisoner over to keep the peace for six months in two sureties of £lO each, or, in default, two months' bard labour. The sureties not being forthcoming, the prisoner went to gaol, and will have to serve a total term ci three months and two weeks.
