At the close six new pledges were taken. STEALING PIGEONS IT ST. HELENS.-011 Saturday, at the St. Helens Police Court, a lad named Richard Jones was charged with stealing six pigeons, valued at Bs., the pro- perty of Thomas Topping.—lt appeared that the prisoner had, on the night of the 9th instant, paid a vimt to prosecu- tor's pigeon cote, at 32, Fenton-street, and carried away the pigeons, and afterwards attempted to sell them. He was apprehended about one o'clock, on Saturday, when return- ing home w‘th his mother. The prisoner, it may be stated, is the son of John Jones, of Oxford-street, who is at present in gaol as a punishment for noisy conduct in the streets. —Prisoner, who bad been previously convicted, was !sent to gaol for a month.

A shocking drowning fatality occurred at Runcorn Docks on Wednesday evening. About a quarter to six, the schooner Cwnavon, lying in the Tidal Dock, was discharg- ing Dart of her cargo of huge masses of stone into the nar- row canal boat Ant, which lay alongside. At the bottom of the boat, it is stated, a block of stone weighing seven tons was placed, and the remainder of the cargo consisted of

stones varying from two to five tons weight. The last block weighing two and a half tons was lowered down the schooner's side into the Ant, and the captain Wm. Musker, who was superintending the loading, remov,d the crane chain from the stone. There are conflicting statements as to what now took place, but the heavy mass suddenly shifted, and disturbing the equilibrium of the boat caused it to capsiz till with water, and sink. The captain escapel itntn.rsion by grasping the crane chain, but confined in the boat's small cabin were his unfortunate wife aged 30, and two boys, aged respectively four years and 16 months. Under these circumstances it was impossible to save them, the only means of getting t.) the boat b.ing by lowering the . ,

water in the dock, which is very deep: it took half an hour to accmplish this, and during thai time workmen were standing helplessly on the dock side watching the water slowly sink. When the big tvlcame visible no time wis lost in descending to the cabin, where the poor mother with a dead child on each arm was fourri cold and lifele's.. The family belonged to Barnton, near Northwich. Until a few minutes before the accicien'., Ms. Masker had been on the schooner deck, but she theo descended, with her two young -
children into her husband's boat to make the tea for her family. One of her buys, about 8 years of age, refused, however, to leave the schooner, and was thus miraculously saved.

wore also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, jowl Lock- wood, INtessrs. John Ashton, Henry Lowe, Joseph Knowles, John Carnpkin, James Derbyshire, W. Whitlow, J. G. Hamilton, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). SERIOUS OUTBREAK OF FEVER AT WESTON POINT. Mr. David John, locum tenens for Dr. Bride, wrote as follows :—I have to report an outbreak of scirlet fever at _ _

Weston Pint. There are altogether three families attacked. I have visited each case, and have endeavoured to ascertain the source of the disease. The first Case occurred at a pro- vision shop occupied by John Dunbavin, whose wife and six children suffered from the disease. My inquiries as to source of infection in this instance have led to no definite result other than it might have been carried here from some distance by an infected person. Owing to the fact that it is a shop, strangers would therefore be more likely to visit it than any other house in the neighbourhood. As regarded the other cases, one occurs at a house in West-street occu- pied by James Whitby, two of whose cbVdren have been attacked. And the remaining case at . _

a house near the school occupied hi Richard Sh iw in which his child aged fire years is now convales- ing. As regtrds the source of infection of the last two elms, I have no doubt but that it is clearly traceable to the Cyst case. lam glad to ha able to state that all the patients are now'convalescent, with the exclation of one of John Dutibavin's children, who is suffering from a sequila of scarlet fever. The usual m.-asu!es as regards disinfection and isolation have been .thcrouubly carried out by your

inspector, Mr. James Farrington. I hopz.. by this 'Means there will 134 no further spread of the disease."—Mr. Farring- ton was ordered to take the usual measures in the matter. TUE ANT4OIiUS WATIIII SUPPLY. The Inrscrobt of NUISANCES submitted a report respect- ing the water supply of that portion of Antrobus, situate near Antrobus school. He stated that the total number of houses, including the school, was 9, with a population of about 101, comprising 22 adults and 72 children, including the scholars attending the school. At the present time the whole of this population was without the water supply owing to the Action taken by the owner of a pump and well, on which the people had for a long time depended. S)me years ago, previous to his (Mr. Farring- ton's) term of office, a well was sunk and a pump erected at the roads' le at the expense of the late Rev. George Eaton, for the benefit of the portion of the township in question, but owing to the well not, being sufficiently deep, together with the defective drainage near the well, he was given to understand that the water was not of a good quality, the well was closed, and the pump was now out of order. tinder the provisions of the Health Act, 1875, he (Mr. Farrington) considered the pump and well now as the property of the Sanitary Authority, and he suggested that the well should be opened and examined with a viee to its being sunk to a greater depth. He believed that if this were done the quality of the water would be greatly improved, as the water in the immediate nsighbuurhood fully confirmed such a belief.— After some consideratiin Mr. Farrington was instructed to carry out his suggestion, and to report to the next meeting. —This concluded the business.

div.head: TILE INQUEST'.
div.p: TILE INQUEST'.

Mr. Ridewav, the coroner, held an inquest on the bodies at the Bridgewater Arms Hotel, yesterday morning. Mr. R Wright was foreman of the jury; and Mr. J. Meadowcroft was preseut as a repreeent itive of the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Co. Mr. R B. Tuft was also present. The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, shortly reletef the facts of the accident, which, he said, were very simple, and the jury would have no difficulty in coming to the cenclu- sion as to what was the cause of death. The point to which he would specialty direct their attention would be whether there was any negligence on the part of any person who had anything to do with the loading of the boat. Since he bad been coroner for this district, the was the most painful in- quest he had ever held. The facts seemed to be simple, but when they thought of the mother and two children being drowned without a chance of being helped, for it appeared they were in the cabin of the boat at the time, there was something very sad about the case. He trusted the jury would give the case their careful attention, and say if there was any blame attaching to anybody or not. William Masker, living in Princess Park, Bernton, near Northwich, said he was a boatman. The bodies, of which the jury had had the view, were those of his wife Emily, and his sons Ardena and Robert. On Wednesday afternoon he was loading his narrow boat " Ant " with stone in the Tidal Dock. The stone was being discharged from the schooner Cwnavon. His boat was registered to hold 35 tons, which, however, she never carried, and on the present oc- caeion Wee ledeu with 31 tons Of stone. The lest stone lowered into the boat by the crane weighed about twO foes and a half, and a skid was put under one end. He then moved the crane chain to one end of the stone so that he could remove the skid. He removed the skid and placed a smeller one under, and then shouted "lower." The order was obeyed by the man at the crane, and the stone gave " bit of a lift," slipped about three inches towards the side of the boat, which heeled over. He called out to the man at the crane to "heave up," but before he could do so the boat had filled with water and sank. The reason the stone could not he " heaved up " was because there was too mnch "stack" chain out. He made an attempt to reach his wife and children, who were in the cabin, but it was impossible to save them. He was almost up to the head in water when he jumped up the schooner side. There were three men at the crane, but be (witness) was placing the stones himself.—The Foreman : Do you think the mis- hap would have occurred if there had been a competent man at the crane? No; I don't think it would.—Were the three men at the crane sober? Yes.—Being Whitsuntide that is the reason I ask. A juryman wishes me to ask did the man at the crane lower the stone gently when you removed the chain from the centre, or whether he lowered it too quick? When the stone got on the boat be lowered it as fast as he could, and then when I shouted out " heave up" there was too much slack clrain.—The Coroner: How far would the stone have to lower" after you removed the skid? Not over five inches.—Mr. Sinned (a juryman) said that if the stone had only that distance to lower, the boat must have been top heavy for the stone to capsize it. The Coroner: Before this last stone was lowered was the boat quite level? As straight as the table is.—A Juryman said anybody used to handling heavy weights, would know that when a great stone of two tons was lowered into a boat almost loaded, if it only meved the slightest, the effect would be great.—ln answer to the Coroner the witness said the man at the break of the crane lowered the stone gently, and then allowed the chain to run well out.—The Coroner: How were you trying to get the stone in position on the boat? The witness replied that he was standing at one side of the stone, which he pushed as well as be could with his hands, and when he shouted to the man at the crane to lower, he was a minute before he did so, and the stone came to him about four inches. In answer to further questions the witness said the man who lowered the last stone, had lower- ed several others, and he had occasion to tell him that if he did not mind he would have the boat over. The man, whom he did not know, only laughed. A juryman fetid they must remember that the loading of the last few stones was the most critical time. The Coroner pointed out to witness that he was responsible for the proper loading of his boat, and if he found he had an incompetent man at the crane he could refuse to go on with the work.—Mr. Meadowcroft (to witness) : What sort of a skid was the second one you used? It was one of my old timber beads which had been broken off. It was not square. It was thicker at one end than the other, and was the shape of a wedge. The Foreman : Well, that is the reason that the stone slipped—Witness the stone did not slip on the wedge at all.—By Mr. Meadowcroft: He told the men on the schooner that if they would lower that stone his boat would be right.—The Coroner: How far from the end of the stone was the chain after you had put small skid under? About six inches. That being so, supposing the crane chain bad been quite tight, and the men had obeyed your order to heave up, what would have been the result? It would have held the boat from going down. If it had been raised one inch the boat would have recovered. He had been captain of a narrow boat for five years. He did not know that there was any restriction, or any rules as to what narrow boats must carry.—ln answer to Mr. Meadowcroft, witness said when he removed the first skid, the stone was stationary at one end, and did not move. —Mr. Meadowcroft: How do you account for the stone slipping if it remained stationary at one end ?—The Coroner said from Musker's statement, he thought the stone bad twisted. Witness stated, in reply to Mr. Meadowcroft, that the stone was lowered nicely into the boat in the first instance, and one end of it was not lifted again. George Tomlinson, of 18, Surrey-street, Runcorn, said he was a weigher for the Bridgewater Nevigation Company. He assisted in loading the Ant on Wednesday. He was counting the stones and seeing the chain put properly round them. He saw the last stone, weighing about 2tone 10ewt., taken from the schooner and lowered to the boat. The boat sank three or four inches when the stone was lowered on to it. He could not see what Mufeeer did with the skids, but he saw him move the chain a little, and. then heard him call to the men to "heave up," so that he could move the chain. The men did so, and Masker did something which he (witness) ceuld not see, and he called out, "Lower." Witness then called, "Lower steady." The man at the crane lowered steady, and witness saw the stone setile down on the boat. He then saw Mocker unhook the chain. The boat was all right, and he turned round to tell the lad to meve the crane. He then heard Masker shout, " Heave up," and saw the boat sinking down. The boat was not overloaded. It was a foot out of water, and the larger stones were put at the bottom of the boat.

Musker was recalled, and questioned by the Coroner, but persisted in saying that he did not unhook the chain. Tomlinson, in answer to the foreman, said the mate of the vessel was at the brake of the crane. He was a capable man.—By Mr.Meadowcroft : The stone was lowered steadily. He could not have done it better himself.

David Roberts, Milford Haven, said he was mate of the Cwmavon, and was helping to load the narrow boat on Wed- nesday last. He understood the working of a crane, and lowered the last stone. He could not 986 what Musker, who was on the narrow boat, did when he was lowering the stone, but afterwards saw bira unhook the chain, and directly afterwards the boat capsizad. He had not been used to lowering into a narrow boat, and could not say whether the boat was properly loaded or not. Richard Edwards, seaman on the schooner, corroborated ; and the Coroner briefly directed the jury, who, after so Tle consideration, returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."

THE EARLESTOWN MUSICAL SOCIETY.—AIiont 13 of the members and friends of the Etrlestown Musical Society had a very pleasant picnic to Frodsham and Overton Hills on Thursday. The party wore conveyed thither in a wagon- ette, leaving Earlestown in the forenoon. The weather was exceedingly favourable for the outing, and all thoroughly enjoyed themselves. The company arrived home at a late hour in the evening. CRUELLY PLATING A Metax.—.4t the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Adam Clegg was charged with cruelly working a mare on the 28;h ult.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—lnspector Campbell, of the Royal Suciety for the Prevention of Cruelty to Aniinals stated that on the date named he saw the defendant driving a black mare attached to a cab going in the direction of Haydoek Park The defendant was very severely PI igging the animal with the whipstock, and was driving too fast for him (witness) to overtake him. When he returned to Newton Station in a short time afterwards, he examined the mare and found aereral bad marks of the whip along the loins. He pointed these out to the defendant, who said he would not do it again, and he hoped witness would not take any notice of it.—The defendant was Ened 103. and come.

The Rev. Canon Barclay presided at the fortnightly meet- ing held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were present the Revs. J. W. A. Tanner, John Lockwood, Messrs., Jno. Ashton, C. Reynolds, J.P., ex-officio, Jno. Highfield, Jas. Darbyshire, Jas. Mclntyre, W. Whittaker. C. Munn- field, J. Campkin, H. Lowe, E. A. Wallington, T. Norman, C. Rigby, Joseph Knowles, Geo. Percival, Geo. Whitlow, Win. Pickering, Joseph Smith, J. G. Hamilton, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). A letter was read from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of a communication from the Board in which they requested their sanction to the proposals of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union to send three Roman Catholic children,l who were at present in the workhouse to the Roman Catholic school at Pantasaph, near Holywell, at a cost not exceeding four shillings per week for each child, The school referred to had been certified by the Board under the statute 25 and 26 Victoria, and it was therefore com- petent for the Guardians to send children to it without the sanction of the Board in individual circumstances. If, how- ever, the amount to tie paid by the Guardians for the main- tenanc3 of each child if a child in the school exceeded the cost of the maintenance in the workhouse, it would be neces- sary for the managers of the school to apply to the Board to sanction the higher rate of payment under section 13 of the 45 and 46 Victoria,—On the motion of Hr. MCINTYRE, a scheme propounded by Mr. Jones for dealing with the storm drainage of the workhouse was approved. On the re- commendation of the Finance Committee, moved by the Rev. JOHN LOCKWOOD, accounts amounting to £l2B 19s 8d were ordered to he paid.—The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board inquiring whether Mr. Tipping, late assistant overseer for Walton, had paid to the treasurer the sum surcharged upon him at the recent audit. The letter concluded "Do you think it possible proceedings could be avoided by giving him notice that if the money is no paid before Friday next, a summons will be issued ?" The CLERK said he was unable to answer that question, as owing to Bank Holiday the treasurer's book had not come in.—The relief business WAS then proceeded with.

GOOD TEMPLARISNI IN SOUTH- WEST LANCASHIRE. DISTRICT LODGE MEETING. A quarterly session of the South-West Lancashire Dis- trict Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Good Templars' Hall, George-street, St. Helens, on Saturday last. There was a larere attendance of deputies and representa- tives from different lodges in the district, the Hope of Earlestown Lodge being represented by Bro. George Clarke, D.M., Bro. John Taylor Bro. John Warburton, L.D., Bro. E. Newman, S.J.T., and Bro. Wm. Aitken, senr., P. Rep., while a number of visitorsattended with them.—Bro. GEORGE Dorms, D.C., of Northumberland District, gave an encourag- ing address, in which he referred to his early conneetion with the Temperance movement, remarking that he had been an abstainer for 47 years, and for 45 years a public advocate of the temperance cause.—Bro. M. BEEBINGTOI, D.C.T., reported on the internal working of the Order, and recommended earnest and persistent efforts in the cause they had espoused. Bro. R. W. KIRKUS, district secretary stated that there were nearly 4,000 members in the adult section, and 1,945 boys and girls in the juvenile order, with 127 adults as honorary members. He also gave the financial report and the report of the Executive, which showed good work done during the quarter, and referred to several changes in the mode of supervising the lodges in the district, and also to a proposed monstre tea party on May 23rd, when the repre- Pentatives of the R.W.G.L. pass through Liverpool, en route for Halifax, Nova Scotia.—Brother 51onnis JONES, D. E.D., dealt with the electoral work of the Order, pointing out that temperance workers could congratulate themselves on the present position of the movement in Parliament and upon the success they had recently achieved. They mast not imagine that the work was done—they had much hard work and opposition to contend with before the work was accom- plished. It would be done, however, and all the sooner by everyone doing his duty. The various report,' were adopted, and the following resolution was unanimously car- ried, On the motion of Brother W. A. BIONALL, seconded by Brother M. JONES, D.E.D., and supported by Bro. John B. Collings, "That in view of the great and rapid advance of temperance principles on public opinion and also among members of Parliament, this District Lodge of South-West Lencaehire of the Independent Order of Good Templets is of opinion that no measure of local option will be satisfactory to the people unless it gives to them the power to veto the granting andrenewal of licenses. whether dispensed by magistrates or a board specially elected for the purpose.." It was else decided that copieA of the re- solution should be forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Home Secretary, the members for the clunty, and to Sir Wilfrid Lawson. It was arranged that the next seesion of the District Ledge should he held at Earlestown on Satur- day, August 25th. A public tea meeting and demonstration were afterwards held.

MAINTEWANCE ORDER.—OU the application of Superin- tendent Barker, the Prescut magistrates, on Tuesday, made an order of 2f! Gcl a week against George Wafter, towards the support of his daughter, Mary Walker, who had been convicted of obtaining boots by false pretences, and sent to a reformatory. Defenaant was a watelmaker earning 25s a week.

Ammar. FAIR AT NEwroN. The usually quiet and secluded appearance of Newton-le-Willows was changed into one of bustle and activity on Thursday, when -the annual May fair was held. In accordance with orders issued by the county authorities, Mr. Worley, law clerk to the Improvement Commissioners, issued notices a short time ago stating that the annual fair for the sale of cows, bulls, oxen, heifers, calves, sheep, goats, and swine would not take place. This, however, did not prevent a goodly number of dealers in horses putting in an appeaitance. The animals ex- hibited were of an average quality, though very few of a high class were on sale. ,Several hundreds of horses wcre brought to the market, and a considerable proportion changed ownerships. The principal attraction to the juve- niles was the end of the village nearest to St. Peter's Church, and opposite the Town Hall. Here a large number of gingeybread, toffy, and not stalls, with numerous "three shots a penny" and other shooting galleries had been erected, and a pretty good trade was done by, the stall- holders. The local publicans also did a 'roaring trade,, ' and the tradespeople generally had increased receipts at the close of the day's proceedings.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. Tlik-EXECUTIOIOF CURLEY:
div.p: LATEST NEWS. Tlik-EXECUTIOIOF CURLEY:
LETTER TO UIS WIFE.

We append the following further details of this execution, which is briefly reported in our inner pages :—The convict retired to rest on Thursday night at twelve o'clock, and rose in the morning about six, looking cairn and refreshed. He went to mass directly Canon Kenneiy and the Rev. Mr. O'Reilly arrived, and partook of the last sacrament. At a quarter to eight his devotions were interrupted, ani Mon- signor Kennedy told him to arise. He obeyed, and the pro- cession was immediately formed, consisting of the convict, two clergymen, the Sub-Shertff (Mr. Ormsby), the governor of the gaol (Mr. Gildea), deputy-governor (Mr. Flewett), Dr. W. A. Carte, and a dozen warders. On the way through the corridor Marwood appeared, putting up his hand to salute the priest. He took his place behind the convict. The Litany for the dying was recited, and Cutley answered the responses in an audible and firm voice. He wore a cru- cifix round his neck. About 10 paces from the scaffold, at a sign from Marwood, there was a halt. Marwood produced his belt and straps, and, whispering in the ear of the culprit, proceeded to pinion. Curley did not offer the slightest resistence. Even when the painful operation was over he stood erect and firm. Directly before his arms were caught in the straps he stretched forth his right hand, and, shaking hands lith the governor, said, "Good-bye, and thank you." He took a farewell look at all present, and seemed to yearn with gratitude as he gazed for the last time on the attendant priests. The re- citation of the Litany was then resumed, the convict praying with intense fervency. At the foot of the scaffold Curley took one more glance at the last mortals to see his end. He then ascended the scaffold lightly, almost springingly. Marwood was quickly at his side, and strapped his legs. He then adjusted his head, lifting it slightly and placed it within the noose, pulling the white cap over the convict's face. Precisely as the clock struck eight the hang- man stepped aside and touched the lever. The drop fell. Daniel Curley was dead. There was no quiver, no motion. Death was instantaneous. Dr. Carte immediately afterwards went to the pit and looked at the convict's face. He died evidently without pain, the features being placid. The drop was about nine feet. About twenty minutes after the execution the two clergymen drove off in a cab. The crowd outside the gaol remained in prayer, saying the Litany for the dead fully twenty minutes after the execution. The crowd then dispersed. In addition to the police and military there were several marines in plain clothes on duty, and they mixed among the crowd.

At half-pat ten the inquest was held in the hoepital of the gaol before Mr. Harty, the District Coroner. Frederick Searle, chief warder, deposed to the execution having been carried out according to law. After some delay, while Dr. Carle was examining the body, the jurors proceeded to view the corpse, which was laid out at the foot of the scaffold, near an open grave. On their return Dr. Carle was called. Lie deposed that death arose from complete severance of the spinal cord high up in the neck, caused by dislocation pro- duced by hanging. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that death ensued from rupture of the spinal cord, caused by hanging, in accordance with the sentence passed at the Commission of ow and terminer, which opened on the 9th of April. The following is the text of the letter which the convict had written to his wife :—" My dear and most ever-beloved wife and children,—l take this opportunity—the last on this deceitful earth—of saying a few words to you, hoping that you will forgive me for the step I took with regard to my trial—l mean for not frying to save myself as others did; but I could not stoop so low or bring myself to do so. My dear wife, I will die as I have lived, faithful to my principles and my country's cause. I will do as all honest men do—bring my secrets to the grave with me, and leave them that is at freedom to enjoy it. Dear wife, I will say no more en this subject, as I have domestic business to speak on, as this, that I will request you to keep a vigilant watch over our dear children. Keep them to their school and religion and off the street, as you yourself know that I dread to see children getting the run of the street. Dar Jane, do not think that because I say tbie that I have not confidence in you. Yes, dear wife, I will die at rest; I know you will do what is just to them. I will also request of you not to let them out of your sight or care to any one as long as you can help it, my dear and faithful wife. Now about yourself. As I have told you before, I will not ask to restrict you in any manner. If you think it well to change your widowed life you can do so with all my wish and blessing, and I never like to see. anyone tied I love. I love liberty. But, my dear wife, if you ever change your life, be very careful in your choice in a companion. Deceitful men! My dear and faithful wife I love you. Excuse me, I cannot speak of this matter, as it was very hard to tear my trustful heart from you and offer it to God—and what a trial! Yes. The base and brutal de- ceiver should be the cause of separating two loving and trustful hearts. But God's will be done that is my only consolation. My dear wife, I will ask of you to be attentive to your religious duties. No matter how much you are engaged in the business of the world, never ne- glect that. My reason for saying so is that I shall die with the hope that we shall meet in the kingdom of Heaven, never to be parted by the power of man. Dear wife, I am sure you will be glad to hear that I die in peace with all men, forgiving enemies. May God for- give them for the injury they have done me. lam happy and at peace with God. Oh! may God protect you and the dear children in this deceitful world. Remember me to Frank, Peter' and Nelly, Mr. and Mrs. Hiland, Granny Misey, and all friend s.—Believe me to be your faithful and loving hw3band, DANIEL CUELEY.—To his affectionate and faithful wife and dear children, Mary, Jane, Michael, Peter, and Daniel. Pray for the soul of your dear husband. May the Lord have mercy on my soul.'; Then followed a num- ber of crosses signifying kisses.

div.head: IMPRISONED AGITATORS ON THE POPE'S CIRCULAR.
div.p: IMPRISONED AGITATORS ON THE POPE'S CIRCULAR.

Mr. Davitt, the founder of the Land League, and Mr. Healy, M.P., who are now confined in Richmond Prison, Dublin, for inflammatory speeches, have both written to Lord Mayor Dawson in reference to the Pope's circular to the Irish bishops. Mr. Davitt says it remains for the Irish people to express in unmistakeable remonstrances their pro- test against the unfounded charges implied in the Papal circular, and their emphatic condemnation of the marner in which their hereditary enemies the Catholic aristocracy of England, hive sought to Obtain from the head of the Catholic Church a sena e.-cathedra pronouncement in keeping with their hatred of the Irish national cause. The Parnell testimonial, he adds, should not be allowed to assume less proportions than a national tribute of £50,000. Mr. Davitt requests, therefore, his name to be added to the Irish Mansion House Committee, and subscribes £lo.—Mr. Healy save it is sought to make the Vatican the ante-chambet of the Birmingham caucus if Ireland will not recognise the attempted induction of Mr. George Errington into the chair of Peter. He asks the Irish people not to make themselves accomplices in the conspiracy against Mr. Parnell, and also subscribes to the fund.

Two workmen were killed and fire seriously injured by a fall ef a haze stack of steel ingots at Dr. Siemen's steel works, Landore, near Swansea, yesterday. Last night's Gazette announces the Queen has conferred the Albert medal of the second class on Henry Hood, cox. swain of the Seaton Carew lifeboat, for gallantry in saying life at the wreck of the Norwegian schooner Atlas, on Long- scitr Rocks, on the 11th March last.

WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.
WARRINGTON.

In Warrington there was a general suspension of business on Whit-Monday, and the glorious weathor caused a large exodus of townspeople, who went far and wide in search of enjoyment. The several railway stations wore their usual holiday aspect, and the streets of the town were for some hours alive with vehicles of every description. Omnibuses, brakes, wagonnettes, and traps were going in every direc- tion, and so great was the demand for conveyances that long before noon there was not a horse to be had on any terms. Frodsham proved as attractive as over to Warringtonians, but some of the townspeople went on to see the quaint and picturesque city of Chester, and others journeyed still further to view the sights of North Wales. Southport and Black- pool and other Lancashire watering places also attracted their share of visitors, and others again proceeded to Liver- pool and Manchester and other neighbouring pleasure re- sorts; while not a few made for Runcorn to take part in the festivities there. Numbers went to Lymm and to Stretton, and those who did not care to make a long journey were to be seen wandering in the fields and lanes about the tawn, or enjoying a quiet walk through the Park, which is now very attractive. Altogether the holiday makers conducted themselves very well, and it was remarked at the railway station that the pleasure-seekers were never before so numerous, so well dressed, or so well-behaved. The day passed off without accident, a circumstance which in itself spoke volumes for the behaviour of the trippers.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

Under a bright blue sky and tinged with golden sunshine dull, dingy Widnes looked its best on Whit-Monday, when tradesmen and workmen made general holiday. Hundreds of people glad to escape beyond sight of the tall, black chimneys, smokeless for the once, and the ugly piles of dirty red brick buildings, left the town in the early morning by the various excursions provided. The platforms at thc railway stations were crowded almost the whole day long, and the traffic was stated to be much greater than on any previous year. The Farnworth Parish Church trip to Windermere was most successful, upwards of 600 persons departing by it from Widnes London and North-Western Railway station at six o'clock, while others were picked up at Appleton, Farnworth, Clock Face, and St. Helens where the train stopped. A delightful day was spent amid the hills and dales, and the charming waters of the Lake district, the return journey being ac- complished by ten o'clock. The members of Widnes Sun- day School Union chose Mattock and Buxton as their desti- nation, and to the number of 300 left the Central station at 7.1,5., arriving at their journey's end shortly before ten. The manifold beauties, and curious natural phenomena of these health resorts were viewed by the excursionists with the utmost pleasure, and they returned to Widnes by ten , o'clock, highly elated with their day's trip. There was the usual excursion to Belle Vise, Manchester, crowded with passengers, while the numerous attractions of Liverpool caused a great exodus from the town to that popular sea- port. Hale, with its rural beauties, was not forgotten. Con- siderable numbers of people booked for that charming spot, and hundreds wended their way across the bridge to witness the festivities in Runcorn. Widnes, however, was not de- serted. Excursionists arrived in the chemical centre to visit friends and relatives, and at certain times of the day the streets presented an animated appearance. The promenade, the one breathing lung of Widnes, was not unlike a fair. Swings, merry-go-rounds, and numerous stalls were erected there and were beseiged by " young men and maidens." The river, too, was alive with small craft, the boat owners doing a brisk businss the whole of the day, RUNCORN,
As Whit-Monday, Runcorn's great annual holiday, ap- proaches, the atmospheric conditions are anxiously scanned for some indication of the weather to be _expected on that

universal gala day. Should dark clouds overhang the town, and their "distilled dews" fall e'er so gently, gloom is thrown over every household and the extensive preparations made for the celebration of the festival seem a solemn mockery. The cold easterly winds which ushered in the "month of flowers" and the snowy hailstones of Friday, re- duced the bright hopes of the scholars, and of their no less interested parents to zero. True seemed the vines— May is a pious fraud of the almanack ; A ghastly parody of real spring, Shaped out of snow and breathed with eastern winds.

But with Saturday came more genial breeses to end, how' ever, in a drizzling rain at night. Sunday, although not cloudless, was fine and bright, and the crimson sunset de- lighted the heart of the dweller in town as well as that of the shepherd, with anticipations of a joyous morrow. The old proverb for once proved true, and on Monday morning Runcorn was canopied with a brilliant blue sky. The air was glorious with golden sunshine, the Parish Church bells, swang by the strong arms of the Gerston ringers, sounded a merry peal; flags fluttered from numerous bailclinets ; and the town presented a scene of gaiety. In the " hives of in- dustry" the hum of labour was not heard. The workmen had ceased to toil for two days, and the people, glad to find their prognostications of a wet, dull holiday falsified, were thronging the streets before nine o'clock. Visitors from the Lancashire side of the river crossed the noble bridge which spans the Mersey in a steady stream, while the railway officials were busily engaged dealing with the extra traffic at the station. Usually on Whit-Monday morning the members of the Friendly Societies, arrayed in the curious and picturesque insignia of i the order, walk in procession through the streets ; but on the present occasion the display was confined to one club, the Star of Freedom Lodge of Oddfellows. Shortly after nine o'clock, the members of this order to the number of about 80 formed a procession at the Rifleman's Arms, Church-street, and paraded the principal thoroughfares of the town, headed by the National School Brass Band. Following the banner were two tall marshalle clothed in s!ains and bearing drawn swcrls, a sight which drew to- gether a large concourse of people, but of scarcely such large proportions as those which have witueseed former demenstra- tiens. This was the only special event of the morning. Runcorn affords no sights for the curious beyond the pretty parish church and the shipping in the decks, and until the Sunday school demonstration in the afternoon the "folly fair," which occupied its usual position, was the chief attraction. And tc this scene of noisy confusion wandered many of the excursionists and " natives" too. When tired of battering the countenance of "Aunt Sally" with wooden balls, "three a penny," the frolicsome youth could see human faces bruised in the booth erected for displays of the "noble art of self-defence," or if he had a taste for the

mysterious, visit the "temple of magic," and view feats of legerdemain. Shooting galleries, "gingerbread stalls," a'nd the multifarious accompaniments of a fair were there, while the deafening din of the rattle, the drum, and the umbel, mixed with the hoarse shouts of the various vendors, must

have been excruciating torture to the unfortunate inhabitants of the neighbourhood. It was pleasing to notice that many preferred to roam among the hoary tombstones of the Parish Church yard, reading the curious epitaphs upon the "moss- grown slabs," than visit this scene of folly ; while others found pleasure in a walk to the ruins of the ancient castle of Halton. At the approach of noon the few tradesmen who had kept open their establishments hoisted their shutters, and the streets became lined with row after row of spectators gathered in anticipation of the demonstration by the Sunday schools. Owing to some slight misunderstanding the scholars of Bethesda school started alone from High-street at one o'clock, and led by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor of the church, proceeded to a field off Halton-road, which had been kindly lent by Mrs. C. Hazlehurst. Then they were joined by St. Luke's branch of the school, the scholars in the procession number- ing about 330. Shortly afterwards the Brunswick Sunday School, which was to lead the united procession of Noncon- formist schools, it having been established in the year 1800, was seen approaching Fountain-square. As it proceeded to Delph Bridge the ether schools took their places in the ranks in the following order:—
Brunswick (Wesleyan) 6OO St. John's Presbyterian 252 Primitive Methodist 293 Mill Brow (Wesleyan) United Methodist Free Church Camden (Wesleyan) Nelson-street (Wesleyan) 194 Mersey Musslons 270

The scene as the scholars, in all about 3,000, marched along the crowded thoroughfares was most picturesque. Bands of music were discoursing sweet sounds; from the scholars ascended strains of vocal harmony; and banners of varied hues reflected the bright sunlight. Each school was led by the minister of the church with which it was connected, and the superintendents occupied positions in the front ranks. The Primitive Methodist scholars marched to the strains of the band belonging to that denomination in War- rington, while Mill-brow, Camden, and the Mersey Missions schools had each the benefit of the services of their own bands of music. After the parade the scholars adjourned to a field near Greenwav-road, lent by Mr. Joseph Savage, and engaged themselves in a variety of out-door games, then returning to their respec- tive schools, where tea had been provided. The schools connected with the Establishment also held their annual fdte. Accompanied by their band, the scholars of the National Schools and the Newtown Mission walked in pro- cessional order to the Vicarage, thence to a field at Higher Runcorn lent by Mr. Ford. Here they were met by the scholars from Weston and Weston Point, and refreshments were distributed. Tho scholars of Trinity school and ite branch, the Ragged school, proceeded to a field near Canal- street, lent by Mr. Horsfield, and after an enjoyable time re- turned to school to partake of tea. In consequence of the rough treatment to which they were subjected last year, the scholars connected with St. Edward's Roman Catholic Church abandoned their procession this year. The Salvation Army, as usual, contrived to bring its proceedings pro- minently before the public. Extraordinary activity was shown on Sunday, and early on Monday morning the mem- bers were put through "knee drill," followed by a parade through the town. As a substitute for the ordinary instru- mentalists, young girls, dressed in pl tin blue dresses, with handkerchiefs of the "Salvation colour" wound round their heads led the way, beating tembourines with dexterity. The unique spectacle was witnessed by hundreds of people, and a great crowd assembled in Dever:shire-square at half- past one, when, according to the announcement a " battery of guns" was in position, and a " tremendous battle " was fought. " Terrific slaughter" wile the dire consequence The services of the Widnes Salvation Army brass band and the aforementioned tambourines were much in in s requst, while some Salvation soldiers attired sang Salvation hymns to rollick- in n leslilY flocked t see them as though they were dbtdrliuege4t,isit.c b riid anti tiphijersey were present from Widnes and jugglers in the fair, and one old lady lifting up her bands In hGly horror, exclaimed " Wt.ll, I doan know what I shall live to see before a dee," her remark having, apparently,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19,1883.

reference to the " maidens " with the tambourines. During I the afternoon tea Wa 3 served in the Foresters' Hall, and ' subsequently there was a "tremendous procession" through the town, the troops "shouting and singing songs of victory," The day's proceedings were concluded by a "large praise and finish up" meeting, at which were an- nounced to speak "A converted drunkard from Cheater; the cornish person, the tnan who drank ale from a cabbage leaf, the converted dancing master. the Salvation beauties. Hallelujah Tom, and a host of Salvation astonishers." If there was an influx of visitors into the town, there was also an exodus of the residents who sought " pleasures haunts " away from familiar scenes. About 16 persons departed for Llandudno by a Liverpool excursion; while the well known beauties of Frodsham and Helsby exercised a potent at- traction over great numbers. Trains for Chester, Liverpool, and Manchester, had their full complement of passengers, about 700 people departing from Runcorn by train during the day. Superintendent Williamson and Inspector Hoil- ingworth are to be complimented on the admirable order which was maintained in the town. On a festival such as we are recording one may expect to see a few drunken men in the streets, but the number of men whose feet seemed to have a most perverse inclination to go wrong, and whose 3,eads seemed much too heavy for their shoulders, and yet wore upon their breast the blue ribbo, was somewhat _ _ _
. We have been supplied with the following particulars of the various schools, which will no doubt be read with in- terest :

CAMDEN SCHOOL. Total number of scholars on books, 505; average attendance, 357; number of officers and teachers, 27 male and 12 female; number of books in library, none ; superintendents, Messrs. G. Hazlehurst, S. C Beckett, H. Randle, and W. J. Shore. The scholars walked through the town with the ether schools, headed by the band, to a field behind Runcorn Soap Company's works. Tea was provided for the children in the school at four o'clock, for adults, at five o'clock, and a general meeting was afterwards held. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SCHOOLS,—Number of scholars on books, 104 boys and 91 girls; average attendance 76 boys and 67 girls; number of teachers, 14 male and 8 female; number of books in library, 348: minister, Rey. This school mustered strongly, the procession consisting of the scholars and a few members of the congregation, numbering 252 They joined the other schools at the fountain, and, on their ' return from the field, sat down to a substantial tea, after which the superintendent, Mr. James Pritchard presided over a very interest.ng meeting. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. E. Williams, and Messrs. Leach., Kirkham, and Humphreys. During the evening a number of recitations were given by the scholars, and a humorous and instructive dialogue, entitled "Wanted, a confidential clerk," was ably rendered by Messrs. Lampshaw, Joseph Dobson, Thomas Dobson, ,f. Gunning, and J. H. Richardson. The choir sang with much spirit of feeling the following anthems: " Won- drous love," 'I shall be satisfied," "Christ arose." This school, headed by their brass band playing appropriate music under the leadership of Mr. George Thomas, left the room at 1-15 p.m., and joined the united procession on Delph Bridge. After leaving I the field they passed along Heath-road, Union-street, I Sewell-street, and Halton-road, and played opposite the residence of Mr. Samuel Taylor, the school treasurer; then returned to the schoolroom, where the children were regaled with cake and tea free of charge. Pickwell; superintendents' Messrs. J. Ashley and R. Hillidge; secretary, Mr. John Fleet. The procession was formed at Regent-street school about 12-45 noon, and headed by the Warrington (Legh-street) Primi- tive Methodist Sabbath School brass band, (the members of which not only gave their services gratuitously, but kindly bore their own expenses, and played in excellent style) joined the other schools, and proceeded along the route chosen to Mr. Savage's field. Subsequently the teachers and scholars returned to the school, where tea was partaken of. Tea being over, Mr. Savage's field was again visited, and various games were indulged in until about 8-30.

D. Thomas; superinten- dent, George Lucy. The scholars took part in the general procession, and then spent the afternoon in a field kindly lent by Mrs. C. Hazlehurst. Tea was subsequently provided in the school-room, where a miscellaneous enter- tainment was held in the evening. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Num- ber of scholars on books, 154 boys, 146 girls; average attendance, 90 boys, 80 girls; number of teachers, 7 male, 8 female ; number of books in library, 0; minister and superintendent, Mr. William Shaw, seamen's and boatmen's missionary. Led by their admirable band, the children of this school formed part of the united procession, after which they returned to the school and were regaled with a sub- stantial tea, and spent the evening in the enjoyment of a variety of games and pastimes. Advantage was taken of the proceedings to present Mrs. King (nee WiNams) with a handsome silver-plated teapot, bearing the following inscrip- tion: "Presented to Miss Williams by the Sunday school teachers in connection with the Mersey Missions to Seamen, on the occasion of her marriage. Marcia 27th, 1883." Mr. George Howard made the presentation with a few appro- priate remarks, and it was accepted and suitably acknow- ledged by Mr. Albert Williams, on behalf of his sister. TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, HALTON.—Num- ber of scholars on books, 120 boys, 101 girls ; average at- tendance, 6/ boys, 65 girls; number of teachers, 10 male, seven female; number of books in library, 368 ; minister, Rev. Sydney Mees; superintendents, Mr. Jne. Gamon, Mr. Hugh Howe,Mr.Joseph Astburg ; secretaries, Mr.J.H.Gamon, Mr. W. H. Bradbury. The children met at the school at 1-30, formed a procession through the village, and then went into a field kindly lent by Mr. W. Nixon, various games were heartily entered into, viz. :—Football, cricket, rounders, ac. Tea was provided in the school about 4-30. The following ladies presided at the tables: Misses Gamon, R. Edwards, Chamberlain, Lightfoot, Astbury, Paunders, Rowe, and C. Edwards. After tea a very pleasant evening was spent, all seeming to enjoy themselves. Thanks are due to Messrs S. Barron, J. Looker, and J. Houghton, senior, who formed the amusement committee, for the able manner in which they carried out their work in putt- ing up the swings for the children. UNITHD FREE CRURCIL—N umber of scholars on books, 121 boys and 117 girls ; average attendance, Si boys and 61 girls; number of teachers, 25 male and 12 female ; number of books in library. 371 ; Minister, Rev. John Billington ; Superintendents, Mr. E. Gandy and Mr. E. Jones. The scholars and friends assembled at the school shortly after 1 o'clock, an being arranged in order, joined the procession at the bottom of Ellesmere-street. Returning to the school via Greenway-road, Regent-street, and Church-et, where'a large numb r of the scholars,:teachers, and their friends had tea, after which an entertainment, consisting of recitations and singing by the scholars, assisted by the choir, was given to a large and very appreciative audience.

div.head: FRODS HAM.
div.p: FRODS HAM.

The festivities usual to Whitsuntide were duly honoured at Frodsham. on Monday, when, contrary to expectations and the prophecy of the weather wise, the "big dram day" was ushered in with bright and bracing weather well worthy of the merrieenonth. The day is generally associated with the parade of friendly societies and we were glad to find that the golden principle of self-help was still predominant in Frodsham. The Foresters' and Oddfellows' Societies made a very creditable appearance each headed by an efficient bend, and the members attended divine service at the Parish Church, the noble proportions of which come out grandly as recently restored and beautified. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. C. G. Hopkinson, vicar of Alvanley, and a most appropriate discourse was preached from the first four verses of the 2nd chapter of Acts. The dulls afterwards made their annual visit to the gentry in the neighbourhood. As in former years, Castle Park, the seat of E. A. Wright, Esq., was open to the public; and a large number availed themselves of the opportunity to inspect the well kept grounds and tastefully arranged conservatory, which presented the appearance of a large nosegay in its varied and choice display of flowers, ferns, ric. The Court Independence of Ancient Foresters dined at the Town Hall, and from the annual statement of accounts has 269 members, and funds amounting to the satisfactory sum of £2,537 7s op., while £278 Bs. 10d. had been paid as sick and funeral money dpring the 'year. The Emblem of Hope Lodge (No. 516) of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows dined at the Bear's Paw Hotel, and the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A , vicar, took the chair, and Dr. Weaver, the vice-chair.—After full justice had been done to the excellent dinner provided, the Rev. H. B. Blogg said it gare him very much pleasure to be present, and to find that the order was so largely supported, and in an excellent speech he advocated the cause of friendly societies as pro- viding a benefit to the families of members and for old age. He wished hearty prosperity to the order, and trusted that as years rolled on they would increase in efficiency and general character of the members, and prove a benefit not only to the society but to the whole parish.—The Secretary (Mr. George Gorst) then read the statement of accounts for the year, from which it appeared that the number of members was 136. The funds amounted to £1,064 2s 311, and 169 Os 9d had been paid as sick and funeral money. The Secretary, in an interesting speech, traced the progress of the society from its formation in the year 1858. and stated that in the first two years they saved £lO 12e 3.1, the next three years £49 Is 4d, the next 10 years .£352 103 111, and the next 10 years £551 17a 91.—Dr. Weaver proposed "Success to the Odd- fellows Society," and remarked that the death rate in friendly societies in the kingdom was 2 in 100, whereas the death rate in this society was 1 in 138. Mr. Peter Riley proposed a vote of thanks to the Vicar for presiding, and the proceedings were brought to a chae.—The Independent Order of Rechabites, Delight of Frodsham Tent, No. 230, did not walk on Monday, but from the annual statement of account which has been handed to us, we find that the num- ber on the books is 68, the total funds amount to 1,216 8s Op, and the sum of £39 16s had been paid as sick and funeral motay durieg the year.
