BURTON WOOD.

STEALING A PAIR OF BOOTS AT EARLEATOWN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, William Harrison, 13 years of age, residing at Burtonwoocl, was charged with stealing on the 10th inst. a pair of boots, value 2s Gcl, the property of Joseph Burchall.—Superintendent Jackson briefly stated the facts of the case, after which Mrs. Burchall was called. She stated that on the previous after- noon the defendant came into the shop with a pair of boots, which he said he wanted repairing. He had a satchel with him, and she thought his manner was somewhat suspicious. She ultimately opened the satchel and saw that he had put in- side a pair of children's boots of the value of 2s GI He had taken them off the counter. P.C. Ivison deposed that he apprehended the prisoner and charged him with the offence, but he made no reply. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and the Bench sentenced him to receive twelve strokes with a birch rod. BRUTAL ASSAULT: HEAVY PENALTY. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before George McCorquodale, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqrs., Wm. Jones was summoned for assaulting Jane Lea, at Burtonwood, on the 28th April.—Mr. Moore. solicitor. Warrington, appeared for the complainant.—Defendant said he would plead guilty, but was aggravated into committing the assault.—Mr. Moore observed that the complainant was the wife of Wm. Lea, re- siding at Burtonwood, and the defendant had committed a most violent assault upon her. During the recent dry weather the complainant placed a tub beneath a spout in order to catch the rain water. The defendant twice knocked it away, and in doing so broke the bottom of the spout. She reprimanded him f.,r his conduct, and he struck her violently on the mouth and also gave her a black eye. She ran into the house, and he followed her there where he again assaulted her.—Jane Lea, the complainant, was called, and gave evi- dence in support of Mr. Moore's statement. The Bench considered the charge a very serious one, and Mr. Moore had used the correct word in describing it as cruel. The de- fendant would be fined 40a and costs.—Mr. Moore asked that the full costs of .the witnesses and his (Mr. Moore's) fee should be allowed.—The Bench remarked that it was not a practice usually adoptcd in that court to allow the advocate's fee, but under the ciretimstauces they would allow it. CHILD WALL.

ALLEGED THEFT FROM A FELLOW LODGER.—At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, James Rigby, gardener, was charged with stealing £lB 103, the property of a coachman, named Arthur Gwilliam. It appeared that the two men lodged together at Childwall. On Monday morning prose- cntor went out, leaving the money and a pair of gloves in the pocket of a coat in his box, and on his return he missed them Information was given to the police, who searched prisoner's box, and found the gloves, but the money was still missing. Under these circumstances Superintendent Barker asked for a remand for a week which was granted.

div.head: DITTON.
div.p: DITTON.
POOR-RATE.—On the application of Mr. Houghton, assist- ant-overseer, the Prescot magistrates on Tuesday sanc- tioned a poor-rate of Is 4d in the pound for the township of Ditton.
HALE.

PIC:SM.—The annual picnic in connection with the Tue- brook Primitive Methodist Band of Hope took place on Menday, at Hale Park, kinuly lent ley Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne, M.P. Waggonettes started from the school at eleyon am., and returned at ten p.:n. The sports, &c., included flat races, egg-and-spoon races, three-leg race, eke., and the party seemed to enjoy themselves to the utmost.

SERIOUS FIRE.---AbOUt four o'clock on Tuesday morning an alarming fire broke out in the stackyard of Mr. W. Turton, of Ivy House Farm, Hale. Joseph Turton, who lives a few yards distant from the farm, saw flames issuing from the stack, and at once went to the fire-station. Within a short time the Royal fire engine, under the charge of Major Dwerryhoese, kiergeant-Instructor Price, and about thirteen volunteer firemen, hastened to the scene. By this time the flames bad made great headway and the stack and a cart standing near were one mass of flame. Unfortunately the supply of water feli short, and the firemen and their assistants had the mortification of seeing the stack con- sumed whilst they were powerless to arrest its progress. The fire raged through the early hours of the morning, and it was not until late in the afternoon that it was ex- tinguished. Police-sergeant Coutts and Police-constable Roberts were present, and rendered every assistance. The cause of the conflagration has not been ascertained, but we may remark that there is no suspicion of incendiarism. The damage amounts to about £3OO, which is covered by insurance in the Royal Fire and Life Office, Liverpool.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

DRUNK AND INCAPABLE AT LYISIM. Michael McGinn labourer, Warburton, was charged at Lymm Police Court on Monday, with having been drunk and incapable that morning about one o'clock. Mr. Simpson, farmer, found the prisoner lying on the roadside helplessly drunk, and being under the impression that prisoner intended doing him some bodily harm, he obtained the assistance of one of his farm labom-ers and took him to the police station.—A. flue of 6s. including costs wan imposed. WHITSUNTIDE AT LYIDL.—Each day this week large numbers of visitors principally from Manchester and Liver- pool, have poured into Lymm, and imparted to the village a lively appearance. On Monday, a large party of cotton porters from Liverpool paid a visit, staying at the Plough Hotel; and a goodly number of persons came from Manchester in boats by the canal. The Rev. J. Callen, of Oughtrington, with a band of temperance people, and the Heatley Druids, headed by the Lymm hand, paraded the village on Mon- day. Thursday and F. idav, however, were regarded as the principal days, for besides several organised Sunday school parties from the city of cotton, which came by special trains, a number of pic-nic parties arrived by or- dinary trains. It was computed that about 1,500 visitors came by train on Thursday and about 1,000 yesterday. The weather throughout the week has been all that could be desired, and the various places of interest in the pic- turesque village, with its sylvan attractions now in all their summer beauty, were well frequented and much ap- preciated by the trippers. NORTH WICFI.

Mr. Coroner Y ,tes held an inquiry at Northwich, on Friday, on the bodies of Benjamin Askew and Mary Jane Lunt, who were drowned in the river Weaver under melan- choly circumstances on Monday. Mr. Askew was returning with his servant from a concert in which he had taken part, and in going along the towing path towards his residence both fell down the bank, which is here about ten feet high, and were drOwned.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

OYER FAta.—The spring fair has been very fairly attended. The amount of stock brought for sale was greatly in excess-of many former years, but owing to fine weather setting in and prospects of plenty of grass, prices for all I kinds of stock were high. Much business was done. _ PADGA.T.E.

A FOWL STEALER SENT TO GAO-L.—On Wednesday, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, John IVhittaker was committed for one month's imprisonment for stealing a fowl from the premises of Elijah Harris, at Padgate, on the 12th November last. Prisoner had only just been discharged from prison, where he bad undergone six months' imprisonment. SOU r a WORTH.- WITH-CROFT.

SCHOOL BOARD . —The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board school on Tuesday evening. There were present—the Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. Richard Turner, James Hatton. Lewis Birchall, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer).—The Attendance- Officer presented his report, which stated that be had visited the various schools in the district, when he found the attendance of the children was not so good as in the pre- vious months, In consequence of some of the children being absent from school sick from whooping cough, severe colds, &c., but he was glad to say that they were now improving, and would soon be able to attend school again. He also stated that he had served three notices on parents for illegal employment of children; also warned several others that unless their children attended school more regularly they would be summoned to appear before the School Board to show a sufficient cause for such absence. He also reported that he had issued summonses against Richard Moss Gi:bert Dean. and John Sharply, of Croft, for breaches of the bye-laws ef the Board (as instructed at the last Board meeting), the cases being heard at the War- rington Petty Nessions, on the 2nd inst., when Moss was fined ss. including costs, and attendance orders were granted in Dean's and Sharpie's cases. The report having been adopted, the Chairman and Clerk read a circular which he had received from the Education Department respecting the revised regulations (issued by the Department to local authorities) as to certificates of age, proficiency, and school attendance (Elementary Education Act, 1876, sec. 24); also calling the attention of the Board to the duties imposed upon local authorities by the provisions of Articles 11 and 15 of the code of 1883 relative to half-time scholars. In- structions havine: been given to the attendance officer respect- ing the same, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

The annual gala in aid of the Wigan Infirmary was held on Monday, in the Public ['ark, kindly lent by the Corpora- tion. The day Was beautifully fine, and there was a very large attendance. In the afternoon there were running and old English sports, and in the evening there WAS an excel- lent display of fireworks. The railway traffic was consider- ably augmented, the day being more generally observed as a holiday then has hitherto been the case. A Primus WOMAN.—A shocking affair, which it is feared may terminate fatally, took place on Tuesday night in Stanley-row, Wigan. Two married women had been been drinking together during the day, and at night a quarrel ensued between them. One, named Maria Goulding, seized a poker and struck the other, known by the nickname of " Cosford," and in striking again hit a young chi:d which was in her arms. The child's nose was broken, and it lost a great quantity of blood, and little hope is entertained of its recovery. Goulding was taken into custody by the police. A CLERICAL DISPLUE.—At the Wigan County Court, on Thursday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkas, judge, and a special jury, the adjourned case of Hammon v. Heins came on for hearing. The plaintiff, the Rev. G. J. Hammon, was formerly a curate at St. George'd Church, Wigan, but in

div.head: Vi7INSFORD.
div.p: Vi7INSFORD.

WINSFORD RIFLE Conrs. This company of the 3rd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers went into camp on Saturday last. Through the kindness of Lord Egerton, of Tatton, the camp is again held in Tatton Park. LAUNCH OF A BTEA3I BARGE AT WINSPORD.—The enterpriAng firm of Deakin and Co. launched, on Saturday, from their slip at Knight's Grange, the largest steam barge on the Weaver. The barge is intended for the salt trade between Winsford and Liverpool, and has been constructed under the superintendence of the foreman of the dockyard and works, Mr. E. Nevrall. It is of the following dimen- sions :—Length, 18 feet; beam, 21 feet; depth of !1011, 10 feet: with a carrying power of 300 tons. The engines are being made at Messrs. Deakin' s works, Just before the steamer left the slip addresses were given by Mr. G. 11. Deakin, one of the firm, and Mr. E. Newall, when the cere- mony of naming the vessel was performed by Master Norman Deakin, who amid cheering named the barge as it took the water "The Acme." Instead of the usual dinner, Messrs. Deakin gave a gratuity of half-a-crown to each of the men.

TEMPERANCE FESTIVAL AT WINSFORD.-011 MondaY, a grand Dissenting temperance festival was held at Winsford. It embraced the teetotallers from each of the chapels of the district and the bands of hope, and was got up by the Wesleyans. Most of the temperance people took part in the procession, and hundreds partook of tea in the Town Hall at its termination. Mr. Massey, confectioner, Winsford, pur- veyed for the company with evident satisfaction, and the children were supplied with buns, tea, atc. in their own school-rooms, or at the Cocoa House. The chief societies represented were the Rechabites, Sons of Temperance, the Gospel Temperance Union, Salvation and Blue Ribbon Army Corps. and the Bands of Hope of the Wesleyan, Free Methodist, Primitive, and Congregational schools .(seven in all), and the Juvenile Sons of Temperance and R.chahites. There were two brass bands in the procession—Northwich (Hartford Corps H) and 'Winsford (Corps E)—and the general effect of the procession was increased by banners and banneretteg, of which there was a great variety. The arrangements were under the management of the following committee: Messrs. Maudsley, Preston, J. Dodd, T. Dodd, J. Cheshire, Curzon, J. Dickenson, G. Newall, J. Billington, W. Hall, W. Brooks, T. Oaks, J. Griffiths, Woolley, T. Hulse, E. Leigh (president), W. Dodd (vice-president), R. Royle (treasurer), and W. McDermid (secretary). A well- attended public meeting was held in the Free Methodist Chapel, under the chairmanship of Mr. Leigh, who was supported by the following speakers: Revs. J. Chisholm, Liverpool; T. Rippon, Warrington; T. Turner, Over; J. T. Maxwell, Over; C. S. Reader. Wharton; W. T. Symons, and Messrs. J. Slater (Mayor of Over), and W. Dodd, late of Southport. Mr. Singleton presided at the organ, and there was a choir of nearly one hundred voices. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

CiTTLE DISEASE IN CREsmtnii.—The Chief Constable of Cheshire has now issued the most favourable report pre- sented for the year. Last week 63 animals remained under treatment for foot-and-mouth disease, of which 46 have re- covered, and as no fresh cases have broken out, only 22 animals remain under treatment in the whole county. Swine fever has also been reduced to one, and sheep scab to four cases.

SERIOrS SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.—A serious accident hap- pened to three men who were engaged in the erection of several houses in front of the new cattle market, near Crewe Railway Station. The scaffold on which they were working gave way and they fell, all sustaining serious injuries. Mr. S. Wood (brother of the contractor) had one of his legs broken just below the knee, the ribs of the second man were fractured, and the third was much bruised.

PRESENTATION AT CREWE.—Mr. Wallace Lumb, son of Mr. Richard Lumb, brewer, of Liverpool, was an Saturday presented with a handsome silver salver, tea and eoffee service, and a dining-room marble and bronze time-piece, by the friends of the Crewe Horticultural Society, in recogni- tion of the valuable services he has rendered to that society as secretary. Councillor Bebbington presided. Councillor Thomas, J.P., made the presentation, and other gentlemen also spoke. NARROW ESCAPE OF THE SHERIFF OF CHESTER- —On Monday Mr. John M'Shattie, Sheriff of Chester, had an ex- ceedingly narrow escape from drowning. Together with seven members of his family and relatives he had entered a pleasure boat on the Dee, when a man who was engaged in preparing the boat for its departure suddenly jumped into it, and the boat capsized. Mr. M'Shattie assisted the other members of the party in grasping the landing-stage and getting out of the water, and then succeeded in seizing the stage himself. Just as he was sinking beneath the water he was nulled on to the bank, and was found to be in a fainting condiron.

CHESTER CATHEDRAL AND THE CAPITULAR ESTATES.-- Dean Howeon has just issued a statement of the funds con- tributed in Cheater Cathedral daring the year 1882, and the processes to which they bad been applied. The expenses connected with the care of the Cathedral, by reason of the consumption of gas and coke being much larger than in pre- vious years, area heavy burden at present upon the working account of the Cathedral, especially (continues the report) as in consequence of the agricultural depression, losses of rent have taken place on the capitular estates during the last four years to the extent af more than £1,500. Revert- ing to what has been done in the Cathedral. the Dean says tbat the whole of the north wall of the chapter-house has been rescued from its state of decay and danger ; the repair of the outer roof of the south transept is now completed, to- wards which the Ecclesiastical Commissioners contributed £l,OOO. Steps will now be taken to complete the vaulting; of the east aisle, one bay of which was done several cen- turies ago. The total cost will, it is estimated, reach £7OO. Poore BA.TES AND PAUPERISM—The followieg figures have been supplied to the Local Govercment Beard by the clerks to the guardians of the county of Chester, showing their receipts and expenditure far the year 1882-3 :—ln this county, with a population of 621,544, £137,173 was ex- pended in relief to the poor, against £138,453 in 1881. being a decrease of £1,280, or 0 9 per cent. The receipts from peon rates amounted to £292,516. from the Treasury, £10,892, and £9.998 from other sources. The expenditure amountA to £323,304. Of this £29.006 were for main- tenance, £5O 220 for out relief, £21,667 for the maintenance of lunatics, £6 498f0r workhouse loans, £18,593 for officers' salaries, &c, £11,189 for incidental expenses, £2.851 for law proceedings, £111,547 for police, £37,778 for highway boards, £2 342 for sanitary purposes, £1.058 for burial boards. £4396 for school boards, £1,898 for school Commit- tees, £2,088 for fees to clergymen and registrars, £2,336 for vaccination. £2,153 for parliamentary registration, £BOl for schoel fees for non-pauper children, £1,278 for payments under the Asessment Acts, and £15,605 for all other pur- poses. The loans and interest outstanding at the end of 1882 amounted to £82,280. CHESHIRE VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.—The Third Battalion of Cheshire Rifle Volunteers- have, as usual, spent Whit- week in camp. The eight companies comprising the bat- talion, having their head-quarters at Altrincham, Knutsford, Northwich Winsford, Cheadle, Sale, and Lymm, marched into camp at Teton Park, Knutsford, on Saturday afternoon, the tents having been fixed the previous day, and every pro- vision made for the comfort of the men. The commissariat was managed by Quartermaster Daggatt, who was for some time attached to the 24th Regiment at Salford Barracks. On entering camp the men were received by Lieut.-Colonel Marshall, Major and Adjutant Braddell, and Major Fox. The Altrincham companies marched to the park under the command of Captain T. A. Jones. The officers in camp, in addition to the above, were Captain Cheshire, Northwich ; Captain Davies, Knutsford ; Captain Maraland, Sale; Cap- tain Butler, Altrincham ; Captain Turner, Winsford ; Cap- tain F. Howarth, Cheadle; Captain J. Bower, Lynem ; Lieutenants Lee Jones, Northwich ; E. D. Schott, Sale; C. C. Wedemeyer, Cheadle; Malcolm Blair, Lymm ; Adden- brooks, Lymm ; Quartermaster Daggett; Surgeon T. More- ton, Northwich ; Surgeon Wm. Agar Renshaw, Altrinchatn ; Surgeon Oh-ell. Wineford. The number of men in camp on Saturday was 672. Of the 122 tents which were pitched 80 were allotted to the men, the remainder being devoted to the officers, the hospital, the guard, and other purposes. There was a large recreation tent, in which varied entertain- ments were given every evening.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board washeld on Thurs- day, Mr. W. Tyrer presiding. There were also present : The Revs. T. Chambers, J. Barnacle, and T. Finegan Messrs. R. Lee, J. Ptnketh, J. Fidler, J. Agnew, W. G. Ashton, S. Marsh, J. Matthews, W. Gerrard, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, J. Jackson, J. Buckley, J. Eatock, J. Griffith, W. Swift, E. Syder, T.Dobell, J. T. Hall, J. Leatherbarrow, and W. Longton.
THE BOARD AND THE AUDITOR.-STRAINED RELATIONS
AND STRONG PROTESTS.

The Local Government Board sent to the Guardians for their examination extracts from the report of the auditor (Mr. Hazlehurst) finding fault with the style of bookkeep- ing used by relieving officers,Stuart, Bullock, and Scannell. The complaints of the auditor bad reference to technicali- ties which cannot well be described apart from the reliev- ing officer's hooks. A correspondence between the officers named and the Local Government Board on the subject was read by the clerk. The Local Government Board re- quested that the imperfections alluded to by the auditor should be remedied in future—The CLURIE remarked that he had replied to one portion of the Local Government Board's letter by stating that the report of the auditor in that particular was not correct. In another communicatios the Local Government Board requested the observations of the Guardians upon a fur- ther extract from the auditor's report, in which Mr. Hazel- buret stated that in consequence of the Guardians not en- forcing prompt payment of the calls due from the overseers of several townships Ira respect to their contributions to the common fund, conaklerable arrears were permitted to ac- crue. As examples the auditor referred to the amount owing by Earlesteern and Widnes, and in a schedule gave particulars of the amounts due from other townships.—The CHAIRMAN said the only question was whether they should notice the eemmunicaiion. The auditor seemed to have gone out of his way in bringing suck matters before the Local Gewernment-Board. It was not the duty of the aux,. tor to keep the overseers of the townships up to the mark in their payments. It was the duty of the Guardians, who in the dkleharge of that duty haearne cognisant of the mq,,,3ors

why calla were not paid, and of these reasons the auditor could not have such perfect know- ledge, In the case of Widnes, for instance, there were peculiar circumstances which caused it to be in arrear, but now they had got a new assistant overseer, and everything was being done to collect those arrears.—Mr. FIDL.ER said with regard to Eecleston, if the Local Government Board was to be written to about the overseers by the auditor they would have to get fresh overseers. He for one would not submit to the supercilious and dictatorial statements m, de to the Local Government Board with respect to the tor- ship of which he WM one of the overseers, (Hear, hear.)-- Mr. HALL moved that the Guardians had no remarks to make upon the Los.al Government Board's letter.—Thy Rev. T. CHAMBERS seconded the motion, and it was c trried unanimously, Mr. FIDLFR observing: They treat us like a lot of school children.

In a still furthcr letter (on hearing the opening of which a Guardian remarked, "The cry is still they come ' ") the same cenoral authority req-eated the views of the Guardians on the following portions cf, the auditor's report :—" The relieving officers of this union are by direction of the Guardians still employed out of their own respective dis- tricts in obtaining particulars of the circumstances of per- sons alleged to be able to contribute to the maimenance of paupers chargeable to the Prescot Union. For instance, one relieving officer, during the last half-year, was absent , two entire days from his district on the prosecution of two inquiries at Newcastle-on-Tyne, Jerrow, Kilburn, &c The CLERK said this was a matter which the Guardians should take up. The object of the auditor's report was, to his mind, to compel the Guardians to appoint an additional officer, which would involve an an- creased expenditure of at least £lOO a year. As the chairman had justly observed in regard to a previous matter, the auditor had travelled out of his way to report upon this matter. The Guardians were the best judges of the necessities of their own union, and if they thought pro- per to appoint a special officer to make the enquiries in question they could do so. They had a standing order that no relieving officer should leave his district without his (the clerk's) consent;and when a relieving officer did leave- his district he provided for his work being done by his brother relieving officers during his absence. The Local Government Board asked for the opinion of the Guardians on this subject, but it was a question whether they should submit to such a requisition.—Mr. Finnan: Certainly not. —The CLERIC said he should like to have an expression of opinion by the Guardians, as he should have to reply to the. letter.—The CHAIRMAN suggested that the Clerk reply that they protested against the auditor in- terfering with matters he had no business ' to interfere with. They had made what they considered suitable and economical arrangements. Not long ago they- had appointed an assistant relieving officer, so that now they had five relieving officers in the Union, and the fact of those officers going out of the district to inquire into the cases re- ferred to did not interfere to any appreciable extent with their other dutiee.—The CLERK remarked that the arrange- ment in operation was a considerable saving of expense. They sent a relieving officer to make inquiries into a parti- cnlar case, and he gathered evidence both as to the ability of the person summoned to pay and as to the age, and so on, of the person chargeable, and this evidence being admissible they saved the expense of bringing witnesses—such, for in- stance, as the cashier of a large firm—from a distance.—Mr. FIDLER was anxious to know whether the auditor attended there in a dual capacity. Was he clerk as well as auditor, or what was he ?—This inquiry was followed by a general conversation, which was interrupted by the CHAIRMAN calling upon Mr. Hartley to read the draft which he had pre- parell of a reply to the main points raised by the auditor.—The draft reply was as follows :---0 My Lords and Gentlemen,— I am directed by the Guardians of this Union to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the 11th lost, with ex- tract from the report made by Mr. George Hazlehurste district auditor, after his audit of the accounts for the half- year ended at Michaelmas last, in which that gentleman thinks fit to complain of the relieving officers being em- ployed in obtaining evidence necessary to be produced to the magistrates when poor relation maintenance orders are to be applied for. I am further desired to say that where the auditor deems reports necessary to you he should be re- quired to give the explanations he receives at the time when from his point of view the cases for report arise, as this would in the opinion of the Guardians render need- less much of the correspondence with which you and they are troubled. lam requested to question the right of the auditor to make such a report as the one sent, and to say that in doing so he travelled out of his way and ex- ceeded his duty. The Guardians strongly protest against what they consider undue and improper interference on the part of the auditor, and they are not disposed to submit to it ; and I am to acquaint you with their determination (not- withstanding their desire to be at all times courteous) to decline making any observations or giving any explanation on this report or any reports of a similar character. They contend that they have discretionary powers; and teeing the best judges of the requirements of their own Union, they are prepared to exercise such powers irrespective of the auditor's repeated attempts to restrain them."—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS moved that the letter drafted by the clerk be forwarded to the Local Government Board. He thought the Guardians were doing quite right in taking no notice of the auditor's remarks about certain townships behind hand, because he believed all of , them were doing their best, and the auditor was quite going out of his way in saving what he had said. As for Hale- wood, he had seen the overseers the day before, and he was told that next time they were only. going to lay a sixpenny rate instead of a three shilling one. To be talked to by the auditor in that way was most unsatisfactory.—The CLERK mentioned a case in which the treasurer had made an error in crediting Windle with £l,OOO which was due to Widnes. The auditor had called upon him in order to rectify the error to alter the books, but he refused to do so as it would have involved upwards of forty alterations, and the proper way in book-keeping was to correct the error with a cross entry. He requested instructions to credit Widnes and debit Windle with £l,OOO, and to issue adjusted contribution orders upon those townships.—On the motion of Mr. DOBELL, seconded by the Rev. T. CHAMBERS, a resolution embodying the clerk's request was unanimously agreed to ; and Mr. Chambers's resolution that the clerk's reply to the Local Government Board be approved and despatched, was carried with similar unanimity. Another letter from the Local Government Board had re- ference to a return required by the auditor of the securities entered into by the relieving officers.—Mr. FIDLER : If this is to go on much further, I shall move for a special meet- ing to consider the auditor's objections.—The CHAIRMAN : Or a special day to take no notice of them—The CLERK: The auditor has adjourned the audit till Tuesday next.— The Rev. T. Ceraernens : Would it be out of order to pro- pose that it be adjourned sine die2—The CLERK: lam afraid he will not be able to proceed with the audit on Tuesday. He will find certain obstacles and difficulties. 'the Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the pro- vision of an outfit for an apprentice whom the Guardians I had sent out. Tbe expense had been objected to by the auditor, and the sanction was in response to an appeal by the Guardians.

div.head: TNT! BURTAL OF PAUPHRS.
div.p: TNT! BURTAL OF PAUPHRS.

A !Ater was read from Mr. Evans, churchwarden, Pres- cot, in answer to a letter from Mr. Hartley, with reference to the burial of paupers in Prescot Churchyard. The letter stated that the Present churchwardens were well aware that the Gu.irdians contributed £lOO towards the enlargement of Preseat Churchyard in 1855, and had the right of interment therein, but they thought it hardly fair that that right should be exercised to the fullest extent, as the Guardians had received the value of that money many times over dur- ing the last 28 years. The churchwardens asked that the right of burial which the Guardians had in other burial places should be exercised.—This letter was referred to the Visiting Committee.

div.head: ALIF.ORD GROSS CRUELTY TO A CHILD.
div.p: ALIF.ORD GROSS CRUELTY TO A CHILD.

A case of what was stated to be gross cruelty to one of the children placed out by the Guardians was brought under the notice of the Board in a report by relieving officer Stuart. The name of the child, a little girl, aged 10, was Mary Ann Anders, and she had been placed out with a John Anders, of 10, Shaw-street, St. Helens. It appeared that the child at- tended Cowley schools, and on Friday last the mistress of that school, Mrs. Baddeley, noticing what appeared to be marks of severe ill-treatment, took her to relieving officer Stuart, who found several abrasions on the child's back and arms and also a mark bebind one of her ears, apparently the result of a blow by the buckle of a strap. In consequence of what he saw Mr. Stuart sent the child back to the workhouse, and reported the case.— Mr. }her, said that when the child was brought in the first instance before the Committee her body was all black and blue, and it appeared that she had been compelled by her foster parents to get up about half-past five every mornisg and clean out two rooms and wait upon some gentlemen, and if all was not properly done she was Beverly thrashed, and she did net get to bed till about eleven o'clock.—Mr. FIDLER said he had never been so unmanned in all his life as when he saw the poor girl, and it seemed to him she had undergone a continual infliction of cruelty. She seemed to have been in a state worse than slavery, and he advised that the foster parents should be prosecuted to the uttermolt.—The child was brought into the room, ;Ad there were several scars shown on her back and arms, although it was stated that many of the marks of ill-usage had abated Eince she was admitted to the workhouse a week ago.—Mr. STUART, re- lieving, officer, stated that his attention had been once be- fore called to what an informant thought to be the cruel treatment of the same chili, and he had at that time warned the foster parents.—Aftea some further zonversation, in the course of which several Guardians ref2rred to the necessity of surprise visits by Uuardians to places where children were placed out, it was agreed that the persons who had, as alleged, illtreated the child in quation- should be prose- cuted ; and on the motion of Mr. 7.O3ATOCK, seconded by Mr. Fintsn, a vote of thanks was plumed to Mrs. Badeley for bringing the •matter under the notice of the relieving officer.

div.head: TiIR _DEATH o,k' MR. TWIST.
div.p: TiIR _DEATH o,k' MR. TWIST.

The CRAIRUAN referred to the loss which- the Board had sustained in the death of MT. Twist, assistant overseer for the township of Windle, rad Mr. FIDLER also referred in eulogistic terms to the good qualities of the deceased.—On the motiou of Mr. LEATRERD&RROW, a letter of condolence was directed to be sent to Mrs. Twist.—Mr. MARSH said that at the next meeting he would move that Mr. Twist's son, who had done the work during his father's protracted illneEs, be appointed to the vacant office.—This concluded the business of public interest._

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thornas lioward was charged under a warrant with committing a brtach of the peace at Golborne, on the 12th January, 1882, and pleading guilty, he was bound over in the sum of £5 tr, Isecp the peace for six months.

JOHN MORLEY, M.P., LAST NIGII r. reegler's Cirque, Liverpool, as famous for its political demoestretions as fur its rquestrian exhibitious, was last might again the scene of a magnifieent Liberal gethering , The meeting vres to give the Liberals of Liverpool an oupor- tennity of hearing ad tresses from Mr. John Morley, the cewly-elected member of Parliament for Newe aide, and Mr. M. emitb, M.P., and a githering such as 'het ehich assem- bled, drawn together eel it was upon a summer's night, was an counistakeble proof of the exteneion of Liberal prin- aseplee iu the city of Liverpool. All parts of the spacious] building were crowded with intro-sted listeners,l who Fpent the time which elapsed between the . 9pening of tee doe's met the cominsneement to the p-oceedings on respendiug to calls for cheers for Mr. Merle, en r. Smith, mad the Littera' leedets; and groaus for Mr. Newdegate au-ti other prutrimeet conservatives. At eight o'clock, the appointed hour, elr. H. D. Hutt, eh iirm in of the Liverpool Leeral Associetiou, !unto his appearance upon the platform accompanied by Mr. Jelin Morley, M.P., Mr. S. Smith, W.. P.. and the leading Liberals of Liverpool and the neigh- bourhood. Tbe entrance of awed gentlemen was the signal for a loud and prolonged outburst of cheering. When quietness Lied tarn restored the Chairman reee and al tutted to the Lim that when they (net met in that piece it was to receive the candidate whom the Council of the Liberal Association hart selected as a et end proper person to represent Liverpool in Parliament. it he pointed out that they were met tied evening as the fe".heral party et Liverpool had not met bcfur,--at least in C 3 recollection. they had won in a fair polhicel fight, in spite of the prestige ot the Town Hall, arid uf the aldermen, the rasjeriey seat, and crest was the ch song when he an- ceunced that they were aseembled that eveniug to welcome 03 majority member fel' Liverpool, Mr. Smith. He ex- peteeed the hope that the existing utrenimily would be cemented so as to enable them at the uext election te give rr. Smith 3 worthy colleague, and then referred in brief complimernary terms to the literary talecurs and election 10 Parliament of Mr. Morley, who the said, entered Parliament abcut the time Mr. Smith did, and he concluded by remarking that it was to such men as bin Morley aid Mr. Smith they looked tor guidance, a re- ar k that was greeted with loud cheers. Mr. T. H. Ismay, who was met on rising to propose the first resolution .with Cries of 3 our tuture member," dealt with the question of obstruction, and moved a resolution declaring the unabated conndence of ihe meeting in the policy. zeal, and devotion of Her Majesty's Gevernrnent, expreeeing its gratitude towards their faithful supporters in both liouses of Parlia- ment and its grievous disappoiutment at the continued parelyeis of leeislatiun, and urging upon Her Maje.sty's Cloisters the paramount necessity of taking prompt measuree to prevent the chef., uction of Wale business, and that a memorial expressing these views be signed by the chairman and forwarded to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. . G. Eitbbone seconded the resolution, which was carried. Hr. S. Steam then rose to reply, and met with a gratifyin reception. At the onset he thanted them very cerdially for act extremely kind reception they had given him, and re- marked that it encouraged him to think that they had not repented of the chute which they made last December, and that they were not dies itistied with the way in which their representative had performed his duties in the House of Com- mons. There were, be said, two key notes in the resolution, thq first of which was unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and the eecond of which Was deep regret, 'mounting to Alarm, at. the paralysis of public bueiness in Parliament. Addressing himself to the last of .these, be said he quite agreed with all that had been said upon that subject. But the Causes of this block of business were, be said, Yore then those that were alluded to. Parliament aeffered from three separate causes of delay. The first of these he styled the congestion of business, the second the excessive hquacity of hon. members, and the third #sv silent and uuavowed obetrnction. He suggested as 'atives of what had become an intollereble evil, an nsion of locel self government, and a steady ; policy of elecentralisaticn. He proceeded to justity 03 policy of the Governmept upon some points which bad been most impugned. He first dealt' with the extremely delicate question of the Affirmation Bill (cheers) and said when he i! voted for the Bill, it was because he could justify that con- ' duct in the sight of both God mad man, fie had clearly come to the conclusion that thele was no alternative before i the House of Commons—there would be no alternative 1 before the House of Commons—except the "leasing of this 1 Affirmation Bill. (Cheers.) Perliement, in !lid judgment - Was not competent to et.Trire into any man's religious o con-religious opinions. (Loud cheers.) He expressed his Leiief that where Christianity relied upon the civil power it weaken, d itself iu co doing—(cheers)—and pointed out that in excluding Mr. Bradlaugh from the House ot Commons they had done incredible injury to 1 the cause of that religion they lied esdoused. , 'They bad made Mr. Bradlaugtt ten - fold more dangerous ' to Christienity than lie was before, and it filled him (Mr. Smith) with the deepest regret to think how well-mean- lug and reliehala people had played into Mr. Bratilatigh's I Lands, and lotn the bends of the cause they abhorred. The responsibility of returning At heisis to Parlieineut rested with those who ?lent theta. (Hear, hear.) He deplored that any Eeglish coreititnency should act as Northampton had done, but as it bed chosen so to act it was not competent for them to stand between it and the min of its chnice. (Hear, hear.) 1 tiebetieved the opening i f the doors of Yartiament to Mr. ' -13redlaugh would take away miue-teettis of its influence and he c.iuld not believe that the British floliee of Commons would ever contain many men of that stamp. (Heir, hear.) He Was not the least afraid of Cbristieuity from the presence of Mr. Bredlaugh in the lama's of Commons. It bad scrvived for 1,16.00 years attacks from every source, and it wouid survive all attacks in the future. Adverting to the state of Ireland, he pointed to the restoration of law and order in that uultappy coun- try, and to the tern ukelele success which had attended the Government in grappling with crime and in bringing ite _perpetrators to jestice. He hoped the time would come When it weuld be peseible for the British Government to , administer the frish Government through Irish members of true loyally and public worth, and WO he thought the IBritish Government should deal with Ireland in the way it dealt with took. where it had made railways anti had spent reillione of money in public works. He I asserted that our foreign affairs was very much safer in the Lands of Mr. Gladstone than in the hands uf Lord Salis- bury, and claimed the support of the meeting fur the Liberal Government te cause it was mere capable of carrying out renome, because it We ...aide ill sympathy with the needs of the British 'people, because it nad a more earnest moral purpose, because it was eetter able to translate philanthropy into practical 'mintier,. (Cheers ) He concluded with sirnply claiming Chair unebered c tafetence in one of the test and ablest 00vernmi-rit4 this country ever had the good fortune to pi;;3t,SS. (Loun cheers.) Mr. JOHN SIOLGLEY, M.P., said he wee, as 90t110 of them knew. a Lenc,shire titan, and therefore he recognised in the Cordiality with which they had received him some- thing oh a Lancashire welcome. (Hear. hear.) But though tier was Linceshire born and LincaNhire bred, he was bound to say that he lied never ad, re srd a !nesting in this county or any other which seemed to him so full of true Liberal impulse and Liberal enthusiasm as the enormoes gathering whicn he lied the honour of addressing theu—(cheers)— and wit, n ne remembered the impression that was made rot only in Lancashire, but throughout all the Liberal party iu En4larld at the result of their election in De- ceader la s —(ciheers)--be could not be surprised that they should gather in such force to receive the cham- pion who led them on to that brilliant victory. (Cheers.) ft would be impertinent in him to:verdure upon any en- ccrrounia upon their representative's zeal, or ability, or intelligence. All he could tell them was that he knew of no borough in England and he might say the same of the House of Commons, in which all r home quanties were not amply recognised, and for sending which to Parliament Live' pool had not received tin gratitude of tie Liberal party. He was glad, therefore, to have the opportunity uf seeing such a member face to face with such ctotistiruents. (lieer, hear.) There were some points upon which, though he agreed with Mr. smith in what be had elequently said as to his Conclusions, ho did not entirely follow Fin as to his premises. (Hear, hear.) So far as the Nortli.amotnn election was cencerned they steed not be at all afraid so far as the conclusion went, he wee ab.colute;y at one with Mr. Smith. As he said three tights ago in his own constituency at Newcastle, when he ; heard Mr. Gladetone use in the most maenificent speech 11 that he had ever heard, or he thought ever should hear' 1 that in his apprehension the opinion of the country wasl areinet the Adirmetion Bill—("No ")—he (Mr. Morley) ventured in hia own mind, with ell respect for the leader in ,1 nffsction fur whom he was second to none, to dcubt ' vehether that wait the case. (Cheers.) lie, for anyo... . , , one, ,Ariald throw no bad words at any man vhcon any c mstitneney in England in tile free exercise of their constitutional choice preferred to send ee their repreeentative to the Howie of Commons. to turn out all the men in the House of Commons, to whose opinions they objected. the Conservative minority wculd be smaller than it is now. (Loud cheers.) As to Irel ind, he was nut sure that he ever thought they ought to be in a state of content or order there until they gave to the Irish members of Parliament and to Irishmen in their own counties and districts a greater voice in the management of their own affairs than they had now. (Loud cheers.) He for one believed, and he would never pretend not to believe, that that country would not be pacified until the English gave it at least the same measure of-self government as we enjoy in Eng- land,—(cheers)--and until our statesmen have found out some way of conciliating their national sentiment. The millions that had been spent in war in South Africa should have been spent on our own people in rescuing from the depths of degradation. into which so many thousands of them were plunged, and in wiping away he blots that stain cur own civilisation. (Hear, hear.) They now beam the Tories were going to meet the Liberals on their own ground with social aud domestic reform. There was something come into existence which he thought they in Liverpool had heard something about—a thing called "Tory democracy." (Loud laughter.) However, they alight be sure that the interests of that party made it impossible for them to compass any of that legislation which a democracy required and de- manded. (Cheers.) Notwitstanding that the Conservatives believed by their alliance with the Irish members they would bye-and-by be able to force the present Ministry to a dissolution, he did not think constituencies like Liverpool and Newcastle were going to change their minds. He asked them to look back upon the past, and see the victories Liberalism had achieved, and recognise the principles by which these victories were achieved, and by them let them stand, and by them they would conquer. (Loud cheers.) I The usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.

div.head: WIDNES OTNSERTATIVE AS4CA.TION. ANNUAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.
div.p: WIDNES OTNSERTATIVE AS4CA.TION. ANNUAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.

The Widnes Conservatives have at last awakened from their lethargy, and are showing some signs of activity, but these are not of a character that need cause alarm to their opponents. The result of the last revision has been highly unfavourable to the Conservative party, and Widnesians must have begun to doubt whether they really had a Con- servative Association in their midst. The usual annual meeting was held in February, 1882, but since that time local Tories have judiciously refrained from the warpath, thinking probably that discretion was the bet- ter part of valour, and that little was to be gained by attempting to compete with more popular opponents in the direction of demonstrations which could only signi- ficantly prove their own weakness. A great blow to the Tories of Widnes has been the removal from the neigh- bourhood of Major Cross, who has recently left Moss Brook, Fa.rnworth, to take up his residence in Wales. The Major was the shining light of the party in the district, and though he is still retained as the supreme head of the association, it is obvious that whatever reflected light the Tories of Widnes have derived from his presence in the past must in future be greatly dimmed if not entirely quenched. The Tories of Widnes are in the un- fortunate position of neither having the vox populi, or local men of light and leading on their. side; and though they ,possess a respectable proportion, but decided minority of the voters on the register, they are well aware that the masses are against them, and that the extension of the franchise must reduce them to an infini- testnal majority ; while they have also to meet the unpleasant fact that the names with which the rise and progress of Widnes is intimately associated are almost with- out exception on the side of the party of progress. The Conservatives, who in other quarters have found unex- pected, and not an altogether welcome alliance in the Irish Catholic community, have received no such aid in Widnes. The Hiberrian population remain apparently tree to the party to whom they owe Catholic Emancipation and the Irish Land Act. The state of the Simm's Cross School-room last evening, when the annual meeting was at last held, was typical of the condition of the Association. Ihe gathering was respectable and representative, but showing no numeri- cal strength or individual weight. With the exception of one local light of the Established Church, ever ready to fill the breach when less determined foemen are wanting, the meeting embraced few whose names, as far as the pub- lic of Widnes is concerned, emerged from the obscurity to which an unkind fats has consigned them. The first an- nouncement of the meeting was the disappointing one that Major Cross, the deservedly popular president of the Aseociation would not be present. In his place, Mr. Lewis was voted to the chair, and we must add, occupied that posi- tion in a manner which, considering the extreme disadvan- tageous circumstances in which he was placed, was highly creditable. The speeches were on a par with the other features of the meeting, and may be aptly described by the French proverb " Beaucoup de bruit pen de fruit" quoted be Lord Bacon, and indeed the whole proceedings might serve capitally as a political rehearsal of the comedy of " Much ado about nothing." The buainess statement, made in a very able manner by the chairman, was full of humiliating confessions, and was of a chiefly negative character. For instance, Mr. Lewis was obliged to admit that the total subscriptions of the society during the past year amounted to only £l6, and it re- quired all his sophistry and all the credulity of his audience to gloss over this ugly fact. He had also to face the circarnstance that the great constitutional party had sustained an undoubted defeat at the last revision, and though he attempted to extenuate this, he did not deny that a gain had actually been made by their opponents. lie very generously complimented Mr. Shores, the honorary secretary of the District Liberal Association, upon his energy and capability. This well-deserved tribute was received in silence by the audience, who perhaps felt somewhat keenly that the result of Mr. Shore's activity in the past had been very disastrous to the Conservatives of Widnes. The rest of the business consisted in the appointment of president, Major Cross being re-elected to this post; of the vice-presidents, Mr. Kidd and the Rev. George Bond, being eppointe,l; and the committee, which was constituted on similar lines to that of last year; and the declaration that Mr. Whiteside had been appointed secretary to the association in the , place of Mr. T. A. Bullough, whom business arrangements I compelled to resign. This first part of the proceedings ' was hurried through in a helter-skelter fashion ;as if these taking part in it were con- scious that the statement of their affairs placed them in a disadvantageous, not to say humiliating, position before the public of Widnes. This completed, however, the Widnesian Tories appeared more at ease, ard proceeded to deliver a series of speeches in which volumes of vituperation and vitriolic abuse were poured forth on the devoted heads of their opponents. A resolution condemning the policy cf the Government was moved by Mr. James White. Mr. Knowles seconded Mr. White's resolution, and it was carried. A resolution was moved by the Rev. George Bend noticing with satisfaction the late defeat of the Government, and urging local Tories to renewed activity. The rest of the proceedings were of a formal nature, and the Widnesian Tories separated after making arrangements for a demonstration in the summer, which they seemed quite confident would convert the inhabitants of the chemical centre to the principles they professed.

div.head: DEMANDING MONEY WITH MENACES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DEMANDING MONEY WITH MENACES AT WARRINGTON.

, A middle-aged man named Thomas Bibby, a clogger, re- siding in Crossley-street, School-brow, was charged at War- rington Borough Court, on Tuesday, before Alderman Holmes and Councillor Monks, with being found on the premises of Mr. James Rhoades Buckton, Fairfield Hall, on Monday night, for the purposes of committing a felony, and demanding money with menaces.—Elizabeth Clutton, par- lour-maid at Fairfield Hall, said on the previous evening, about 10 o'clock, there were four loud knocks at the hall door. She went to the door, where she saw the prisoner, and she asked him what he wanted. He said he wanted to see her master. She asked "What master ?" and the pri- soner replied "The master of the house." She again asked him what he wanted, and he said he wanted her master on business, and wanted some money. She enquired his name, and prisoner said "1 am a gentleman, and I wish to see your master." He then added "Are you going? If you don't, there are more at the back of me." Mr. Buckten men came to the door. The knocks were very loud ones, and she would have been much afraid had not her master been at home.—Mr. Buckton said that shortly after 10 o'clock, on Monday night, he heard four loud knocks at his front door, and had previously heard his dog in the yard howling. He heard the discussion at the door and went there, and found the prisoner standing on the steps. Thc prisoner must have passed through two other gates before he got to a front door which was in an en- closed space. He asked the prisoner what he wanted, and he said " who are you ? Aro you the master of the house ?" Witness said he was, and the prisoner then said " I want Is you must give me Is." He afterwards said "You must find me lodging," and he (witness) told him he would. Pri- soner then said very deliberately and distinctly " You must give me 1s,:I have ten snore men here," and he repeated the statement at witness's request. He asked where the men were, and the prisoner, turning half round, said " behind those trees." He thought it a matter of some seriousness, and that it was his duty to take further notice of it. He sent round to secure the gate so as to prevent the prisoner's escape, and kept the prisoner in the house until the police l catne.—Prisoner : Oh, dear, it is hard. I asked his name, !, and he would not tell me. If he had told me his name I i would have gone off.—Witness, in reply to the Chief Con- stable, said this was not the firat time men had visited his ' house. He had had to send one man away at 12 o'clock at night.—P.S. Cox said about half-past ten o'clock on Monday night he was sent for to Mr. Backton's house, Fairfield Hall, and found the prisoner sitting OR the stairs. lie ViciS then perfectly sober iVitnese charged the prisoner with being there for an unlaw- ful purpose, and he said " I have come here to claim my • place; ([is mine."—Prisoner said he only wanted to know the cceunier's name —On being asked if he had anythiug .o s.ay why he should n,t be convicted, the prisoner replied, 4' I say I have no right to be here. I think it is very hard , if a man can't I eas there and ask his name. I reckon myself a better :Ilan than he is. (Laughter ) Und that"— The etstaml Chief Conetable : Don't be initsudent.—Mr. Bucktoe : I have no hesitation in saying this man was perf(ctly sober. - —The Cider Constable: And perfectly sins; but he treats this as a lark.—Alderman Holmes: You will have to go to prison for a ment'a. lam sorry to see a respectable looking .. man Lilco you in a position of this sort.
