WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Wednesday. Pre- sent: Messrs. J. Greening (chairman), Derbyshire, Har- rison Appleton, Brown, Cartwright, Mackie, Jolley, Owen, Worthington, Hunt, Grange, Cooper, J. Houghtou, Siddeley. Greenall, W. Houghton Walmsley, Swinton, Blackhuret, Roberts, Kilshall, Jeans:Caldwell, and Sutton (clerk). THE NEW SCHOOLS: REMOVAL OF TILE CHILDREN.—STATE OF THE YARDS. The minutes of the Schools Committee, dated Bth inst., stated that the superintendent was directed to proceed with the removal of the children to Pedgate as soon as practi- cable. The sub-committee was directed to carry out the instructions given previously by the Board to purchase the necessary furniture for the teachers' residence and other apartments at the industrial echools at Padgate forthwith. —At a meeting on the 15th instant, the medical officer re- ported the health of the children as good as usual. The sub-committee reported that they had obtained tenders from cabinet makers for the supply of furniture for the superin- tenuent's house; and the committee having carefully examined the same, recommended that Mr. Mounfield's ten- der for sitting-room, and Mr. Mareh's tender for bedroom furniture, be accepted.—Mr. Mines reported on the Bth inst, that he commenced the removal of the school furniture on Monday morning to Padgate. On his arrival at the homes in company with the chairman (Mr. Greening) and the architect (Mr. Pierpoint) some doubt was ezpreseed by these gentlemen as to the wisdom of finally removing the children until the yards had been re-laid with cement, and the gas and water closet arrangements completed. He should, therefore, be glad if the committee would give some definite instructions on this matter. He recommended the immediate purchase of such additional furniture as might be necessary for the commit- tee-room, offices, teachers' house, and other apartments, in order to facilitate the work of removal. Reporting on the 15th instant, Mr. Mines said the children were removed from the Barracks to the new schools on Monday afternoon. On examination of the new premises before occupation, he found several defects existing, such as wash-house floor de- fective (drainage), tower cistern out of order, and cemented yards broken up on surface.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and the Rev. G. F. RoRERTS seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. JOLLEY, referring to the condition of the yards, suggested that the committee should ascertain the depth of the foundation, the quality of the concrete, and break open the cement to test it, and said if it was not , found to be of the right quality the Board ought not to be called upon to pay for it, but that the man who had done the work should be called upon to replace it with proper material. There was a rumour abroad that the work had been imperfectly dcne. The CHAIRMAN said the committee had seen the condition of the yards which were certainly in a very bad state, and it was decided that the committee should take the matter intO consideration, and give such orders as they thought fit for the repair of the yard.—Mr. MACKIE asked if the medical officer was satisfied with the condition of the buildings.—The CLERK said Dr. Spinks examined the premises a fortnight or three weeks ago, and had certified that they were fit for habitation ; and the certi- ficate was sent to the Local Government Board, by whom it was approved.—Mr. BLACKHURST : The sanitary condition of the schools is perfect.—The CHAIRMAN supposed the specifications stipulated that a certain depth of concrete was to be put in the yards, and that it was to be composed of certain materials. They had paid Mr. Pierpoint for seeing that the specifications were adhered to, and had also paid a commission for superintending the building; and it was hardly to be expected that Major Cartwright, Mr. Derby- shire, and other members of the committee should go to the schools and ECO the work done.—Mr. JOLLEY said he did not ask that.—The CHAIRMAN said if the Board had no con- fidence in their surveyor they must get one in whom they had confidence. No member of committee could be expected to act as clerk of works, when they had appointed one at a weekly salary.—Mr. BROWN said if the work had been done according to contract, let it be ever so bad, the builder had nothing to do with it, but if the architect had permitted the builder to use concrete not of the material he contracted to use, in his opinion the Board ought to hold the architect re- sponsible for negligence of overseership. They had paid their architect for preparing plans and specifications and superintending the work, and he held that if the architect had certified as to the correctness of the work the Board should took to him in case of defects.—Mr. DARBY/MIRE said they employed a clerk of works who was expected to look after these matters; but he might say for the informa- tion of the Board that they dispensed with the services of the clerk of works before the yards were cemented, so that he was not responsible for what had since been done.—Mr. OWEN remarked that he felt inclined to move a resolution that they had no confidence in either the clerk of works or architect. He thought the Board should appoint a well qualified person to compare the work with the plans and specifications the builder had had to work by. He should like every particle of work done since the clerk of works left examined.—Mr. HARRISON said there was a little doubt as to who was to blame, road the Board ought to be careful as to how they set about to rectify this matter. Was the ash- phalte laid in accordance with the specifications of the ar- chitect? That was a crucial question, and the next was whether the specification was of such a character that if it I had been carried out it would have avoided the present defective condition of the asphalte ? If the archi- tect's mode of making the asphalte would not stand the weather, clearly he was responsible and not the man who did the work. If on the other hand the architect's mode of mixing the concrete was of a character that would stand any ordinary wea.ther and wear and tear, then the question arose, did the contractor put in such an amount of asphalte as answered to the specification of the architect. These were the questions the Board had to consider.—The CHAIRMAN said the Committee would be in a position to report on the matter at the next Board meeting.—Mr. BLACIIICUST said he could throw a little light on the subject. At the time the asphelte was being laid by some reason or other when the work was partially done the man stopped operations, and Mr. Napier, the builder, then- employed another man; but the materials be used were not of the right quality.—The Rev. G. F. Rometers pointed that the slates in the roofs were not of the same colour.—Mr. DAREysniKii said there were a few slates here and there of a different colour to the rest, but they were no worse for that although they looked bad in the roof. He was glad Mr. Blackhurst had given an explanation about the concrete. The man who was doing the work could not obtain payment from his employer, Mr. Napier, and stepped work. In a fortnight or three weeks he returned and commenced work with the material he left on the ground, which, however, in the interval had perished and ought not to have been used. There were a great many things that the architect and Build- ing Committee knew about, and be thought if the Board would leave them to the committee they would do their best. The committee were as surly as the Board that these things had turned out as they had, and they blamed the archiect. —Ultimately the minutes were confirmed. THE BOARD AND ITS BUSINESS. Mr. MACKIE' rose at a quarter to 12 and proposed that the remainder of the business be adjourned to the next Board meeting, and that the relief cases be taken. He pointed out that he was only able to give two hours to the business on 'Wednesdays, and as he was anxious to take his share in the granting of relief he suggested that the Board should revert to the old practise of hearing the applications for relief first. He referred to the hardship of keeping the poor people waiting until the special business of the Board bad been dis- posed of.—Mr. DARRySIitHE denied that the poor people suffered any hardship, and stated that the applicants for re- lief were only asked to come at 12 o'clock. Mr. HARRISON: Are they net hear now?—Mr. Danisysertnst : No.—The CLERK said he had not known any case since the new arrange- merit of the business in which applicants had been kept more than one or two hours.—Mr. HARRISON was certain of the efficacy and advantage of adopting Dr. Mackie's suggestion. It was well known the administration of relief by that Board was confined to very few members indeed. There were some gentlemen who never stopped to take relief Cases, but the hearing of those ceses constituted the lona fide hard work of the Board, and if gentlemen did not stop to take relief cases they were certainly not fulfilling the obligation cast upon them. If they took relief cases first gentlemen would stop for the special tueiness, and thus they would always secure a proper number of persons to watch over the interests of the ratepayers as well as the in- terests of the poor.—The CHAIRMAN said a great many years ago the Board took the relief cases until eleven o'clock, and then went on with special business, after which they took the remairider of the relief cases, so that some of the poor people had to wait a long time. The conduct of the business, he thought, was settled at the first meeting; but if it was the wish of the Board—and he should like them to be unanimous if possible—that an alteration should be made, he did not know that there was anything to prevent such alteration. Notice of motion would, however, have to be given.—Mr. Jb:ANs fully endorsed the motion by Dr. Mackie. He would just as soon sit there two hours administering relief as sit two hours listening to speeches. (Hear, hear ) He thought most of them had something to do, and could not sit very long, and therefore it would be a great improvement if they could take the re- lief business tirst.—Maj m CARTWRIGHT &aid the chairman bad adopted that morning the very plan Dr. Mackie had suggested, for previous to the commencement of the special business he administered relief. He was quite agreeable to the relief cases bing taken front 10 to 11 o'clock in the morning.—tr. J. Florian:met : Say half-past nine.]-1t was only a suggestion, and if the Board were in favour of it they would have to give 14 days' noiice of the proposed alteration. He gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that the relief crises he taken from half-past 9 to 11 ,o'clock.—Mr. littower sail the chairman would remember th at the relief cases were formerly taken from 10 to 11 o'clock, and that certain gentlemen never put in an ap- pearance until 11 o'clock, and as toon as the special business was over they look their dep rrt ore. It all depended upon thorn individually as to whether they would devote them- selves to ad,nioister relief in a proper menher ; arid he did not think they load had sufficient experience to warrant them depatiug from the arrangement made at the first meeting of the Board.—The CLERK pointed out that they could not make any alteration without the sanction of tit'', Local Government Boa: d. It was true that cer- tain gentlemen used to go At 11 o'clock, stay for au hour and then go away. Mr. Hari ison had sat in the chair alone for hours administering relief, and le felt FO much anxiety about that state of things that the change was made, and it had not happened since.—Major CAIMTRLORT said they had gut as good a Board now NA they had bad for years. Tile tillaiciians would attend, and they were as likely to get as gout! an attendance of member- for the special business commencing at eleven o'clock as
they did now with the special business commencing at tt o'clock.
TILE EX-CHAIRMAN SURCHARGED.

The CIARS. read the follewiog entries by Mr. Hazlehnrst, the auditor :.—"I do hereby certify that in the accounts of the Guardians of the Warrington Union for the half-year ended at Lady Day, 1883, I have disallowed the sum of £l3 81. 10d. as a payment illegally made out of the funds of the said Uoien ; and I find that George Blackhurst, Esquire, late chairman of the Union, authorised the making of the said illegal payment, and I do hereby surcharge the 3aid George Blackhurst with the said sum."—"ln the accounts of the Warrington Uaion for the half-year ended Lady Day, 180, I disallowed the sum of £l3 Bs. 10d. charged therein as and for a payment made to Messrs. , Ridgway and Worslev, solicitors, in respect of a , bill of costs for professional services rendered, on the following grounds, viz, because the said bill of costs had net been passed by the Clerk of the Peace or other authorised taxing officer, as required by the Act 7 and 8 Victoria, cap. 101, sec 39."—Mr. HARRISON : If I were " George Black- hurst, Esquire," I would not pay it.—Mr. BLACKFILRST said he should not do so.—The CLERK said it would need a formal appeal. The auditor had been on very good terms all round. This was all the bueiness.

THE UNION INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS REMOVAL OF THE CHILDREN. At length the final step towards the fulfilment of the long cherished desire of the Guardians of the Poor to bring up the children under their care apart from the influences of pauperism has been taken. On Monday the children marched to the new industrial schools in Padgate, and took possession of the premises in which their scholastic and in- dustrial education will henceforth be conducted. For the past fire years the subject of the removal of the children from the Workhouse has been constantly under the con- sideration of the Guardians, and in 1879 circumstances arose which necessitated the transfer of the juveniles to the bar- racks in Wilson Patten-street vacated by the 4th Royal Lancashire Militia, which place they temporarily entered in January, 1880. About this time the Guardians, who had been on the look out for a site for the erection of a perma- nent industrial school, pnrehased land in Padgate; and plans having been prepared, and the contract let, the found- tion stone of the new institution was laid on the 7th October, 1880, by the then chairman of the Board, the late Mr. W. E. Winstanlev' who was the chief advocate for the separation of the schools from the Workhouse. The build- ings are now complete, and form a handsome and pleasantly situated block, which never fails to arrest the attention of travellers through radgate on the Cheshire Lines Railway. The premises are of a plain Gothic charac- ter, and have been built of brick made on rho ground, relieved with dressings of terracotta. The principal building is the school, which will accommodate 200 scholars, and on either aide the school buildings are two cottage houses, each of which will accommodate 50 children. The houses on the west side are occupied by the boys, and those on the east by the girls, and they contain on the ground floor dining, work, and store rooms, kitchea. pantry, matron's sitting- room, with enclosed yard and outoffices, while the chamber floor of each house contains three dormitories of 50 beds. There is also a lodge and a house for the superintendent. The contract for the erection of the above was entrusted to Mr. Napier,of Manchester for £8,690,but since then an addi- tional contract for £2,200 has been entered into by Mr. Wm Porter, builder, Warrington, for the erection of wash houses, laundries, committee, waiting, and store rooms, superintendent's office, etc., which were not included in the original plans, but which were subsequently found requisite. Leads of baggage were last week sent from the Barracks to the new schools, and on Whit-Monday, as already stated, the children went to their new homes. Headed by the school band, they, to the number of 165, quitted the Bar- racks, about five o'clock, and proceeded through the town to Padgate, followed by three lorries, containing the remainder of the baggage. The procession, resembling that of troops on the march, was witnessed by a large number of townspeople, and about 300 persons, accompanied the children to Padgate, where the vicar and other inhabitants turned out to welcome their new neighbours.

THE RES . D. S. PROSSER'S REPLY TO MR. REED. Under the auspices of the Eerlestown and District Liberal Club, the Rev. D. S. Proeser, of Walkden, near Bolton-le- Moors, delivered a lecture in the Co-operative Hall, Earle- street, Eerlestown, on Wednesdey evening, on "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform; a reply to Mr. H. Byron Reed." ['here was a large and enthusiastic audience. On the rev. lecturer taking his zest upon the platform he was very warmly welcomed. There were also upon the platform Messrs. W. Urquhart, George Owen, Charles Kelly, G. F. Aveline, and P. Hall ; and Messrs. Thomas Howard, and C. A. Luff man (secretaries.) Mr. THOS. HOWARD explained that Mr. Charles Pilking- ton, who had been announced to preside, was unable to be present; and that Mr. A. McCorquodale could not attend; I also that he had received letters apologising for absence from several leading Liberals in the neighbourhood, as well as the ministers of the various Dissenting denominations in the town. One from the Rev. James Alhett, the Congrega- tionalist minister, who is in Ireland at the present time, read as follows :—" 1, High-street, Carrickfergus, Ireland, Itith May, 1833.—Dear air,—l have only just received the invitation kiedly sent through you to attend the lecture on Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform, to he given in the Co. operative Hall to-morrow evening. As the outgoing mail leaves almost immediately after the delivery of letters I have no time to do more than heartily wish for you a most useful and successful meeting. If I had been at home I should have been OR the platform of Pave, Retrenchment, and Reform.—Yours truly, JAMES ALLA:I-T.—Mr. Thomas Howard. secretary of the Liberal Club, Earlestown." Mr. Howard added that in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Pilkington, it was the wish of the committee that Mr. Hall should preside. Mr. Herd, then took the chair, and briefly introduced the lecturer, remarking that the audience would have a treat, and bespeaking for him a fair hearing. The Rev. D. S. PROSSER, on rising, was received with much applause. Ile said ha would not ask them to give him a fair hearing—he took it for granted that they would do so. There was a very wise piece of advice, which recurred to his memory that evening, and which was applic- able to their gathering. It was" Hear the other side." (Hear, hear.) He presumed they were there to follow that advice. They had had one side of the subject presented to them, and that evening they were to have the other side. He took it to be very useful to the community at large when those political questiens were presented from the standpoints of the two great parties in the State. In that way public opinion was formed, the information of the masses was in- cresstd and an influence was exerted which was helpful to good legislation oven in the Houses of Parliament. It was very desirable inpublic meetings where they heard matters discussed from a Liberal or from a Conservative point of view that they should observe moderation in language, and that they should be careful to abstain from anything like mere abuse. No good could possibly come from such tac- tics, and toe sooner they were dismissed from Liberal and Conservative platforms the better it would be for the people as a whole. (Hear, hear.) He had had the opportunity of looking through an extended report of a lecture by Mr. Reed,on "Peace, Retrenchment and Reform," and amid much of which one could approve, he certainly thought it was to be regretted that Mr. Reed did occasionally descend to mere abuse. He hoped in that matter he would not fol- low a bad example that night. (Hear, hear.) For example be found, if correctly reported, that Mr. Reed charged the Liberals with having made common cause with our foreign enemies during the reign of the last Tory Government. Nitl a word in substantiation of so grave a charge was uttered so far as he (Mr. Prosser) could gather from the report. A more serious statement could not have been made, and certainly should not have been made, with- out some evidence being adduced to support it. It came strange, too, from the other side, when they remembered that Lord Beaconsfield and the Marquis of Salisbury went to the Berlin Congress with a secret treaty made with Russia; and in view of that fact it was really surprising they should have a charge of that kind hurled against a whole party whose patriotism no one had ever had ream in to doubt. (Hear, hear.) Then Mr. Reed thought Mr. Gladstone in his Midlothian addresses and other addresses and publications had magnified the Bulgarian atrocities and made capital out of them. But he (Mr. Prosser) respect- frilly submitted it was impossible to magnify them—that they were in themselves so great and horrible that exaggeration was really out of court. They would remember that when the meetings were held ttefonghout the country they were not party meetings at the first. T hey were meetings irrespective of politics, town's meetings and public gatherings, and all joined in denounc- ing the horrors, the reports of which were appearing in the daily Press. They would remember that Lord Beaconsfield spoke of the reports as "coffee house babble," and likened those who believed in them to the three tailors of Tocley- sereet. But the reports which came threuge the columns o'f the Daily Nato were substautieted by the reports of the Secretary of the Legation of the United States of America; and at last Mr. Baring was sent out by our own Cameros- dem Government, and he substantiated the accounts that had reached this country. The result was an investigation which showed that in those atrocities there were between 15.000 and 16.000 slain, the greater number being women and children. No less than over 70 villages had been destroyed. It was to the honour of this country that such a tide of indignation should have passed over it, and one of the things for which Mr. Gladstone would be honoured in the future by coming generations would be the part he took on behalf of the weak and the helpless, the part ha took in championing the cause of the Bulgarian Christians. (Ap- plause.) He noticed that Mr. Reed had a good deal to say about Radicalism ; and, judging from the report, Mr. Reed seemed to think that the Kadicals were really the Cabinet at the present time. But unfortunately, in the judement of many, the Radicals lead never been the govern- ing power in connection with the State; they had never been the governing power in coranection with the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) In the present Government—if they carefully looked through the names of chose who constituted the Cabinet they would find that the Radicals were not in a majority. If they cerefally went down the lists of the Liberal party they would find that the Radicals were not in a majority; and it seemed strange, seeing that they were in a minority, that so much should be said about them by their Conservative friend. Many of them wished that they were in a majority. (Applause.) One speaker had said that Radicalism was simply Liberalism in earnest, and he thought that was a judgment which many were inclined to agree with. Peace, retrenchment, and reform would be much more sure, and perhaps they would stand a greater chance of being pressed to their logical issue. I Mr. Reed had a convert for his chairman that evening— (laughter)—and there was no reason for a man turning round if he could only satisfy himself that his reason was l good. What was the reason of the chairman changing from I a supporter of Mr. Gladstone to a supporter of Lord Beaconsfield ? His first cause was the disestablishment of the Irish Church. But Earl Beaccnsfield had himself de- clared that the great bane of Ireland was an alien church, and in any other country but Ireland such a state of affairs 1 would bring about a revolution. Revolution was the only cure; but Ireland was weak and could not indulge in revo- lution, hence she was to be pitied. What had been the result of the dieestablishment of the Irish Church ? To-day I it was healthier, stronger, better, and doing more for the Ination and her Great Head than ever she did with the I emoluments and the thraldom of the state. He I thought it was an example, and a very en- couraging one fcr them to disestablish our I National Church. They would simply say to those who held I her in bondage, loose her and let her go free from the power I which binds her, to go forth on a nobler omission, and to do more for God and humanity than was possible under pre- sent conditions. Mr. Reed said that Mr. Gladstone had been making an effort to gain the admission into Parliament of lan Atheist. As a matter of fact, an Atheist could be elected 1 to day and take his seat in Parliament as a member of the IBritish House of Commons. They had no law to prevent I an Atheist fro.n taking his seat as a member of the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Atheists had been elected, had taken the oath, and sat in the House. Sir Stafford Northcote himself said that if Mr. Bradlaugh hal without demnr or remark taken the oath, the Conservatives would I not have interfered. There was an admission that seemed to be fatal to the policy they had since pur- sited. Mr. Bradlaugh declared that the oath was nothing to him, and as he had a right to affirm in a court of law be judged that he had a right to affirm in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) He was not alone lin that action. There were several eminent legal authorities who held the same opinion; and Sir John Holker, who bad been the Conservative Attorney-General, and who was at that time the Tory member for " Proud Preston," held that Mr. Bradlaugh was right in his view of the law—(applause) —and would not join his party in trying to oppose him. They all knew what had followed since. By the opposition that had been called into action against him they had given Mr. Bradlaugh popularity, they had enabled him to pose as a martyr, made his case a great constitutional question, and had made his books to circulate by tens of thousands, making him tichond so far from religion having been in any way beeetned it had been worsted by being dragged into such a conflict. Who were they weo were in favour of the town of Northampton having her right ? If they looked over the House of Commons and the country, he ventured to say that they would compare in morality, and in their Christian character and life, very favourably with those who opposed it. (Applause.) It was the tight of the Catholics over again ; it was the fleit or the Jews, it was the tight of the Nonconformists, and it brought to their minds the old lines that bed been verified a I:malted tienee—

Freedom's battle once begun, Bequeathed by bleeding sire to son. 'lllJugh baffled ott, is ever won, and thus the principles of liberty and justice would at last certainly win the day. (Lend cheers.) He knew oi no one to whom the social and atheistical views coultl be more repulsive, repugnant, and odious than to Mr. Gla4utone, and it was all the more to his honour and credit that knowing as they did how he abominated tltese views that be allowed his judgment to guide him in the convict. He maintained that Mr. Gladstone and those who took the same view were far truer to the spirit a the New Toetament than we those who were taking the opposite course. (Cheers.) It was amusing to find that their Conservative friends adopted such a title as Peace, retrenchment, and reform- .1 for a lecture as it unquestionably belonged to the Liberals. They could only hope as they had begun to take the names that by-and-bye they would take the principle?, and then they would have a conversion of the Conservaalves of the country to sound Liberalism The questin peAct ought not to be a party

question, but unfortunately for the nation it sometimes' became a party question. He was afraid that neither of the two great parties were altogether blameless in relation to that matter. (Hear, hear.) No one could look tack at the Liberal Administrations for the paet fifty years without a feeling of regret and humiliation. 7.1t00 many in connection with the Liberal party were willing enough on slight provocation to go to war, and I too many of the Liberal party throughout the country also caught the contagion of the war spirit. Any Ministry that went into war would be pretty certain to find that there was a goodly amount of jingoism in the land. (Applause) He maintained that the Crimean war was not war of either party, as no Ministry could have remained in power without going to war. The nation was infuriate, the war spirit had got possession of the people, with the ex- cep!ion of a few like John Brig,ht—(applause)—who kept their heads,. and it would not have mattered a fig which party was in office for war was inevitable. The Radials had no real position at that time; and he thought they would bear him out that just as Liberalism had developed into Radicalism, and a Radical element had pervaded the party, the war spirit had been held in check. One of the surest preventives against unnecessary war would be for Radicalism to still developo itself until it became doalinant. (Applause.) . If they considered recent Liberal and Tory administrations there was a very great difference between the two in the natter of war. If they went back to the Zulu war they had a declara- tion from the Government that they admitted that war was a mistake, that it was unnecessary, and that they had been led into it by a representative of theirs in that far off land. Rverythin.g was done to revent the Government from entering into the Afghan war, and they remembered how Lord Lawrence predicted what would happen. Though be died before the end, his prediction was abundantly ful- filled. When they took those two wars they had to consider the Eastern Question. He knew the Eastern Question was apparently settled by the Berlin Congress without this country being actually engaged in war, though they were within measereable distance of it. They would remember that they were so near to it that the Earl of Derby and the ' Earl of Carnarvon left the Cabinet because they saw how near to the brink of the precipice the Government had brought the nation. licit the Government was to blame for the war that did take place. If the Government had only preserved the concert of Europe and worked with the other great powers as they were asked to do, that war would never have happened. Turkey would never have gone to war with Russia if England with the other great powers had only taken a stand as the other great powers were anxious England should do. The guilt of that war with all its horrors and suffering rested upon the Tory Government of the last Parliament. (Loud cheers.) When the present Government came into office they had the Boers war, a legacy of their predecessors. They had the honesty to make peace with them, and he thought nothing that had occurred in connection with our Government was more to the honour of the Government than that they should have made peace when we were smarting under defeat, the pride • of the nation bad been wounded, and when there were troops and everything on the spet which would have ensured them victory in another encounter. They raised themselves above such considerations, and in the moral conscience of the country their action was approved. Instead of the chaos to which the late Government had brought Afghanistan, there was row regular order and settled government, and there was every prospect of prosperity being at last realised by that unhappy people. Who was responsible for the Egyptian difficulty? Who introduced the Dual Control and so joined us to France ? Not Mr. Gladstone or the Liberal Government. It was the last Government and it was that Dual Control which fettered this country and which led to the complica- tions, which resulted in war. Had it not been for that they would never have had the Egyptian campaign; and when they were forced into it by the policy of the late Govern- ment surely it was a matter for thankfulness that the cam- paign was so short, so briliant, and so successful. As far as any responsibility for that unhappy incident in the history ; of the present Government was concerned, that responsi- bility lies at the door of the last Conservative Administra- tion. (Applause.) A good deal bad been said about re- trenchment which was a matter of interest to all. They I were told that the present Government had not redeemed its pledgee of retrenchment, and that the expenditure ot ' the nation had really increased instead of decreased. To have a fair comparison between Liberalism and Toryism in connection with expenditure, they must in all fairness take a series of . years. He had with him a small pocket chart showing since 1860 the expenditure under Conservative and under Liberal Govern- ments. Beginning with the year 1860 they had an expen- diture under a Liberal Government of £69,000,000. It went up in 1861 to £72,000,000, a very great Hatt, but it gradually went down until in 1865 it stood at £65 000,000, thus showing a great deal of declension under Liberal rule, while industry flourished and peace was maintained. After the Conservatives came into power the expenditure in 1866-7 went up to £67,000,000, and the next year to £71,000,000. Then the Liberals got into oiNce again, and in 1808-9 the expenditure went up to the enormous sum of £74,000,000, the highest sum it had ever reached up to that time. That was rather humiliating, particularly to the Liberals who were in power, but when they looked at the Budget and estimates for the year they found that they had to pay a Tory debt for the Abyssinian war amounting to £4,800,000. When they had got rid of the Tory liabilities the expendi- ture came down the next year to £68,000,000. In 1872 it went up to £69,000,000, and in the next year to the highest sum it had reached, £76.000,000. In that amount was found £3,196,000 for the Alabama claims, far cheaper after ail than any war, however short and however successful it could have been. (Applause). Having got rid of that liability, the next year the expenditure came down to £74,000,000, and then, they would remember, the Govern• ment of the" spirited foreign policy" took office. Of course, as a matter of Cause and effect, the exnenditure went up to £76,000.000, the next year to £7,000000. the next year to £85,000,000—(A voice "Natural results" and loud laughter.) —and the last year which they were in power it actually came down by the enormous sum of £l,ooo,ooo—it got down to £84,000,000. Then the present administration came in, and in the first year the expenditure was lowered to £83,000,000, hut they must mark the% in that sum they had to pay £2,347,000 on account of Earl Beaconsfield's policy. In the next year 1881-2 the expenditure went up to £85,000,000, equalling the amount of the highest year in the Tory administration. In that amount they had to pay on aceount of Earl Beaconsfield's war £3,842,000, in the first part of the year, and at a later period they had to ply £2,170,000 more, making a total of some £7,000:600 in con- nection with the £85,000.000, and bringing it down, if it had not been for the obligations of the past Government, to £78,000,000. In the face of such facts and figures as those they need not be afraid of comparison with their Conserva- tive friends. (Hear, hear.) lie obserieed that trade pros- pered more under Liberal Governments than under Conser- vative Administrations, and he said there teas more confi- dence that things would go on better. Mr. Reed had ventured to say very little about the question of reform. Reform belon i ged to Liberalism, and the great reforms n re- lation to the franchise had come from the Liberal party. He said it advisedly, although be knew who wen the Prime Minister and who was the Chancellor of the Exchequer when the last Reform Bill was passed. They all too slightly ap- preciated the boon conferred upon this country by the Reform Bill of 1832, for every great reform affecting the community even within our own time had been the result of that Reform Bill ; and if it had not been for that Bill the great measures in which they rejoiced would never have been written upon the Statute book. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Prosser alluded to the struggles and excitement at the time the Reform Bill was passed, and subsequently spoke on the beneficent en- actments that followed, mentioning the Bills for allowing Quakers and Moravians to affirm ; the Emancipation of Slaves, the Poor-Law Amendment Act, the Educet;on Acts, kc. The country was, now on the eve of another reform Bill, and the Tories would probably strive to neutralise its effects. In reference to the county franchise he said the country was rapidly ripening fore something else— manhood suffrage. (Applause.) If a man discharged his duty as a citizen; bore no taint or crime, and bore his share of the taxation, then he should be recognised as a citizen, and instead of being privileged to have a vote it should be regarded as a right. (Load cheers.) If they wanted a thorough Reform Thll, and something like equal electoral power throughout the country they must keep a Liberal ministry in office, for they might be certain that if the Tories had to do anything of the kind it would be through compulsion, and they would try to neutralise its effects. Nothing bat the strictest watchfulness, scrutiny, and fidelity on their parts would secure them the measures they needed and required; and it was their duty, not only , to hand down the privileges to their eons, bnt try to d vel- ope and perfect the rights they possessed. They bad their hope only in the Liberal party, and if they did their best personally and as a party, then every injustice would be. brought to an end and every grievance would be redressed, They must remember that if they were tialiting for the right they were not fighting for the riglet alone, hut for victery. They could not put back the clock; the forces of tha tittle were for them, as Mr. Gladstone. once said, and he lixedeto see his own prophecy fulfilled. So he would say, in sr:amain- sion, the forces of the time were for them still— For truth is truth, Since right is right, And truth the end must win, To doub, would be disloyalty, And to falter would be sin."

(Loud and prolonged cheers.) After a few remarks from the Chairman, Mr. V:A. Lure.- max moved a hearty vote of thonks to the Iceturer,,whicb WAS seconded by lr. G. F. div.head: TIIE WARRINGTON HORSE STEALING CASES
div.p: TIIE WARRINGTON HORSE STEALING CASES

COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONERS. On Tuesday, Henry Hankinson, and James Hill, were charged on remand, At Warrington Borough Court, with having stolen from a field in Howley, on the 19th April, one grey mare, and one mouse coloured mare, value £l2, the property of George Howard.—The prosecutor, a general broker, residing at Bennett-street, said he rested a field called the Wharf Meadow field for grazing purposes. He remembered on the night of the 19th April between the hours of eight and ten, he saw in the field two horses one a grey mare, and the other a mouse coloured mare. They were then all right. He valued the two horses together at £l2. On the morning of the 20th April he went to the field and found the animals were gone. He examined the fence, and could find no gap. He had not since seen the horses, and he gave information to the police. Hugh Dean, horse slaughterer, Newton Heath, near Man- chester, said he knew the prisoner Hankinson. On Friday morning, the 20th April, he went to his (witness's) premises. i There was another man with him, but he could not recognise the second prisoner as the man. He brought two hones, one chesnut or cream coloured mare, and the other a grey mare. Hankinson was in the habit of taking horses to his establish- ment for a man named Pilling, of Warrington. He said he had left Pilling, and he was going to buy "these things himself. He had no doubt he could buy a great many, and supposed witness could buy them from him. The prisoner gave his name as John Whittaker, Ducie-street, Warrington, and it was entered in die regieter. Witnese bought the ani- mals for 25s each, and paid £2 103 to Hankinson. The horses were afterwards slaughtered. Hankinson and the man who was with him then left. By Mr, Hunt: He had heard the prosecutor state that the horses were worth £l2, but he did not think they were worth more than the amount he gave for them. He had bought many better animals.—On bsing asked if he had any questions to ask the witness, Hankineon said £2 was all the money he received for the hotses.—lnspector Berry said on Tueeday morning, the Bth instant, the prisoner Hankinson was in custody at the Warrington Police Station on a charge of vagrancy, when he charged him with having, in company with the prisoner Hill, who had not then been apprehended, stolen from a field in Howley, Warrington, on the night of Thursday, April 19th, one grey mare and one mouse coloured mare, together of the value of £l2, the property of George Howard. He cautioned the prisoner, and he then replied " I can't help it. I have nothing to say, only I sold the two first horses to Mr. Dean for £1 each. His yards is at Newton Heath." He further charged the prisoner with stealing, on the night of Tuesday, the 24th April, one bay mare value £7, the property of ' George Maguire. He replied "The other horse I sold for £1 to a man in Salford who I don't know." I When prisoner Hill was apprehended he charged the two prisoners toeether, on the 9th instant, with the offence. He read over ifankinson's former reply, and he said it was cor- rect. Hill replied "On Thursday, the same night, I was standing in Buttermarket-street with a mate. Hankinson shouted me away and asked me if I knew of any horses fit to take to the knacker's yard. I said "Well, I have seen one or two down Howley:" He (Hankinson) said "I should like to take them to-night or to-morrow night, and he asked me if I would come with him." I said "I did not mind : I might go to-night as to-morrow night." We went, and got a rope, cut this, and made halters of it ; and we went in a field near Mersey Mills. belonging to George Howard. We caught two horses and put the alters on them and took them along the Mersey- hank to Weolston, and came out at Sandiway half-way house, and went through Manchester to Dean's knacker- yard, Newton Heath. He (Hankinson) went to Mr Dean, and brought him out to look at the horses. Hankinson asked Mr. Dean what the two horses were worth. After Mr. Dean examined the horses Hankinson told me to take them into the yard. I did so I asked Hankinson how much he had got for them. He said two sovereigns, and gave one to me ?—The prisoners who had now nothing te say were com- mitted to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. Both prisoners were then charged with stealing from the same field on the 24th April, one bay mare, value £7, the property of George Maguire, —George Maguire, licensed hawker, Bank-street, deposed that he had a hay mare, and on the night of the 24th. of April, between nine and ten o'clock he put it in the field. Next morning about four o'clock he went to the field and found the horse was gone. He examined the field closely and saw there were no gaps by which the animarcould get out of the field, Ho valued the animal at £7, and gave in- formation to the police. He next saw the horse in Salford in the possession of a man named Paxton, and identified it as his.—William Derbyshire, cattle jobber, 78, Ellesmere- street, Patricroft, slid that at 8 o'clock on Wednesday morn- ing, the 26th April, lie saw the prisoner at Eccles. He was talking to a butcher when time prisoners wont by with a bay horse. lie asked them wherellthey were going, and Hank- inson replied "to Newton Heath." He said he would take them to a man who would give them more than they would get at Newton Heath. He took them to a man named Ker- shaw in Greengeite, Silford. Kershaw examined the horse, and told the prisoners they had better take it to the knackers, as it was not worth much to him. After some conversation Kershiw offered them £l, which Hankinson accepted. Wit- ness was ordered by Kershaw to take the horse to a field, and on his way he met a man named Paxton, to whom he sold the animal for £2 7s. 6d.—John Kershaw, buicher and hossedealer, 93, Cireenga,e, Salford, was the next Witness. He eeid on the 25th April the last witness and the prisoner Hankiuson went to his shop. '1 he latter said he had a horse to sell, and witness asked him where it was. He said it was in a back itreet, and when he (witness) sew it he said it was no use to him, and he had better take it to the knackers. ,yitnese, Darbyehire' and ilinkineon then went to Fotlaer- gill's beerhouee in St. Stephen-street while Hill held the horse outside. After some bargaining he offered Hankiason isa, which he accepted. Henkineon then said he would bevel to horses to sell on the Monday, and gave him his aldress.l He ordered Derbyshire to take the horse to the field, but he crune back and brought 365., having sold it.— fespector Berry said he charged both prisoners with the sec,eul charge. Hankinson replied, " The ether horse I sold to a into in &Alford I don't know." Hill made a full con- t. elion of the part he took, and said Hankinson give him 63 6d. Witness went on the night of the 9th met, to Sal- ,enl, •ind with the assistance of the Selford detectives 'raced the horse to the possession of a man named Jcbn Paxton, of Salford, of whom he had since recovered it,— The prisoners were committed for trial on this otarge also.

IN PARLIAMENT SESSION, 1883.— MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. Resolution of Owners and Ratepayers passed at a meeting I. eld at the Public Hall, on the Bth day of May, 1883, approv- ing of a resolution passed by the Courcil of the Borough of arringtrn on the 17'h day of April, 1883, in opposition to a Bill in the present F•ess,on of P4rliament, intituled a Bill to au- thorise the c wstruction of a ship canal to Manchester, and for other purposes. TDat this meeting hav'ng considered the said resolution, and the Council of this Borough he.ving been advised that the pro- vi.ions of the Manchester Snip Canal BM were prejudicial to the int rests represented by them, and the Co,mcil having on the 17th day of April last unanimously resolved to take all necessary proceedings as may he deemed expedi-mt for the due protection of the tights and intarests of the Borough vf War- ringtmn as represented by them, It is unanimou,ly resolved : That the resolution passed by the Council at a meeting held on the 17th day of April, 1883, be approved and confi and that the Couneit do take all necessary steps befo.e Parliament in opposition to the Sill for the due protection of the rights and interests of this Borough, and that the costs, charges, and expenses incurred and to be incurred thereby bd harge.l upon the Borough Fund and Borough Rate. Dated this lith day of May, 1883. JOHN CROBFIELD, Mayor. WM. KY. BROOK, Town Clerk.

TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further encourag- ing amongst their consumers the use of gas for cooking and other purposes. aye now prepared to sell, let on hire, or pur- chase lease, GAS COOKING STOVES, at a small half-yearly rent charge. All Stoves will be selected from the best makers for economy in the consumption of gas, and perfection in cook- ing. At the Durham City Sessions, on Thursday morning, George Park, landlord of the Fighting Cocks Hotel, applied for a summons against local members of the Salvation Army. He said that every Sunday morning they congre- gated in front of his house and vilified publicans, created great annoyance, brawling and playing tambourines called his house a den of infamy, and told these going in that they were going to bell. He had been 13 years in tinsi- ness, paid his license and rates, and he asked for protec- tion. The magistrates granted a summons. A Plymouth correspondent states that for some months a gentleman named Leycester, of London, and his wife and nieco have been residing on Love Nand, on the Cornish coast. They lived a very reserved life, never visiting the mainland, but were known to spend their time in fishing and shooting, the lady being as clever with the rifle as her hus- band, On Wednesday the three went out in a boat too small fur the open sea, shooting porpoises. On Thursday the boat was found bottom up near Love. The only clue to their relatives was an envelope found at their house, addressed "Mrs. Levcester, Belgrave-square, London." POST 0-FFICE SAVINGS BANKs.—A return just issued by the Postmaster-General, shows that the amount received from depositors in the Post Office Savings Banks, 'last year, from January 1 to December 31 was £12,821,230, which, added to the deposits previously in the bank and the interest thereon, made a total of £49,907,355. On the other hand, the repayment to depositors amounted to £10,869,533, leaving the amount due to depositors £30,037,821. Of that sum £29.715,518 was lodged with the Commissioner for the Reduction of the National Debt for investment. The ex- penses of management last year were £221,652. Mr. John Morley, M.P., was on Thursday night enter- tained at a banquet by the Liverpool Refers Club, in cele- bration of his return for Newcastle. In responding to the toast of his health, the hon member spoke of the block of public business in Parliament, and said the aim of the Op- position Tory and Irish alliance appeared to be to rob legis- lation of its value and the Legislature of its honour and dignity. It was, in his opinion, eminently desirable that a strenuous agitation for better popular representation should be commenced, in order that the expressed wishes of the nation might be carried into effect. Mr. S. Smith, M.P., also spoke. Hawarden Castle and Park were on Tuesday visited by a large number of holiday makers, and Mr. Gladstone, on crossing the grounds, was "button-holed" by a deputation from the Bilston (Staffordshire) Liberal Association, who presented an address in which the Premier's services to his country were glowingly acknowledged. In reply, the right bon gentleman intimated the pleasure with:which he received these tokens of respect and approbation, rspecially as he now could look back on a closing career. Subsequently the crowd of visitors absolutely "mobbed" Mr. Gladstone, and he was obliged to say a few words to his enthusiastic ad- mirers before retiring to Hawarden Rectory. CRYING FALSE NEws.—A man named John Dougherty was charged at the Liverpool Police Court, on Tueeday, with obtaining money by false pretences. About half-past seven o'clock on Monday evening the prisoner, who was selling papers in Hanover-street, was crying out "Horrible suicide of Timothy Kelly; " "Great excitement in Dublin." A passer-by bought a paper from him, paying for itone penny, and not findieg the alleged suicide in it spoke to the pri- soner, who thereupon became very abusive. The prisoner was then given into custody. Is answer to the charge he said," I must do something for a living." The prisoner was ordered to be kept in custody till six o'clock in the even- ing. Information just received from Lloyd's states that the American ship W. H. Starbuck, from San Francisco, has put into Felmouth for orders, and reports that she encountered a terrine cyclone off Cape Horn on the sth of March, and the vessel was hove to for 36 hours, during which her cargo shifted and her lower top sails were blown away. On March the 7th a wreck was sighted to the southward. The W. H. Starbuck bore down upon her, and found her to be the barque Chiara, of Genoa, 600 tons register. All the Chiara's boats were smashed, bulwarks and houses washed away, and she was totally dismasted. The captain, four sailors, and two passengers were rescued. The chief officer and nine men had been washed overboard, two days previously, and lost. LIBERATION :Or THE IMPRISONED SKYE CROFTERS.— The three Skye crofters, John Macpherson, John Morrison, and Donald Macleod, who on the 15th March were sen- tenced to two months' imprisonment for breach of Court of Sessions interdict, were liberated on Tuesday from the Cal- ton Jail, Edinburgh, where they had been incarcerated. On leaving the prison they were met by a number of their sym- pathisers, and headed by a couple of pipers they proceeded to the Ship Hotel where they were entertained to breakfast by their friends, to the number of about 40. The chair was occupied by Major Macleod, Esklaank, who, in the course of a short address, counselled the crofters to keep the law as it now stood, but not to give up the idea of getting it altered. In the afternoon the crofters left for Glasgow. Morrison and Macleod will remain in the city for a day or two, but Macpherson proceeded direct to Skye, where he will give evidence on Saturday before the Royal Commissioners. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—There was only a holiday market on Tuesday. In the absence of any actual transactions to teat values prices are nominally un- changed from last week. For focal and district brands of pig iron competing here quotations remain on the basis of 458 to 465, less 2i for forge end foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but contracts which have kept makers going are fast running off without being replaced by new orders, and a reduction of the output is in contempla- tion in some quarters. For finished iron the basis of prices remains at £6 ss. In exceptional cases makers are well supplied with orders, but generally works are with difficulty kept going with deliveries on account of contracts and the few new orders which come in.—Business, so far as the coal trade of this immediate district is concerned, is now practi- cally suspended. Prior to the holidays there has been an extra pressure to get in supplies both of house-fire and manufacturing classes of fuel in anticipation of the stoppage of the pits, and prices have been steady at late rates, the average quotations at the pit mouth remaining about as under :—Best caal, Os to 98 6.1 ; seconds, 7s to 78 &l; com- mon house-fire coals, 63 to 6e Gel; steam and forge coals, 5s 6d to 5s 9d; burgy, 4s al to ss; best slack, 3s 9d up to •Is 3d; and common sorts, 3s to 3s 6d per ton. The ship- ping trade shows no improvement, and with only a very dull demand. Lancashire steam coal is to be bought at about 7e to 7s Gd per ton delivered at the Garaton docks or the high level, Liverpool. THE Leeorn MARKET.—The labour market is in an un- settled state owing to strikes and wages disputee. Building in London and the provinces ie brisk, and outdoor labour of all kinds is plentiful. The colliery districts are in a dis- turbed state, and a serious strike has just commenced in North Staffordshire, nearly 10.000 colliers having come out on strike against a reduction in-wages of 10 per cent. In most northern ports marine engineers and shipbuilders are busy, and the Tyneside engineers, after some agitation, have obtained an advance in wages of d per hour. At Middles- borough the workmen at one firm have turned out against a 5 per cent. reduction. At Birmingham hardware manufac- turers and gunmakera are busy, and nailmakers are well ern- ployed, while a slight fletness pervades the shoe-rivet trade. At Sunderland the bottle-makers' strike is finished. A dis- pute has arisen at some engineering firms on wages and also shop regulations. A number of ship-platers and helpers have left Sunderland and gone to work in a new shipyard at , Amsterdam. Alt the Elartlepools the iron trade is quiet. At Sheffield the strike in the file trade has assumed large proportione. About 2,000 workmen are now standing idle, and the effect of the increased American tariff is making itself felt in the cutlery branch. Many table-knife manufac- turers are leaving for the United States and elsewhere, and the scarcity of ivory is telling unfavourably in many branches of the trade. At Glasgow the sugar refineries are busy. At Stoke-upon-Trent the miners have struck against alO per cent. reduction. In the Cornish mining districts labour is only fairly employed, owing to the cheapness of tin. In the textile trades there is very little change, but one fact it is pleasing to note is the conclusion of the weavers' strike at Huddersfield, most of the wort:people hav- ing resumed work. At Manchester there is an improvement in the demand for labour; and at Leeds most of the fac- tories are fully employed. At Leicester ald Nottingham the hosiery trade is quiet, and the lace and Zurtain trade also' and at Nottingham many machines are standing idle. At Bradford and Halifax workpeople are only on regular time. In the principal seats of the shoe trade labour is in fair de- mand; and in agricultural districts good labourers are wanted. Emigration seems increasing to all parts.—Labour News.
